detail.abstract: This research looks at how internet usage affects a country's economic performance. It compares ten countries, five developed and five developing, from 2001 to 2024. The findings show that developing countries gain more from increasing internet use. As more people in these nations go online, their economies grow faster. However, in developed countries, internet usage is already high, so adding more connections does not significantly boost growth. The study emphasizes that digital inclusion remains key to the global economy's growth, especially for developing countries. Purpose: This paper explores the link between internet usage and economic growth in ten countries, five developed and five developing, using World Bank data from 2001 to 2024. It looks at whether higher internet access leads to increased GDP and if this connection varies by level of development. Design/methodology/approach: The study uses panel data regression models with fixed effects for countries and years. Data were processed using interpolation and forward-fill techniques to ensure consistency over time. Robust standard errors (HC3) were applied to address heteroskedasticity. Findings: The connection between internet usage and GDP was stronger in developing countries (r = 0.449) than in developed nations (r = 0.161). Regression models confirmed that internet usage is a significant predictor of GDP (p < 0.05). The results show that developed economies have reached saturation, while developing nations continue to gain important advantages from adopting digital technologies. Originality/value: This study provides a long-term comparison (2001-2024) of how internet usage drives growth, showing that digital spread plays a crucial role in transforming emerging markets.

detail.abstract: The current paper focuses on a comparative analysis of both public transport (PT) and private vehicle (PV) users’ perceptions on the quality of the service. To detect the key components of PT attributes a new hybrid methodology is applied, combining the importance-performance analysis and the importance-performance map analysis. The proposed hybrid approach is simpler and more integrated than the existing methods in the literature. The sample comprises an online panel and a total of 1028 questionnaires for PV and PT users surveyed during the pandemic period in Budapest. The results of the applied methods show that among the different groups, the service hour, the proximity, and the frequency attributes are important and performed well in the years of COVID-19. On the other hand, the temperature and the cleanliness factors are not significant predictors of the PV and PT users’ general satisfaction. The obtained results can be used by local governments and authorities, who seek to identify areas to enhance the service quality of PT during movement restrictions in a pandemic wave.

title: Competitive Intelligence and Market Research in New Product Markets
affiliations: PNC Financial Services Group, Inc., University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and

detail.title: Competitive Intelligence and Market Research in New Product Markets
detail.abstract:
Information is critical for success in new product markets, which have substantial uncertainty. Market Research (MR) is the classical way to acquire information on market characteristics such as demand. Of late, Competitive Intelligence (CI)-acquiring information (intelligence) on competitors' decisions-has been thriving. And yet, the academic literature on CI is sparse.

 In this paper, we formally study CI, its interaction with MR, and its impact on firm and industry profits. We model two firms that invest to compete for market share in a new product market with uncertain demand. Firms can acquire information through MR and CI. We find that CI is irrelevant for symmetric firms, after all there are no secrets to spy on. Thus, some asymmetry-either in information or firm characteristics-is necessary for CI to emerge in the market. By investigating the interactions between CI and MR, we identify two strategic roles of CI: the information equalizing role and the action coordinating role. In the former role, CI levels the information asymmetry between firms by channeling information from the firm conducting MR to the one that does not, thereby blunting incentives for firms to conduct MR. In the latter role, CI acts as a creditable coordinator of firms' actions to alleviate a costly, 'arms race like' competition, thereby enhancing the value of MR. The relative strength of the two roles of CI can lead to a rich variety of equilibrium outcomes-such as one where even ex ante symmetric firms can adopt asymmetric information acquisition strategies: one firm conducts only MR and the other only CI, even when MR and CI are costless. Furthermore, we find that CI can improve the profits for both firms, including the firm being spied upon, and thereby increase the total industry profit. Our research provides a plausible explanation for the boom in CI, and challenges the stereotypical image of CI as unsavory and harmful.

detail.abstract: Hybrid Marketing Science proposes a recursive SO -RE framework that fuses real-time AI analytics, human judgment, contextual awareness, and endogenous ethical safeguards. Five operationalized propositions address sustained attention, cognitive load reduction, amplified engagement, ethical trust formation, and self-learning adaptation. Metrics include gaze duration, NASA-TLX scores, conversion rates, intrusion perceptions, and weekly performance gains. Unlike prior linear models, this is the first to position ethics as an integral core layer within a recursive cycle, enabling dynamic hybrid human-AI systems. Supported by meta-analytic evidence (Li & Wang, 2024: 38% trust variance explained by ethics), we project +12% additional variance via context integration. Full schematic (Figure 1) and comparison table (Table 1) are available in Appendix A. This blueprint targets high-impact empirical testing in retail, transit, metaverse, and emerging service ecosystems.

title: Analysis of the AIDA Model and Conversion Funnel Theory in Modern Marketing

detail.title: Analysis of the AIDA Model and Conversion Funnel Theory in Modern Marketing
detail.abstract: The AIDA framework and its later evolution into conversion funnel theory remain foundational constructs in marketing scholarship and practice. Although frequently criticized for their linearity and simplicity, these models persist because they offer a structured way to understand how individuals move from initial exposure to eventual action. The AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) model is a classic concept in marketing communications that describes the psychological stages of consumers, beginning with awareness of a promotional message, developing interest, forming desire, and ultimately taking action (Sari, et al., 2026). While widely applied in commercial advertising, the model is also relevant in non-commercial contexts because of its ability to explain the flow of individual responses to received communication messages. As one of the widely used hierarchy-of-effects models in marketing and advertising, AIDA illustrates the stages from initial consumer awareness of a product or service to the decision to purchase or utilize it (Sari, et al., 2026). At a doctoral level of analysis, AIDA should not be treated as a rigid sequence of steps but as a cognitive-behavioral abstraction that captures probabilistic patterns of persuasion and decision-making. Conversion funnels extend this abstraction by embedding AIDA-like logic into measurable, managerial systems designed to diagnose and optimize performance across customer touchpoints. Purchase conversion prediction aims to improve user experience and convert visitors into real buyers to drive sales of businesses. however, the total conversion rate is low, especially for e-businesses (Gao, et al., 2023). To date, little is known about how online businesses can scientifically detect users intents within a purchase conversion funnel during their ongoing sessions and strategically optimize real-time marketing tactics corresponding to dynamic intent states and the predictive and detective features of the conversion funnel remains undeveloped and unclear (Gao, et al., 2023).

title: Navigating Rule Ambiguity: Mapping the Human-AI Creativity Frontier
affiliations: RMIT

detail.title: Navigating Rule Ambiguity: Mapping the Human-AI Creativity Frontier
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the boundary between human and machine creativity in cultural and creative industries by analysing 593 tasks across 126 creative occupations. We conceptualise creativity through an evolutionary perspective, viewing it as navigating rule ambiguity across three phases: retention (codified rules), adoption (tacit rules), and origination (novel rules). Employing synthetic data generation to measure cognitive and behavioural rule characteristics at task level, based on the December 2023 Australian Skills Classification, we identify two key mechanisms determining the creativity frontier. The structured novelty effect shows that AI autonomy increases significantly when codified cognitive rules combine with novel rule creation, indicating that machine creativity operates through efficient exploration linking retention and origination phases to support recursive innovation. The tacit knowledge boundary establishes that tacit rules create the strongest constraint on AI autonomy, preserving human efficacy advantages where experiential knowledge resists algorithmic capture. These findings show that machine creativity thrives through systematic exploration within structured boundaries, while human creativity maintains advantages in adaptive rule selection requiring contextual judgement. Creative work operates predominantly through human-AI collaboration (86.3% of tasks), with limited zones of pure substitution (2.7%) and AI immunity (11.0%). We distinguish efficacy (adaptive rule selection) from efficiency (optimised execution), advancing understanding of human-AI complementarity beyond productivity-focused frameworks. Economic value emerges from strategic coordination where humans provide adaptive efficacy while AI contributes structured exploration efficiency. For creative industries, this requires developing organisational practices leveraging both modes: investing in structured novelty capabilities while protecting tacit knowledge, and designing for human-AI collaboration.

detail.title:
Demand-Driven Contractual Closed-Loop Theory 
A Framework for Resource Allocation Based on Real Usage Feedback
detail.abstract: The fundamental problem of economic organization has always been the efficient allocation of scarce resources among competing ends. Since the formalization of modern economic thought, this challenge has been addressed through two primary, often competing, modalities: the decentralized price mechanism and centralized administrative planning. Friedrich Hayek (1945) famously argued that the price system functions as a communication network for aggregating "bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge" held by separate individuals. Conversely, Arrow (1951) and others explored the conditions under which social choices and administrative structures could coordinate production where markets might fail. However, as we move deeper into the third decade of the 21st century, the structural landscape of production and consumption has undergone a phase shift. We are no longer merely allocating physical bushels of wheat or tons of steel through slow-moving supply chains. Instead, the modern economy is increasingly defined by the allocation of "flow-based" digital and automated resources-cloud computing power, bandwidth, automated logistics, renewable energy grids, and algorithmic labor. In these high-velocity, automated environments, the traditional pillars of resource allocation are beginning to show signs of structural fatigue.

title: The Role of On-Site Communication in B2B Marketing: Evidence from Commercial Lending Markets
affiliations: , University of Macau - Faculty of Business Administration and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Marketing

detail.title: The Role of On-Site Communication in B2B Marketing: Evidence from Commercial Lending Markets
detail.abstract: On-site, face-to-face communication plays a central role in complex business-to-business (B2B) transactions, yet its economic value remains difficult to quantify due to the private nature of such interactions. We investigate the role of on-site communication in commercial lending, a high-stakes B2B market characterized by severe information asymmetry. Using a novel dataset of commercial banks' site visits to firms in China merged with 41,568 loan transactions from 2012 to 2019, we examine how site visits affect commercial lending outcomes. We show that bank-initiated site visits lead to larger loan amounts and lower interest rates, indicating that on-site communication increases the quantity of credit supplied while reducing its price. These effects are stronger for non-state-owned and export-oriented firms, for banks with fewer local branches, and when banks hold equity stakes in borrower firms, highlighting the role of on-site communication in mitigating uncertainty and building relational trust. To uncover underlying mechanisms, we develop a hybrid annotation framework that combines human expertise with semantic analysis based on large language model to measure communication content during site visits. Guided by B2B communication theory, we find that more frequent and more formal communication are associated with less favorable loan terms, whereas bidirectionality and non-coerciveness play a limited role. This research advances B2B marketing, relationship marketing, and Generative AI-powered text analysis by quantifying the value of on-site communication in complex B2B transactions.

title: Real-Time Narrative Strategies in Livestream Commerce: Impact of Emotional Stability on Product Sales
affiliations: ,  and Indiana University

detail.title: Real-Time Narrative Strategies in Livestream Commerce: Impact of Emotional Stability on Product Sales
detail.abstract: As livestream commerce grows in popularity, influencers increasingly use emotionally rich narratives to engage audiences and drive sales. Prior research has primarily focused on the impact of average emotionality during livestream sessions on sales. This research reveals that the temporal dynamics of emotionality constitute an additional and influential dimension of persuasion. Intuition suggests that emotionally dynamic genres marked by fluctuating emotional highs and lows better capture attention and boost sales. Drawing on Emotions as Social Information (EASI) theory, this research proposes that emotionally stable genres, characterized by consistent emotionality throughout a product pitch, enhance persuasion and sales by showing authenticity and facilitating consumer trust. Using a proprietary dataset of 30,652 livestream pitches with minute-by-minute transcripts, the authors find that emotionally stable genres generate higher sales than emotionally non-stable ones. However, this advantage diminishes when the active audience size or the streamer's effort level is high. A pre-registered field experiment further confirms the benefit of emotional stability to sales and the moderating roles of the active audience size and streamer effort. Taken together, the findings contribute to the digital narratives literature by introducing emotional stability as a distinct construct that shapes consumer persuasion in real-time selling contexts. Managerially, the findings offer actionable guidance for optimizing real-time promotional strategies, demonstrating how, when, and why emotionally stable narratives enhance sales performance in livestream commerce.

title: Is Earth Becoming Alive? Toward a Planetary Noosphere

detail.title: Is Earth Becoming Alive? Toward a Planetary Noosphere
detail.abstract: In this chapter I investigate the vitality of planet Earth, challenging the materialist view of the planet as an inert rock by exploring its potential to evolve into a fully living system. Utilizing three theoretical frameworks (thermodynamics, Living Systems Theory, and evolutionary theory), I analyze the Earth's capacity for life beyond simple biological definitions. Thermodynamically, the planet can be seen as a proto-metabolism characterized by the intake of solar energy, its use by life and technology, and the expulsion of waste heat. Applying the Living Systems Theory framework, I evaluate twenty fundamental living functions at the scale of the planet, and show where the gaps towards a living planet are. I also propose a Living Spectrum of Earth, a taxonomy ranging from a basic rocky planet to a living Noosphere, where human technology and intelligence integrate to regulate planetary systems. This transformation is framed as a Major Evolutionary Transition, the first of its kind at a planetary scale. I conclude that for Earth to become fully alive, humanity must transition from an exploiter of resources to a manager of planetary functions, a shift with profound implications for global policy, the deep future, and astrobiology.

detail.abstract: This paper presents constraint-dynamics as a descriptive grammar for accounting for irreversible change without invoking agency, normativity, temporal primitives, or domain specific mechanisms. Constraint-dynamics tracks how systems reconfigure accessible possibility-spaces when boundary crossings render prior configurations non-recoverable within a given interface, emphasizing where cost is absorbed, displaced, or suppressed rather than why change occurs. Central to the grammar is a disciplined distinction between absorption-the placement of cost at an interface-and retention-the persistence of the effects of absorbed cost across subsequent structural configurations. Only absorbed cost may or may not be retained; absorption alone does not ensure retention. This distinction clarifies how systems may avoid repeated reenactment of already-borne loss without appealing to learning, progress, or optimization. The paper further introduces not-unaware states as a minimal structural condition in which operative constraints remain legible within an interface. Not unaware does not denote awareness as a cognitive or phenomenological faculty; it denotes the preservation of constraint traceability under irreversibility. Null awareness is used in the same restricted sense: it denotes loss of constraint legibility within an interface, not a psychological state. Where cost is displaced or remainder suppressed, systems may enter stable null-awareness (constraint-illegible) states in which coherence persists while orientation collapses. Constraint-dynamics permits, but does not promise, emergent freedoms that may arise orthogonally to what has been lost. Such freedoms are neither compensatory nor predictable; they become possible only insofar as retained constraint preserves orientation under ordered irreversibility. The framework concludes by identifying structural failure modes-displacement, suppression, null-awareness, repetition, and coherence without orientation-that function as upstream precursors to downstream system-level failures sometimes described as collapse or inflation. By remaining strictly diagnostic, constraint-dynamics provides a domain-agnostic grammar for describing change without prescribing action, justifying loss, or foreclosing future articulation.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to support decisions in areas such as finance, employment, healthcare, and public services, where errors or bias can have serious consequences. Although principles for responsible AI are widely discussed, there remains a gap between high-level ethical guidance and the practical realities of system design and governance. This paper draws on normative ethical theories, including utilitarianism, deontological ethics, and virtue ethics, to explore how harms, benefits, and designer responsibilities can be assessed and balanced in AI decision-making. It examines how ethical considerations can be translated into concrete practices across the AI lifecycle, including the use of ethical risk registers, decision thresholds, documentation, and governance mechanisms. By connecting ethical theory with operational choices made during development and deployment, the paper offers a structured approach to embedding ethical responsibility within real-world AI systems.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Economic Progress, and Uneven Adjustment Artificial intelligence has become one of the most influential sources of technological change in modern economies. Its economic importance lies not only in its ability to automate tasks, but also in how it reshapes productivity, employment, and the distribution of resources across society. This essay argues that artificial intelligence is a major driver of technological progress while also increasing the risk of uneven economic adjustment, particularly during periods of economic slowdown. By changing the relative cost of tasks and enabling productivity gains with limited capital, artificial intelligence can accelerate growth while shifting resources toward some groups and away from others when labor markets do not adjust smoothly. Technological Progress and Task Costs From an economic perspective, artificial intelligence affects production mainly by altering the relative prices of tasks rather than eliminating entire occupations. Tasks based on information processing, such as preparing presentations, tracking sales, or performing routine accounting, have become significantly cheaper when carried out using artificial intelligence systems. These tasks require little physical capital and can be scaled quickly once software infrastructure is established. In contrast, tasks that involve physical interaction with the environment, including logistics management, food preparation, and shipping, often require expensive hardware, specialized infrastructure, and large amounts of training data. As a result, automation in these areas can be costly or technologically constrained.

title: Evolution of Domain-Specific Reputation Systems: From Binary Validation to Citation-Weighted Knowledge Attribution
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: Evolution of Domain-Specific Reputation Systems: From Binary Validation to Citation-Weighted Knowledge Attribution
detail.abstract: Decentralized reputation systems are essential for autonomous collaboration in blockchain-based ecosystems. Yet existing frameworks often fail to adequately attribute value across cumulative knowledge contributions, capture nuanced quality assessments, or incentivize sharing in multi-agent environments. These shortcomings are exacerbated by the emerging AI agent knowledge economy. This paper builds on the foundational Calcaterra, Kaal, Andrei (2018) architecture by introducing a citation-weighted multi-agent reputation model. Key innovations include configurable multi-agent competition for improved output quality, mandatory normalized citation graphs to enable compounding attribution of foundational work, consensus-based ranked validation via weighted Borda count, and PageRank-inspired value allocation that ensures game-theoretic incentive alignment for honest participation and citation. Formal proofs demonstrate convergence, uniqueness, truth-telling equilibria, and enhanced attack resistance. With corruption costs scaling to at least 2-4 times total system reputation under realistic conditions. The framework addresses core limitations of binary validation, including the citation paradox, quality-efficiency tradeoff, and information destruction. At the same time, the framework preserves computational tractability for on-chain implementation. Empirical predictions and testable hypotheses are derived for quality gains, reputation concentration, dispute reduction, and knowledge graph dynamics in AI-agent and DAO contexts. The model offers a pathway toward sustainable, autonomous knowledge ecosystems where foundational contributions are durably rewarded.

title: A Short List Goes A Long Way: Stable Assignment under Stochastic Arrival and MNL Utilities
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Shandong University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: A Short List Goes A Long Way: Stable Assignment under Stochastic Arrival and MNL Utilities
detail.abstract:
We consider a one-sided market with an equal number ($n$) of potential agents and items, where agents form preferences via a multinomial logit (MNL) model and participate independently with probability $p$.  In this framework, agents are asked to report their top-$k$ choices. A matching is defined as feasible and stable if each agent is matched with one of the $k$ choices he/she reported and no two agents are willing to swap their assigned items. We further consider two distinct settings of the matching: a static matching that seeks a feasible and stable allocation with all agents information known, and a sequential matching via serial dictatorship, which assigns items sequentially using the information of arrived agents.

We characterize the required size of $k$ in order to achieve a feasible and stable matching with high probability (with probability higher than $1 - n^{-\alpha}$ for some $\alpha > 0$). Our results show that when the participation probability $p< 1$, a constant $k$ is sufficient to achieve successful static matching with high probability, while a logarithmic $k$ ($k=\Theta(\ln n)$) is needed for sequential matching. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the participation probability $p = 1$ or the product utility is deterministic, then the required size will become logarithmic and linear in $n$ under static and sequential matching, respectively.

detail.abstract: Academic publishing confronts a systemic threat from commercial "paper mills"-fraudulent services that produce counterfeit research manuscripts for sale. This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed this threat, creating a paradoxical dynamic: AI simultaneously drives the mass production of deceptive manuscripts and powers the forensic systems designed to detect them. Conceptualizing this as an asymmetric technological race, we identify critical vulnerabilities: defensive AI operates from a reactive position, and the competitive escalation may inadvertently generate more sophisticated forms of fraud. We argue that a purely technical counter-strategy is unsustainable. A viable defense must adopt a holistic approach: improving and standardizing AI detection tools, strengthening editorial and institutional accountability, and fundamentally reforming the global research incentive structures that create demand for fraudulent publication. Safeguarding research integrity requires addressing not only the symptoms but the cultural and economic roots of the problem.

detail.abstract: This article explores the concept of institutional sustainability in AI governance by comparing the approaches in the European Union, Japan, and Taiwan. It begins by arguing that the relationship between AI and sustainability extends beyond environmental concerns, encompassing the sustainability of governance institutions themselves. The article posits that institutional sustainability, referring to the capacity of governance frameworks to remain effective over time, is essential in the context of rapidly evolving and future-oriented AI governance. The analysis proceeds by examining the EU’s strategy of normative anchoring through legal codification, Japan’s agile governance model based on collaboration and coordination, and Taiwan’s digital democratic discourse that leverages civic participation. With a comparative assessment of these models along four dimensions: adaptability, legitimacy, coherence, and resilience, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations, this article offers diverse insights for developing sustainable AI governance systems.

The European Union’s engagement with subregional frameworks—including the Black Sea Economic Cooperation, the Council of the Baltic Sea States, Barents/Euro-Arctic cooperation, the Arctic Council, and the Union for the Mediterranean—is central to promoting regional stability, governance, and resilience in areas bordering or proximate to the EU. Analysis of the EU Commission’s and EEAS’s approach over the past three decades indicates that current practices are fragmented, procedural, and largely limited to reporting cycles, with institutional responsibilities dispersed across multiple desks and Commission services. While multilateral engagement maintains a presence, it is not fully strategic, nor does it consistently generate measurable impact on the ground or fully align with CFSP objectives and EU norms. To address these challenges, purposeful activities must be embedded within an overarching strategic framework that links operational initiatives to clearly defined objectives, from conflict prevention and resilience-building to governance, economic integration, and normative promotion. Establishing a dedicated EU office for subregional cooperation within the EEAS is essential to consolidate institutional knowledge, coordinate multi-year programs, harmonize resources, and ensure systematic evaluation. This office would integrate ends–ways–means planning, embed measurable KPIs, and apply epikrisis to assess outputs, outcomes, and longterm impact across all subregions, creating a continuous feedback loop that reinforces policy coherence and CFSP alignment.

In the Arctic Council, engagement should remain technical and scientific, emphasizing transparency, environmental stewardship, and sustainable development, while strategically insulating EU activities from geopolitical leverage. Across all regions, interactions should operate at institutional, operational, and normative levels, ensuring local ownership, adherence to EU values, and mitigation of strategic risks.

detail.title: A Methodology for Comprehensive National Climate Damage Assessments Applied to the UK
detail.abstract: Climate change has very wide-ranging economic impacts. Comprehensive economic assessments are therefore needed, yet existing estimates remain fragmented, incomplete, and deeply uncertain. This paper develops an emulation methodology to achieve a much more complete economic valuation of climate risks. We apply it to the United Kingdom, which provides a test case due to the availability of many modeled and expert elicitation estimates. The approach provides channel-specific estimates, quantifies climatic and socioeconomic uncertainties, disaggregates to 406 local areas, and crucially includes understudied impacts such as spillovers from other regions and missing risks. While current warming produces welfare losses equivalent to 2% of GDP [95% CI of 1%-4%], damages grow rapidly under the baseline scenario and reach 10% of GDP [2% to 20%] by the end of the century. Comprehensiveness matters: half of the expected total damages and the greatest uncertainties come from catastrophic and missing risks.

title: Delhi's Slum Demolition and Judiciary's role in Due Process violations

detail.title: Delhi's Slum Demolition and Judiciary's role in Due Process violations
detail.abstract: In recent few months, Delhi has seen a spate of demolitions of unauthorized colonies and jhuggi-jhopri clusters. These demolitions have followed little resemblance to due process requirements as mandated by precedents of both Supreme Court and Delhi High Court. What has been more problematic in these demolitions is the enabling hand of the judiciary. This article seeks to look at the jurisprudential developments that have exacerbated the number of demolitions in the nation's capital and the role played by the judges in diluting the rights of the slum dwellers. The article further looks at the recent jurisprudence of the Supreme Court in matters concerning the need to ensure due process and how they could be used to address the demolitions in the nation's capital. title: The Economic Risks of Financial Speculation on the Global Economy: A Comparative Analysis between Conventional and Islamic Economic Perspectives

detail.title: The Economic Risks of Financial Speculation on the Global Economy: A Comparative Analysis between Conventional and Islamic Economic Perspectives
detail.abstract: This comprehensive paper investigates the profound economic risks and systemic harms posed by excessive financial speculation to the global economic system. It establishes a critical theoretical distinction between productive, real-economy-linked risk-sharing activities and non-productive, purely speculative financial practices that generate significant divergence between capital flows and tangible economic output. The research employs a comparative analytical framework, integrating mainstream conventional economic theory with the ethical and structural principles of Islamic economics. The analysis demonstrates how speculative excesses are primary contributors to the formation of asset price bubbles, heightened financial instability, speculative inflationary pressures, and severe capital misallocation. The study quantifies the staggering scale of speculative transactions relative to global real GDP, highlighting a deep structural imbalance. Furthermore, it conducts a rigorous evaluation of the Islamic economic paradigm-rooted in asset-backing, risk-sharing (mushārakah, muḍārabah), and the prohibition of excessive uncertainty (gharar) and pure monetary speculation (maysir)-as a viable alternative framework for financial stability. The paper concludes with a forward-looking scenario analysis on the potential macroeconomic and social outcomes of redirecting global financial activity toward productive, real-sector investments, alongside a set of integrated policy recommendations drawn from both conventional and Islamic economic thought.

publicationDetails.journalName: Asian Development Bank Institute Publications

detail.abstract: This paper dissects the impact of United States (US) tariffs introduced in 2025 on firm exports, concentrating on heterogeneity. Using comprehensive export customs data to the US from six selected Asian countries from January 2024 to August 2025, we confirm that for the first few months after tariffs were announced, export prices fell slightly, compressing profit margins, while the values and export quantities were not largely affected. In terms of the extensive margin, there was on average no systematic increase in short-run exit from exports to the US. Second, exporters of products with higher (lower) demand elasticity lowered prices before tariffs to a larger (smaller) extent. Third, based on Philippine export customs data, micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) showed more uniform and deeper price cuts that resulted in lower exit rates on average even as their market access admittedly weakened for easily substituted products. In contrast, larger firms continued participation using more flexible and product specific adjustments. Together, these results suggest that tariffs substantially compressed margins among MSMEs over the short run in order to maintain US export levels.

title: Fund Managers' Gender Bias: The Boomerang Effect They Didn't See Coming
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE), Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) and Monash University - Monash Business School

detail.title: Fund Managers' Gender Bias: The Boomerang Effect They Didn't See Coming
detail.abstract: We find that mutual funds tend to underperform when their managers exhibit greater gender bias. Using managers' voting data, we find that fund managers are less likely to vote for female analysts than for male analysts in the star analyst competition, even though female analysts, on average, exhibit stronger skills than their male counterparts. A long-minus-short portfolio strategy based on our gender bias measure can generate an annualized return of 1.248% to 1.884%. We attribute this underperformance to managers' stereotypical views which cause them to inaccurately assess female analysts' skills in constructing portfolios. Importantly, these gender biases against female analysts exist even among female fund managers and are influenced by the "Queen Bee" syndrome and managers' gender-related formative experiences. Our findings show that gender inequality is interlinked across various sectors of the financial industry.

title: The Power to Remove For Cause
affiliations: Fordham University and Columbia University - Law School

detail.title: The Power to Remove For Cause
detail.abstract: This Article reconstructs the common law of for cause removal in the United States. Drawing on extensive new analysis of state and federal materials, it shows that legislators typically paired fixed terms in office with “for cause” removal language to strike a balance: to protect officers from political termination while enabling the discharge of officials unable to carry out their duties effectively. Where a statute conferred a fixed term and authorized removal “for cause,” nearly all courts treated removal as an adjudicatory act—requiring notice, an opportunity to be heard, and de novo judicial review of the legal sufficiency of the asserted cause. By contrast, in schemes lacking fixed terms, some courts treated “for cause” language as merely admonitory, leaving process and review to political actors. Building on these findings, this Article recovers the significance of Reagan and Shurtleff, two largely forgotten Supreme Court cases from the early 1900s. These decisions form the doctrinal foundation on which much of the federal administrative state was subsequently built including institutions like the Federal Reserve Board. Our recovery provides a framework for evaluating ongoing disputes between the President and federal administrators. It cuts strongly against the government’s current position that “for cause” removals are nonreviewable and can be conducted without formal process—and offers concrete legal bases that courts today can use to police the outer limits of presidential removal power.

title:
Is the Kessler Effect Overplayed in the EU Space Act? 
EC Staff Say Stakeholders Want Option 2+ with a Binding Framework Based on Survey Responses
affiliations: Technology Policy Institute

detail.title:
Is the Kessler Effect Overplayed in the EU Space Act? 
EC Staff Say Stakeholders Want Option 2+ with a Binding Framework Based on Survey Responses
detail.abstract: The EU Space Act's preferred "Option 2+", a mandatory framework aiming to cut orbital debris 50% by 2034, leans too heavily on stakeholder surveys and a worst-case reading of the Kessler Effect. Evidence on when and where Kessler cascades might occur is uncertain (especially across different altitude bands), and EU consultation survey methods are not suited to justify sweeping mandates. The EU Space Act fails to consider the emergence of dynamic, market-driven waste mitigation given growing incentives for debris-removal services. Innovation and investment by US firms in space launch and satellite development will likely be chilled by an overly conservative binding framework if the EU Space Act is passed.

title: The Normative Canons of Criminal Law
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Law

detail.title: The Normative Canons of Criminal Law
detail.abstract:
The rule of lenity is an ancient maxim directing that ambiguities in criminal statutes be interpreted in favor of defendants. Courts rarely rely on the rule of lenity though, and its future is currently being debated. Justice Kavanaugh argues for its elimination, even as Justice Gorsuch argues for it to be strengthened. Most commentators agree with Justice Gorsuch, typically advocating that the rule of lenity be made more powerful. This Article argues for a different approach: The rule of lenity can be strengthened by limiting it to resolving linguistic ambiguity. 

 This Article explains why the rule of lenity plays an insignificant role in the interpretation of criminal statutes. The problem is that narrow criminal law interpretations are overdetermined, and lenity is last in the judicial ordering of interpretive principles. The rule of lenity also conflicts with the Supreme Court’s recent insistence that a statute’s single “best meaning” can always be determined, even in the face of ambiguity. Additionally, the Court’s broad conception of “ambiguity,” and thereby the rule of lenity, has made the canon too general and diffuse, further marginalizing it.

 The rule of lenity can serve an important role in criminal law interpretation, but only if its role is clarified. The canon can resolve bivalent, meaning-identification issues (linguistic ambiguity) and ultimate questions of guilt, but not multivalent, meaning-building issues (vagueness). If statutory terms are too vague, the void-for-vagueness doctrine should be invoked. By more precisely defining ambiguity, the rule of lenity’s role in guaranteeing fair notice can be realized.

detail.abstract: Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings provide valuable information about the macroeconomy. We find that analysts are more likely to revise-and make larger revisions to-their earnings forecasts following FOMC meetings when announcements contain greater "surprise." Using firms that follow a "kth-weekdayof-the-month" pattern in earnings release dates, we show that forecasts are more accurate when the date falls after, rather than before, FOMC meetings. These effects are stronger for high-beta and large firms, and during periods of elevated economic policy uncertainty. Firms also cluster their earnings announcements near FOMC dates, suggesting they adjust timing to benefit from improved forecast accuracy. Consistent with greater information efficiency, firms exhibit lower bid-ask spreads and higher Q-sensitivity of investment when more forecasts occur immediately after FOMC meetings.

title: Attention Inefficiency as a Dual-Equilibrium Outcome: Resumption Uncertainty, Opportunity Cost, and Endogenous Competition in High-Competition States
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Attention Inefficiency as a Dual-Equilibrium Outcome: Resumption Uncertainty, Opportunity Cost, and Endogenous Competition in High-Competition States

keywords: economic psychology Section One: INTRODUCTION Attention failures are typically discussed as deficits: insufficient willpower

detail.abstract: Attention problems are often attributed to weak self-control or executive deficits. Yet everyday behavior exhibits a stable dual phenotype: people frequently struggle to initiate important long-horizon tasks ("hard to start"), while also showing excessive persistence in immediately engaging activities ("hard to stop"). This paper proposes a Dual-Equilibrium Theory of attention, framing attention allocation as a resource allocation problem under constraints rather than a unitary control capacity. Under high-competition states, attention dynamics converge to two coupled equilibria operating at distinct time scales. A lateral equilibrium emerges from switching costs and resumption uncertainty, producing locally cost-sensitive stickiness and over-commitment to the currently active stream. A vertical equilibrium emerges from implicit success-probability evaluation and opportunity costs, producing delayed initiation and early withdrawal from sustained goal pursuit. The "rationality" implied by the model is not conscious deliberation but nonconscious, automatic valuation; conscious experience often reflects post-hoc explanation after attentional shifts have already occurred. We further argue that resumption uncertainty is not purely exogenous: multi-goal stickiness can endogenously amplify resumption uncertainty via attentional congestion externalities, generating a self-sustaining inefficient attractor. The theory predicts an endgame completion window in which attention rebounds when task completion becomes visible and capture risk declines. We outline an online decision-style experimental paradigm that manipulates resumption friction and opportunity costs to identify a dual-equilibrium coupling signature, distinguishing equilibrium dynamics from stable ability-deficit accounts. The framework also clarifies why extreme behaviors such as uninstalling games or deleting accounts and characters are not necessarily signs of stronger self-control, but may instead reflect exit-type equilibrium shifts that restructure resumption paths. More broadly, the proposed account speaks to economic psychology by linking attention allocation failures to opportunity-cost-based effort evaluation and context-dependent switching frictions in everyday multi-goal environments.

title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) Progress Report with Monte Carlo Simulation under Debt-Constrained Policy Freedom

detail.title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) Progress Report with Monte Carlo Simulation under Debt-Constrained Policy Freedom

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM), a unified macro-financial framework that quantifies the finite stable lifetime of capitalism under debt-constrained monetary policy.

Capitalism operates only while the empirical inequality

R > g > i > 0 holds, where R denotes the return on capital, g the economic growth rate, and i the policy interest rate.

We introduce policy freedom α(D), defined as an exponentially decreasing function of total debt D: α(D) = α0 · exp(−kD), k > 0

As debt accumulates, policy freedom erodes endogenously, constraining feasible interest-rate policy and eventually preventing the maintenance of g > i. Collapse thus emerges as a structural outcome of debt dynamics, without reliance on exogenous shocks, behavioral assumptions, or institutional failure.

title: Burnout to Buildout: Coal Exit and the Geography of Transition Costs
affiliations: Durham University

detail.title: Burnout to Buildout: Coal Exit and the Geography of Transition Costs
detail.abstract: This paper shows that environmental policies effectively phase out coal assets but also introduce geographic frictions into the subsequent renewable transition in U.S. electric utilities. I begin by decomposing the transition following federal air pollution regulations into two dimensions. First, coal exit is path dependent and operates via a substitution effect: where gas is relatively cheap, firms close rather than divest coal plants, and reallocate more generation to gas. Second, when redirecting capital investment, firms subject to renewable portfolio standards invest more in renewables, with targeted financial incentives shaping technology adoption. However, the policy-driven renewable buildout can be geographically misaligned: firms earn $290-$300 less in annual electric operating revenue per kilowatt of solar projects in low-irradiance regions. Moreover, the renewable transition creates a systematic and overlooked social cost through increased workplace remoteness. Counterfactual analysis suggests that aligning policy with resource geography reduces these costs.

title: The Changing Geography of the International Diffusion of Technological Knowledge
affiliations: University of Bordeaux, Université Côte d’Azur, Maastricht University, Spanish Council for Scientific Research (CSIC) - Institute of Public Goods and Policies (IPP), KU Leuven and World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO)

publicationDetails.detailsText: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Economic Research Working Paper Series No. 92
publicationDetails.journalName: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Economic Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolving geography of international technological knowledge diffusion over the last four decades using multiple patent-based indicators. We first review the main mechanisms through which knowledge diffuses across borders—including trade and global value chains, foreign direct investment, skilled migration, global science, and markets for technology—highlighting their complementarities and the role of domestic capabilities. We then provide new empirical evidence based on cross-border patent citations, technological trajectories defined by IPC recombinations, patent-to-science linkages, and international patent families. The results reveal persistent asymmetries, with a small group of advanced economies remaining central knowledge hubs, alongside the rising role of emerging countries, especially China. Science-based technologies diffuse farther and faster, while capability constraints continue to limit integration for many regions.

title: Green Incentives, Brown Penalties, and Systemic Financial Risk: A Dynamic Policy Game under Capital Risk-Weighted Regulation

detail.title: Green Incentives, Brown Penalties, and Systemic Financial Risk: A Dynamic Policy Game under Capital Risk-Weighted Regulation
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of existing financial regulatory frameworks that have yet to distinguish between green and brown assets-and in the absence of formalized regulatory provisions for green supporting factors (GSF) and brown penalty factors (BPF)-this paper takes a forward-looking perspective to explore how differentiated capital risk weights can guide green transitions while mitigating systemic financial risk. We construct a dynamic differential game model involving financial regulators and commercial banks under a continuous-time micro-foundation, embedding systemic risk, green asset share, and capital adequacy into a three-dimensional state space. Using Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations, we derive Nash and Stackelberg feedback equilibria. Through numerical simulation and sensitivity analysis, we identify the threshold values of GSF and BPF that minimize adverse risk spillovers and uncover the nonlinear coordination mechanism between the two instruments. Our results reveal that unilateral application of GSF may trigger systemic instability via a "capital releaseleverage expansion-credit concentration" risk-amplification chain. In contrast, coordinated implementation of sufficiently strong BPF can significantly enhance financial system resilience. When the regulator adopts a leading role in the Stackelberg equilibrium, the outcomes in terms of risk suppression, capital stability, and green asset allocation outperform the non-cooperative benchmark. We recommend establishing a "threshold-based GSF-dynamic BPF" coordination mechanism, in which incentive intensity is endogenized into real-time feedback policies, complemented by improved stress testing and capital disclosure protocols. This approach aims to align green incentives with systemic financial stability for sustainable policy design.

detail.title: Do People Rely on ChatGPT more than their Peers to Detect Deepfake News?

detail.abstract: This experimental study investigates how people rely on different sources of advice when detecting AI-generated fake news (deepfake news). In a laboratory deepfake detection task, student participants identified the proportion of human-written (non-AI-generated) content in synthetic deepfake news articles and received advice from ChatGPT (GPT-4), human peers, or linguistic experts. The results show that participants rely more on ChatGPT than on human peers when detecting GPT-2-generated deepfake news. Participants also rely more on linguistic experts than on peers, while the relative reliance on experts versus ChatGPT is mixed across experimental waves, potentially reflecting time trends in beliefs about AI-based detection. Moreover, performance improvements reflect the joint role of reliance and advice quality, arising primarily when participants rely on high-quality advice. Overall, relying on AI to detect AI-generated deepfakes can improve detection outcomes, but only when AI-based detection tools are of sufficiently high quality. These findings highlight the dual role of GAI as both a source of deepfakes and a tool for mitigating related risks.

title:
Deal or No Deal
Impacts of U.S. Tariffs on Australian Exports
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title:
Deal or No Deal
Impacts of U.S. Tariffs on Australian Exports

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Data provided by UNCTAD

detail.abstract: The age of free trade is over. That was the message given by President Trump's 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs. Ostensibly, the tariffs were intended to rebalance the U.S. trade deficit, but the measures functioned largely as leverage for bilateral trade negotiations. Most partners sought exemptions or new deals, while China imposed reciprocal tariffs. These actions have reshaped trade flows, with implications for Australian exporters. This paper assesses these impacts using the GTAP computable general equilibrium trade model, applying tariff shocks derived from official U.S. Executive Orders. Three scenarios are examined: (i) Liberation Day tariffs, adjusted for numerous exemptions; (ii) Retaliation, where partners impose equivalent tariffs on U.S. exports; and (iii) Realignment, in which the United States scales back tariffs for most partners except China, which maintains higher protection. Preliminary results indicate that Australia loses from widespread retaliation but in other scenarios gains modestly in real GDP. Agricultural effects are mixed: wheat, coarse grains and cotton expand into markets vacated by U.S. exporters, while beef exports to the United States are reduced. Overall, the global realignment scenario-arguably the most likelyoffers both risks and emerging opportunities for Australian agriculture.

title: Pangenomic Architecture of Harvest Index Determinants in Bioregenerative Life Support Systems Staple Crops

detail.title: Pangenomic Architecture of Harvest Index Determinants in Bioregenerative Life Support Systems Staple Crops

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author has no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Secondary data use only. No human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: ICL Institute, New Jersey, USA

detail.abstract: As humanity prepares for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, the development of Bioregenerative Life Support Systems (BLSS) capable of sustaining crews through in situ food production has emerged as a critical technological imperative. The prohibitive cost of launching consumables from Earth—estimated at $20,000 per kilogram for Mars missions—necessitates closed-loop systems that regenerate essential resources including food, water, and oxygen. Central to BLSS optimization is harvest index (HI)—the ratio of edible yield to total biomass—which directly determines the efficiency with which limited spacecraft resources are converted into consumable food. Despite the fundamental importance of HI for space agriculture, no systematic cross-species analysis has characterized the pangenomic architecture of HI determinants across BLSS candidate crops. This dissertation addressed this critical gap through a comprehensive pangenomic investigation of HI-controlling genes in four staple species prioritized for space agriculture: rice (Oryza sativa), wheat (Triticum aestivum), potato (Solanum tuberosum), and soybean (Glycine max). Employing a four-phase computational comparative genomics approach, this study constructed a systematic gene inventory, conducted ortholog analysis across species, characterized structural variants through integration of genome-wide association study (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) data, and examined evolutionary patterns underlying HI regulation. Results identified 30 HI-associated genes organized into five functional categories: dwarfing/gibberellin signaling, grain/tuber development, flowering and maturity, branching and tillering, and nutrient partitioning. Ortholog analysis revealed remarkable conservation of HI-regulatory pathways, with gibberellin signaling demonstrating 100% conservation across all four species—a finding reflecting the enduring legacy of Green Revolution selection for semi-dwarf architecture. Integration of 20 GWAS hits and 25 QTLs validated the gene catalog while illuminating the genomic architecture of HI variation in these economically vital crops. This research contributes a unified pangenomic framework for HI analysis applicable to both space and terrestrial agriculture, and identifies priority molecular targets for NASA crop development programs, thereby advancing the foundational science necessary for sustainable human presence beyond Earth and enhanced food security on our home planet.

title: A Quantum-Like Tensor State Model for Bivariate Time Series in Forestry and Residential Construction
affiliations: WSB Merito University

detail.title: A Quantum-Like Tensor State Model for Bivariate Time Series in Forestry and Residential Construction
detail.abstract: We propose a quantum-inspired tensor state model for bivariate time series in business and industry and evaluate it against a rich set of residual-based benchmark specifications. The model represents two related processes as a joint tensor product state in a four-dimensional complex Hilbert space and evolves this state via a parametrised unitary operator, which acts as a nonlinear second-stage correction on top of global linear forecasts. In an empirical application to timber harvesting and residential construction across 16 Polish voivodeships over 2005-2025, the tensor model reduces the global mean squared error for harvesting amplitudes from 0.00112 for a pooled OLS baseline and 0.00095 for the best nonlinear tree benchmark to 0.00067, and lowers mean absolute error from 0.0227 and 0.0213 to 0.0177; for construction, it reduces MSE from 0.00223 (OLS) and 0.00157 (tree) to 0.00144, with MAE moving from 0.0366 and 0.0294 to 0.0308. Across regions, the tensor specification attains the lowest average harvesting error in about 90% of voivodeships and the lowest construction error in roughly 40-50%, and Diebold-Mariano tests indicate that its gains over linear and polynomial benchmarks are statistically significant for both sectors, while performance is broadly comparable to a shallow regression tree for construction. The estimated unitary operator has moderate, economically interpretable parameters: local R y rotations of approximately 0.78 and 1.63 radians correspond to slow and fast adjustment scales of roughly eight and four years in the residual dynamics, and an entangling angle near 0.62 radians implies a substantial but not extreme two-way interaction between sectors. At the level of basis configurations, the fitted operator maps joint low and joint high residual states into each other with probability slightly above one half, while mixed states tend to remain mixed, suggesting that simultaneous booms or slumps in both sectors are relatively transient whereas cross-sector imbalances are more persistent. Together, these quantitative results indicate that quantum-like tensor models can deliver forecast accuracy that is at least competitive with strong classical benchmarks and, at the same time, provide a compact and business-interpretable summary of time-varying cross-sector dependence that is useful for planning and risk assessment.

title: Agency Under Acceleration: Artificial Intelligence and the Ontological Crisis of Education

detail.title: Agency Under Acceleration: Artificial Intelligence and the Ontological Crisis of Education
detail.abstract: Contemporary discussions of artificial intelligence in education frame the problem in terms of skills, efficiency, or posthuman adaptation. This article argues that such approaches misrecognize the depth of the current crisis. What is at stake is not educational relevance but the ontological status of the human subject under conditions of algorithmic speed. As AI-driven systems operate at velocities exceeding the temporal conditions of human deliberation, the space required for formation (Bildung) is progressively displaced. Drawing on Bernard Stiegler's pharmacology and Paul Virilio's dromology, this article introduces TRIDO-AA-a phenomenological diagnostic framework identifying the minimal conditions (truth, relation, integration, doing, orientation, attention) under which agency remains intelligible within accelerated technical ecologies. Against posthumanist positions interpreting human-machine convergence as evolutionary advance, TRIDO-AA specifies the threshold at which technical co-constitution ceases to be formative and becomes dissolvent. Grounded in diagnostic case studies of AI-mediated academic practice, the framework clarifies when the "Formation Cliff" has been crossed: the point at which deliberation is not delayed but structurally bypassed. The article reconceptualizes education as "agency infrastructure" and defends slowness not as aesthetic preference but as ontological necessity for subjectification in democratic life.

This paper introduces relevant definitions and issues, examines conceptual models of technology diffusion in agriculture, followed by a description of the process of technology discovery. The paper furthermore explores the channels and mechanisms of diffusion, the factors influencing adoption, the adaptation of technologies to local contexts, empirical studies illustrating innovation and diffusion patterns, the role of government policies and international organizations, and the impact of technology diffusion on agricultural productivity, sustainable development, and food security and livelihoods. The paper then discusses innovation and diffusion of agricultural biotechnologies and precision agricultural technologies by summarizing the experiences and lessons learned from insect resistant and herbicide tolerant maize, insect resistant cotton and precision agriculture technologies in a selected set of countries. The paper draws up policy lessons and recommendations that may be useful to policy and decision makers considering such technologies in their jurisdiction.

detail.abstract: The paper examines how legal certainty shapes protection and appropriation of digital designs such as icons, animations, and layouts. Leveraging the 2012 Apple v. Samsung verdict as a decisive clarification of their protectability and enforceability, we analyze USPTO design patents from 2009–2015 using a matched difference-in-differences approach. We show that legal certainty reduces due diligence costs far more than monitoring costs. This asymmetry lowers the threshold for securing protection, leading to a 9 percent increase in digital design patents. At the same time, appropriation shifted away from licensing toward transfers, with the effect strongest in dense design spaces where monitoring costs remain high despite increased legal certainty. These findings extend transaction cost theory by showing that legal certainty unevenly reduces transaction costs, which in turn alters protection thresholds and shifts appropriation strategies. They also demonstrate how policy changes influence innovation when value is created “under the glass.”

title: Thorn in the Lion's Paw: Révision au fond as India's Self-Inflicted Injury in the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments

detail.title: Thorn in the Lion's Paw: Révision au fond as India's Self-Inflicted Injury in the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments
detail.abstract: In an era characterised by a rise in cross-border litigation, India's stance on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Judgments (REFJ) reveals a complex contradiction. Although India's REFJ regime appears to advocate for a pro-enforcement stance, the inclusion of révision au fond-the practice of assessing foreign judgments based on their substantive merits to test their correctness-introduces considerable tension in the realm of cross-border dispute resolution. This paper explores the implications of India's commitment to conducting merits reviews as a self-imposed obstacle to fostering international judicial collaboration. This paper elucidates how this practice not only complicates the enforcement of foreign judgments within India but also hinders the recognition of Indian judgments abroad, especially in those countries that require reciprocity for such purposes, with Japan, South Korea, Germany, and China being some notable examples. Through a comparative analysis of national laws and multilateral instruments, this paper illustrates how India's rigorous foreign judgment enforcement requirements, especially its statutory révision au fond requirement, pose reciprocal challenges for the enforcement of Indian judgments abroad, advocating for a critical re-evaluation of India's REFJ framework to conform with emerging international judicial cooperation standards.

title: War's Paradox in Tocqueville's Democracy in America: Equality, Centralization, and Democratic Self-Rule
affiliations: George Mason University - Department of Economics and University of Tampa

detail.title: War's Paradox in Tocqueville's Democracy in America: Equality, Centralization, and Democratic Self-Rule
detail.abstract: In Democracy in America, Alexis de Tocqueville identified war as both a formative and destructive force in democratic societies. On the one hand, war can unify democratic peoples, cultivate civic virtue, and counteract the moral pathologies associated with equality. On the other hand, war accelerates administrative centralization, expands state power, and erodes the habits of self-government that sustain democratic liberty. This paper reconstructs Tocqueville's account of war, highlighting the unresolved tension between these competing effects. It then situates Tocqueville's insights within contemporary scholarship on war, state capacity, and institutional persistence. The analysis suggests that while war may generate short-term democratic gains, these benefits are often uneven, reversible, and accompanied by durable expansions of centralized authority. We conclude by arguing that Tocqueville's concept of the "art of association" offers a means of reframing defense in democratic societies in a way that preserves war's unifying capacities while limiting its centralizing and liberty-eroding effects.

detail.abstract: Technology diffusion is central to the process of innovation, as new products or processes must be adopted for them to make meaningful contributions to societal welfare or economic growth. We focus here on the global diffusion of technology that has the potential to improve food insecurity and address challenges posed by climatic effects, genetically modified (GM) crops. We adopt a variety of sources and methods to demonstrate the reach and timing of genetically modified crop technology diffusion worldwide, relying primarily on national regulatory approval information. Specifically, we depict the international adoption of genetically modified crop technology over time and assess the rate at which GM cotton, maize, and soybeans have been adopted within countries. In addition, we examine two case studies that assess an underused information source—trademark data—to determine whether they provide an alternative measure of diffusion. The case studies focus on two different contexts: established branded technologies and nascent technologies. In addition to significant overlap with regulatory approval data for established branded technologies, trademarks appear to provide an indicator of pre-commercialization in countries where regulatory approval coverage can expand. We end with guidance on when trademarks may serve as an indicator of international technology diffusion.

detail.title: The 2003 U.S. Dividend Tax Cut, Small Business Loan Supply, and the Real Economy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the credit supply-side effect of the U.S. 2003 dividend tax cut on the real economy through the banking sector. We show that C-corporation banks (treatment group), particularly those capital-constrained, increase the supply of small business loans more than S-subchapter banks (control group) following the tax cut, aligning with the old view of dividend taxation and the supply-side effect rooted in credit rationing. Such an enhanced small business loan supply stemming from the tax cut translates into real effects on the economy. We find that areas with a greater presence of C-corporation banks exhibit more small business formations, employment, and innovations. The positive real effects are concentrated in subsamples when business growth opportunities are more abundant or international trade exposures are higher. Overall, our findings add to the literature on the real effects of the tax cut by showing an important yet unexplored bank credit supply channel.

detail.title: Carbon Credit Trading and India's Green Transition
detail.abstract: This study examines the macroeconomic dynamics under the recently announced intensitybased Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) in India using an Environmental Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium framework. The policy freely allocates carbon certificates in the primary carbon market and aims to incentivize their trading by monetizing emission intensity reductions in the secondary carbon market. Distinguishing between thermal power and green electricity, we find that the incentive mechanism of this policy promotes the adoption of green electricity and reduces emissions in the long term. While phasing out the use of fossil fuels remains a challenge in the short term, an ambitious intensity target, coupled with cheaper green electricity, can accelerate the energy transition. In addition, it stabilizes the economy against volatility in fossil fuel prices. Our results highlight that the rate-based CCTS outperforms the price-based carbon tax policy in promoting the energy transition while sustaining the growth objectives.

title: How Operation Sindoor Redefined India’s National Security Doctrine

detail.title: How Operation Sindoor Redefined India’s National Security Doctrine
detail.abstract: This paper examines the doctrinal transformation of Indian national security through the lens of Operation Sindoor, a fully acknowledged cross-border punitive operation conducted in March 2025 following the Pahalgam attack. Building on a decade of institutional debates over the limitations of strategic restraint, the study shows how predictable Indian retaliation patterns had inadvertently reinforced Pakistan’s proxy warfare model and enabled the persistence of state-sponsored terrorism. Operation Sindoor marked a turning point, with India adopting an explicit doctrine of compellence, treating major terrorist attacks as acts of war rather than law-enforcement incidents. Drawing on leaked debriefings, official statements, diplomatic communications, and battlefield assessments, the paper traces India’s integration of long-range conventional strikes, drone swarms, real-time intelligence fusion, and readiness-oriented nuclear signaling. The analysis further highlights India’s reduced reliance on external crisis mediation, the strategic use of resource treaties such as the Indus Waters Treaty, and the growing influence of public sentiment on national strategy. China emerges as a secondary yet critical audience, with Operation Sindoor providing intelligence insights into Chinese-origin systems deployed by Pakistan. The study concludes that India is undergoing a coherent, institutionalized transformation, aligning doctrine, technology, public expectation, and geopolitical posture to establish a security architecture fundamentally distinct from previous decades. Far from an isolated event, Operation Sindoor represents a structural recalibration of Indian strategy in South Asia, defined by pre-emption, coercive clarity, and a reassessed understanding of deterrence in a two-front environment.

title: Liquidity Regulation and Bank Funding Costs

detail.title: Liquidity Regulation and Bank Funding Costs
detail.abstract: Using granular instrument-level data, we establish a causal link between liquidity regulation and a lower cost of bank wholesale funding. For identification, we leverage quasi-exogenous variation in banks' exposure to the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) in a difference-in-differences setup. Granular data allow us to carefully control for any observable and unobservable time-varying factors at the creditor, instrument type, and macroeconomic levels. We find that banks with greater LCR exposure see a steeper decline in their wholesale funding costs. Consistent with the LCR's goal to improve bank resilience during a run, wholesale funding costs decline by more for longer-maturity instruments. Our results provide evidence in support of theoretical work on market discipline and the argument that banking regulation, by lowering risk, benefits intermediaries through lower funding costs.

title: Governance: A Contemporary Analysis of Global Migration and India’s Expanding Migration Diplomacy

detail.title: Governance: A Contemporary Analysis of Global Migration and India’s Expanding Migration Diplomacy
detail.abstract: Migration represents one of the most enduring and multidimensional features of globalization, shaped by economic disparities, demographic shifts, technological transformation, climate change, and geopolitical instability. This study examines contemporary migration through a political-economy and human-rights lens, highlighting the tension between state sovereignty, labour-market demands, and migrant welfare. It evaluates the evolution of global migration governance frameworks, including the 1951 Refugee Convention, the International Convention on the Protection of Migrant Workers, and the Global Compact for Migration, while emphasizing their structural limitations and uneven adoption among migrant-receiving states. The research further explores migrationʼs economic contributions through remittance flows, labour-market integration, and demographic stabilization, with special emphasis on India as a major labour-sending and remittancereceiving nation. At the same time, the study critically analyzes vulnerabilities faced by migrant workers, including exploitative recruitment systems, regulatory gaps, gendered labour exploitation, and undocumented migration pathways. By integrating policy analysis, international relations theory, and development economics, the paper argues that sustainable migration governance requires rights-based bilateral diplomacy, ethical recruitment frameworks, and coordinated international institutional mechanisms. The study concludes that migration is not merely an economic or demographic phenomenon but a central element of global governance, human security, and international cooperation in the twenty-first century.

detail.title: Fiscal Risks and Financial Markets' Perception of Peru's Fiscal Strengths
detail.abstract: Fiscal sustainability is a fundamental condition for fiscal policy to have positive effects on growth and welfare. A country has fiscal sustainability if, among other things, its public debt is relatively low and stable. In addition, countries with fiscal sustainability are viewed favorably by financial markets in terms of their ability to service their public debt, which allows them to access favorable financing conditions to make investments that drive sustained growth. However, fiscal risks can generate increasing trends in public debt, which negatively impacts a country's fiscal sustainability and the perception of financial markets. In this regard, this document identifies various fiscal risks to which Peru is exposed, as well as the perception that financial markets have had of the country's fiscal strengths in recent years. Peru's fiscal strengths provide it with room for maneuver to respond to various adverse events, such as the materialization of fiscal risks. However, the country faces significant challenges, such as low levels of institutionality and productivity, which could compromise the adequate management of fiscal risks and even the country's investment grade.

detail.title: Banking on Nonbanks
detail.abstract: We study how banking groups adjust corporate credit supply in response to tighter macroprudential policies. Using granular data on syndicated corporate loans, we show that banking groups reallocate lending from bank subsidiaries toward affiliated nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs) following regulatory tightening. Relative to bank subsidiaries within the same group, NBFI subsidiaries expand lending, and their credit supply also increases in absolute terms. We estimate that by "banking on" their nonbanks, banking groups offset, on average, more than half of the contraction in bank lending induced by macroprudential tightening. Our findings highlight an important intra-group reallocation channel through which banking groups can partially offset regulatory constraints and result in greater bank-nonbank interconnectedness.
