detail.abstract:
Background: Smartphone-related neck disorders predominantly focus on postural kinematics and muscle activation patterns. The cervico-thoracic fascial system's role in altered load transmission during prolonged mobile device use remains uncharacterized. This study investigates fascial densification, shear-strain impairment, and myofascial force transmission dysfunction in smartphone users.
Objective: To evaluate cervico-thoracic fascial biomechanical alterations in chronic smartphone users compared to controls, and to assess the efficacy of fascial-specific physiotherapy intervention in restoring load transfer mechanics. Methods: A prospective controlled trial enrolled 84 participants (42 smartphone-exposed ≥6 hours daily for ≥2 years; 42 matched controls <2 hours daily). Fascial stiffness was quantified via high-frequency shear-wave elastography (SWE) at C4-C5 and T4-T5 levels. Dynamic fascial glide was assessed through B-mode ultrasonography during cervical flexion-extension and smartphone simulation postures. Superficial and deep cervical muscle recruitment patterns were evaluated via surface electromyography (sEMG) and intramuscular fine-wire EMG during graded cervical isometric flexion (12 N, 24 N, 36 N, 48 N). Cervical flexor endurance (CFE) was measured via pressure biofeedback dynamometry. Pressure pain threshold (PPT) at cervical, upper-thoracic, and lower-thoracic sites was determined via mechanical algometry. The intervention group (n=42) received 12 weeks of fascial-specific manual therapy combined with motor control retraining targeting deep cervical flexor–fascial coupling. Traditional cervical stabilization exercise served as the active control. Primary Outcome: Change in fascial shear modulus (kPa) from baseline to 12 weeks. Secondary Outcomes: Fascial glide displacement (mm), EMG recruitment ratio (deep:superficial normalized RMS), cervical flexor endurance time (seconds), PPT (kPa), and Neck Disability Index (NDI). Results: Smartphone users demonstrated significantly elevated cervico-thoracic fascial stiffness compared to controls (mean fascial shear modulus: 18.4±3.2 kPa vs. 11.6±2.1 kPa, p<0.001). Dynamic fascial glide was substantially impaired in the exposed group (glide displacement: 2.1±0.8 mm vs. 4.3±1.2 mm, p<0.001). Deep:superficial EMG recruitment ratio was significantly elevated, indicating preferential superficial muscle dominance (ratio: 0.42±0.15 vs. 0.68±0.18, p<0.001). Following 12-week fascial-specific intervention, exposed participants demonstrated significant improvements in fascial stiffness (reduction: 4.1±1.8 kPa, 22.3% change, p<0.001), fascial glide restoration (improvement: 1.8±0.9 mm, p<0.001), normalized EMG recruitment (improvement toward control values, p=0.002), and cervical flexor endurance (improvement: 18.4±8.6 seconds, p<0.001). The traditional exercise control group achieved modest improvements in endurance (9.2±6.4 seconds, p=0.031) with negligible changes in fascial metrics. NDI scores improved significantly more in the fascial-specific group (reduction: 8.4±3.2 points vs. 3.1±2.8 points, p<0.001). Conclusions: This investigation provides multimodal objective evidence that chronic smartphone use induces quantifiable cervico-thoracic fascial densification and compromised myofascial load transmission. Fascial stiffness represents a novel, biomechanically meaningful outcome reflecting functional impairment distinct from muscle activation patterns alone. Fascial-specific physiotherapy combining manual mobilization with motor control retraining targeting deep flexor–fascial coupling demonstrates superior efficacy compared to conventional exercise protocols, suggesting that addressing fascial substrate pathology should constitute a cornerstone of smartphone-related neck disorder management

detail.abstract: In earlier work [1], a curvature-minimum variational principle (CMV) for the Riemann ξ-function was proposed as a geometric reformulation of the Riemann Hypothesis. The present paper provides a conceptual clarification of that framework, identifying the correct asymptotic regime and scaling structure. We introduce a renormalized curvature ratio R(σ, t) = f ′′ t (σ)/f ′′ t (1/2) and show that universal behavior emerges in the shrinking window regime |σ-1/2| ∼ 1/ log T. While this regime is well-established in the mean-value literature for ζ ′ /ζ [2], we demonstrate that it is also the natural setting for our curvature observable. Our analysis yields several results at different levels of rigor: (1) a proven structural factor A struct = 2 arising universally from the product form |ξ| 2 ; (2) a numerically verified α-plateau phenomenon (variation < 4%) confirming the regime applicability; (3) a conjectured statistical factor A stat = 1/(2π) from zero density heuristics. We also falsify three heuristics from [1]: complete Weyl-scale cancellation, pair correlation integral identification, and unconditional RH ⇒ CMV. The numerical evidence is intended to validate the scaling structure and regime identification rather than to establish asymptotic convergence. This work should be read as a regime-identification and renormalization analysis rather than an asymptotic proof; its primary contribution is conceptual clarity and falsification of incorrect heuristics. The present work should be viewed as analogous to identifying the correct scaling limit in statistical mechanics before attempting a thermodynamic limit: the regime must be established first.

detail.title: Biology and Finance
detail.abstract: This review introduces a biological framework for understanding financial behavior, centered on evolutionary mismatch theory. We argue that human decision systems, optimized for ancestral environments rather than modern financial markets, generate systematic departures from rational benchmarks. We organize the interdisciplinary literature into three domains: (i) biological endowments that drive persistent cross-sectional heterogeneity, (ii) biological states that produce within-individual variation over short horizons, and (iii) biological aggregation, where synchronized physiological responses to environmental cues scale into market-level sentiment and anomalies. We conclude by outlining an agenda to integrate these mechanisms into asset pricing, corporate finance, and household finance research.

detail.title: India’s Political Economy in Comparative Perspective With China and Singapore
detail.abstract: This study traces the long-term evolution of India’s economic trajectory from independence in 1947 to the contemporary reform era, examining how ideological policy choices, institutional capacity, governance stability, and global integration have shaped India’s relative position in the world economy. It analyzes the structural effects of centralized planning, nationalization, and regulatory overreach during the early post-independence decades, highlighting their impact on productivity, capital formation, and international competitiveness. Through a comparative political economy lens, the paper contrasts India’s development path with the market-oriented reconstruction models of Japan, West Germany, and Singapore, as well as China’s reform-driven transformation. Successive political regimes are evaluated, emphasizing the links between governance quality, fiscal discipline, infrastructure development, and institutional reform in determining economic outcomes. Special focus is given to India’s transition from state-dominated industrial policy toward liberalization, structural reforms, and digital-economic integration. The study argues that India’s delayed but sustained shift toward market-compatible institutions, infrastructure expansion, and financial formalization reflects a structural recalibration rather than cyclical growth. The findings contribute to broader debates on development strategy, governance capacity, and the political economy of emerging global powers.

title: Reverse IPOs and Their Legal Implications in the Brazilian Capital Markets: A Deep Structural, Economic, and Regulatory Inquiry

detail.title: Reverse IPOs and Their Legal Implications in the Brazilian Capital Markets: A Deep Structural, Economic, and Regulatory Inquiry
detail.abstract: This paper advances a comprehensive and structurally dense examination of reverse initial public offerings (reverse IPOs) in the Brazilian capital markets, situating the phenomenon within a broader theoretical framework that combines law and economics, regulatory theory, institutional analysis, and the political economy of financial markets. Reverse IPOs, while formally executed through lawful corporate transactions, generate economic, informational, and systemic consequences that closely mirror those produced by traditional IPOs. These consequences include profound transformations in the issuer's informational environment, the redistribution of risks among market participants, and the activation of trust mechanisms that sustain market integrity. The article argues that reverse IPOs expose structural vulnerabilities inherent in disclosure-based regulatory regimes when confronted with sophisticated forms of regulatory arbitrage. It explores the incentive structures driving these transactions, the market failures they exacerbate-particularly adverse selection, moral hazard, and information opacity-and the normative challenges they pose to securities regulation. The analysis further examines the scope and limits of regulatory intervention by the Brazilian Securities Commission (CVM), emphasizing functional equivalence, fiduciary accountability, compliance architecture, and proportional enforcement as central organizing principles. The paper concludes that reverse IPOs demand not incremental adjustments, but a conceptually refined regulatory understanding capable of reconciling financial innovation with investor protection, legal certainty, and institutional legitimacy.

These results suggest that bike-sharing infrastructure generates public-safety co-benefits by increasing street activity and informal surveillance.

detail.abstract: I synthesize publicly available data to analyze how U.S. household income and spending evolved between 2013 and 2024, and discuss policy implications. Using Consumer Expenditure Survey data supplemented with Personal Consumption Expenditures and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau data, I analyze expanded household spending, incorporating third-party healthcare and education spending, and credit card interest. I find that real incomes for the average household kept pace with rising expenses, but households in the bottom two income quintiles consistently spent more than they earned. When third-party spending on behalf of consumers is included, healthcare emerges as the largest and fastest-growing expense, alongside shelter, with food and vehicles the other two major expense categories driving household budgets. By contrast, any other spending category represents a relatively small share of total household expenditures in aggregate data. I argue that meaningful policy interventions aimed at improving affordability must primarily address four large structural cost categories: shelter (via increased supply, reducing construction costs, and helping renters become homeowners); healthcare (via transparency and fixing incentives); and food and vehicles (via trade and competition).

detail.abstract:
This paper presents Resilient Value Economy (RVE 2.0), a policy architecture aimed at strengthening economic and social stability through a clearly defined survival floor and a motivation-layer growth framework. RVE 2.0 departs from conventional Universal Basic Income (UBI) proposals by defining the baseline as a scientifically calculated minimum sufficient for health and cognitive functioning, explicitly excluding lifestyle or comfort guarantees. This design preserves work incentives, social differentiation, and fiscal discipline.

The framework combines a transparent survival baseline with mechanisms such as an Employer Base Tax, wholesale-cost provisioning of basic goods, merit-based educational grants, and compact infrastructure planning to reduce structural costs and limit rent-seeking. Capital allocation remains market-driven, with reduced pressure on passive real estate enabling reallocation toward productive investment or low-risk financing of the stabilized base economy.

Governance is organized around insulated expert institutions, layered authority, and anti-gaming design. Implementation follows a staged pathway—epistemic disclosure, accounting-only pilots, regional deployment, and external stress validation—allowing policymakers to test, measure, and adjust the system without systemic disruption. Methodological specifications are addressed in companion work.

title: The Theory of Behavior - A Fundamental Comprehensive Algorithm for Human Behavior

detail.abstract: The behavioral sciences have notably failed to have the reliability demanded of harder science disciplines, a condition largely attributed to the plethora and diversity of variables impacting the human Lebenswelt. In this paper we address this issue by focusing on the mathematical assessment process-the one used to manage the variables. In doing so, we isolate and identify that assessment process utilizing a retooled behaviorism foundation, build it in a physiological environment modified by experiences of a personal as well as sociological base as established by genetics and refined by history. The result is a theory of behavior that operates with a Bayesian logic independent of individual attributes. We then demonstrate how variables work with this process in a probabilistic, dynamic and multiscalar environment, yielding a fundamental comprehensive theory for human behavior.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an original theoretical framework-termed "Economic Behavior Quantum" (EBQ)-that takes the completed "goods-payment" exchange as the fundamental analytical unit and introducing an action-based evolutionary principle. Traditional economic theories typically center on agents, goods, or equilibrium states, which increasingly struggle to explain innovation-driven growth, digital platforms, and high-frequency, information-intensive economic activity. To address these limitations, this study defines the Economic Behavior Element (EBE) as the minimal analytically irreducible unit of economic reality, identified as a completed goods-payment exchange. Building on this behavioral foundation, the paper develops a multi-layered structural framework consisting of behavior chains, networks, groups, fields, and flows, through which micro-level transactions aggregate into meso-and macro-level economic structures. To explain the directionality of economic evolution, the concept of Economic Action Quantity (EAQ) is introduced as an integrated systemic cost-force functional encompassing transaction costs, time costs, information frictions, coordination costs, and uncertainty. Drawing inspiration from analytical mechanics, the paper formulates a Principle of Least Action for Economic Systems, AN ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR QUANTUM FRAMEWORK 2 stating that economic evolution exhibits a statistical tendency toward structural configurations characterized by relatively lower cumulative action. Within this framework, technological progress and digitalization are interpreted as processes that restructure information space, compress behavioral paths, and reduce systemic action, rather than as exogenous efficiency shocks. The theory provides a unified explanation for key features of the digital economy, including platform dominance, network effects, and rapid structural transformation. Rather than offering prescriptive policy rules, the framework provides a novel, open, and behavior-centered analytical architecture, inviting further formalization and empirical validation in the digital era.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is purely theoretical and conceptual in nature and does not involve human participants, personal data, clinical material, surveys, or experiments. Therefore, formal ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.

detail.abstract: The use of economic levers of pressure is capable of altering political behavior during periods of escalating tension, reducing the probability of aggression regardless of subjective domestic and foreign-policy factors as well as interpretations of an opponent's intentions. In this paper, Surprise Attack Bonds (SAB) are analyzed within the logic of forms of ex-ante economic collateral applicable in the prewar period. It is shown that the mutual collateral use of SAB-including scenarios of exchange, joint or crossdepositing-affects political decision-making processes in the phase of intensified confrontation and also forms an institutionalized commitment device shaping the strategic expectations of the parties under conditions of high uncertainty (Schelling, 1960; Fearon, 1995; Powell, 2006). Such an approach complements traditional deterrence models, reducing the probability of military conflicts arising from mistaken expectations, information asymmetries, and in a number of cases even conscious striving for war. Whereas in previous works of the cycle SAB were analyzed primarily as sanctioning and investment instruments, in the present study they are conceptualized as contractual collateral intended to stabilize decisions in the phase of pre-conflict escalation.

keywords: Contracts of Guarantee under Indian Law
Unequal Bargaining Power in Standard Form Contracts

detail.abstract:
Contracts of guarantee play an important role in supporting commercial and banking transactions under Indian law. Governed by the Indian Contract Act, 1872, these contracts give statutory protections to sureties, who are treated as favored debtors. However, modern commercial practices are increasingly challenging this protection. In today’s banking transactions, contracts of guarantee are mostly standard-form agreements, leaving individual sureties with little to no power to negotiate.

This paper looks into whether the legal protections for sureties under Indian law are effective when guarantees are made under conditions of unequal bargaining power. Using a doctrinal and analytical approach, the study examines relevant laws, court decisions, and academic commentary to evaluate how courts recognize and deal with power imbalances in guaranteed contracts. It shows the judiciary’s preference for strictly enforcing guarantee agreements while engaging little with doctrines like unconscionability and substantive consent in financial situations.

The study concludes that while Indian law offers formal protections for sureties, this protection is largely ineffective in practice due to unequal bargaining power, and the strict enforcement of standard-form guarantee contracts. The paper argues for a more nuanced judicial approach that balances commercial certainty with real fairness.

detail.abstract: Job creation in the United States is typically measured through direct payroll employment and firm-level hiring. However, this approach fails to capture a significant category of economic activity generated through distressed property redevelopment. This paper introduces the concept of hidden employment-distributed, non-payroll job creation that arises through the acquisition, rehabilitation, and reuse of abandoned or stigmatized real estate assets. Drawing on over two decades of applied redevelopment experience across multiple U.S. jurisdictions, the paper demonstrates how distressed asset projects generate sustained employment for contractors, tradespeople, engineers, inspectors, real estate professionals, material suppliers, and local service providers without creating a single traditional "job opening." Because these employment effects are fragmented, temporary, and transaction-based, they are systematically undercounted in conventional labor statistics. The paper argues that distressed property redevelopment constitutes a scalable employment engine with national economic importance and that policy frameworks which fail to recognize this mechanism underestimate both private-sector contribution and public benefit.

title: Adaptive Reuse of Abandoned Public Infrastructure as a National Economic Strategy

detail.title: Adaptive Reuse of Abandoned Public Infrastructure as a National Economic Strategy
detail.abstract: Across the United States, billions of dollars in publicly funded infrastructure remain abandoned, underutilized, or slated for demolition. Former jails, schools, hospitals, municipal buildings, and rural public facilities impose ongoing fiscal and social costs on communities while contributing little to economic recovery. This paper argues that the persistent abandonment of public infrastructure represents a national economic failure rooted not in feasibility constraints, but in fear, regulatory ambiguity, and institutional inertia. Drawing on applied redevelopment experience across multiple U.S. jurisdictions, the paper frames adaptive reuse of public infrastructure as a scalable national economic strategy that preserves embedded public capital, generates distributed employment, and reduces taxpayer burden without requiring new public spending. The findings suggest that practitioner-led reuse offers a faster and more resilient path to revitalization than demolition or greenfield replacement and that policy frameworks should prioritize reuse-first approaches to infrastructure redevelopment.

title: From Tilt to System: A Practitioner’s Framework for Managing Cognitive Biases in Retail Trading

detail.title: From Tilt to System: A Practitioner’s Framework for Managing Cognitive Biases in Retail Trading
detail.abstract: This paper presents a practitioner-derived framework for identifying, categorizing, and mitigating cognitive biases in retail trading, developed over 13 years of active market participation (2013-2026). While behavioral finance literature extensively documents the existence and prevalence of cognitive biases among retail investors-including the disposition effect (Odean, 1998), overconfidence (Barber & Odean, 2001), and loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)-relatively few studies offer structured, practitioner-tested methodologies for their systematic management in real-time trading environments. This study addresses that gap by proposing a four-layer bias management framework grounded in the author's publicly verifiable track record of 242 published trading ideas on TradingView over a period of more than 4 years (October 2021-February 2026), multiple Editor's Pick awards from TradingView's editorial board, and 13 years of live market experience across forex, equities, commodities, and cryptocurrency markets. The framework integrates volume analysis and Wyckoff methodology as structural tools that reduce reliance on subjective judgment, thereby limiting the operational space for cognitive biases. The paper identifies four primary emotional states that amplify cognitive biases in practice-fear, greed, hope, and tilt-and proposes specific mechanical countermeasures for each. The practical significance lies in bridging the gap between academic behavioral finance research and the operational reality of individual traders.

title: The Educational Deep State: Theorizing Relational Sovereignty and Functional Substitution in Fragile Bureaucracies

detail.title: The Educational Deep State: Theorizing Relational Sovereignty and Functional Substitution in Fragile Bureaucracies

detail.abstract: Public administration theory traditionally views informal networks as either supplementary to or subversive of the state. This article challenges this binary by theorizing the "Educational Deep State"-a permanent, parallel, and sovereign infrastructure of elite relational networks that functionally displaces stagnant state bureaucracies to ensure service excellence. Using the case of elite Thai secondary education, we document the emergence of the State-Substituted Social Enterprise (SSE). We provide empirical evidence of a "Relational Moat" where formal state access suffers an 86.4% failure rate while informal networks achieve 100% permeability. We further identify the "Shadow Balance Sheet" as a mechanism of fiscal secession and "Rational Decoupling" as a strategic rejection of state-mandated "Zombie Metrics." This article contributes to the literature on informal institutions by arguing that in high-stakes environments, quality is an emergent property of the "Productive Shadow" rather than a top-down delivery of the formal state.

detail.title: Normalization and Instrumental Variables in Demand-Supply Equilibria: A Graphical Identification Approach
detail.abstract: This note studies graphical identification in the canonical competitive demand-supply model. Using Pearl's (2009) latent projection with explicit demand and supply shocks, it derives an acyclic directed mixed graph (ADMG) representation that accommodates equilibrium feedback while preserving standard econometric assumptions. Within this framework, the familiar instrumental-variables estimand arises on observables, but graphical identification of a structural slope requires an explicit normalization of the structural equations. When price is normalized as the dependent variable in the demand equation, Pearl's instrumental-variables identification theorem applies directly to recover the demand slope; an alternative normalization yields identification of the supply slope. An extension to instruments with side effects shows how graphical separation criteria make the required conditioning set and resulting estimand transparent when conventional IV arguments become cumbersome. The results clarify the relationship between reduced-form equilibrium representations and structural causal identification in simultaneous-equation models.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the RFS Framework, a novel synthetic model for assessing long-term national economic success and resilience. The model posits that sustainable prosperity is achieved only when an economy simultaneously satisfies three measurable, mutually reinforcing criteria: Real (R), focusing on financial stability and debt sustainability (JEL: G01); Free (F), emphasizing institutional quality, property rights, and the rule of law (JEL: P14); and Sophisticated (S), measuring productive knowledge and technological complexity (JEL: O43). We argue that traditional, unidimensional metrics like GDP growth fail to capture the structural fragility, institutional quality, and technological depth necessary for resilience. The RFS Framework synthesizes contributions from Post-Keynesian economics, New Institutional Economics, and modern Economic Complexity theory to overcome the limitations of single-focus growth models. We present a detailed methodology for constructing the RFS Composite Index, incorporating metrics such as Adjusted Net Savings and the Economic Complexity Index. An econometric model is proposed for empirical testing, and an initial comparative analysis of diverse global economies demonstrates the framework's diagnostic power in identifying structural imbalances. The central hypothesis is that high RFS Index scores are significantly correlated with superior, long-term macroeconomic stability and prosperity.

title: Patent Cooperation Treaty as a Catalyst for India’s Economic Growth: Analysing IP Simplification and Foreign Direct Investment Inflows
affiliations: Christ (Deemed to be University), Pune, Lavasa and Christ (Deemed to be University), Pune, Lavasa

detail.title: Patent Cooperation Treaty as a Catalyst for India’s Economic Growth: Analysing IP Simplification and Foreign Direct Investment Inflows
detail.abstract:
An intellectual property system revolution, the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), lies in a two-fold trigger mechanism that secures the sovereignty of innovation and international integration as the cornerstone of global integration. The linkage between the PCT-induced IP simplification and the FDI inflows are widely explored in this overarching review of the literature which poses the question whether the streamline patent procedures indeed stimulate qualitative economic change or simply attract portfolio-seeking capital whose effect on development is indistinguishable. Since its application in 1998, the PCT has dramatically transformed the location of India in the global innovation systems by bringing a method of individual global patent application instead of traditional bilateral filing systems that are characterised by territorial fragmentation and discrepancies in procedural terms. This research question lies at the core of the critical difference in quantitative FDI measures and qualitative developmental implications. In particular, it poses the question as to whether investment of PCT leads to major investment in R&D, transfer of technology, wisdom spillovers and employment generation, or whether PCT sustains dependency structures stressing market-dominance strategies over local capacity-building. The study combines the multifaceted research in the areas of the legal harmonization, econometric analysis, and the innovation management. It shows that investment choices between CECA(Comprehensive Economic Coorporation Agreement)/CEPA(Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement) member countries that have strong IPR regulations have a strong correlation with the 44 percentage point boom of India in IP filings (2020-2025), but reveals a lot of variances regarding sectoral heterogeneity, regional differentiation, and MSME uptake. 

Although it goes without saying that intensified patent protection attracts technology-intensive foreign direct investment and triggers innovative inventions that fulfill the three patentability criteria of India, namely, novelty, inventiveness, and practical applicability, overprotective enforcement of patent laws presents a threat of knowledge stagnation and social and economic imbalances. This is a fine balance that is captured in Section 39 of Indian Patent Act that mandates Indian residents to seek prior permission when filing foreign patent applications in a way that foreign international involvement is considered with national security needs. This study ultimately makes PCT not only a procedural convenience but also a strategic national capital-a strategically significant instrument the maximization of which demands evidence-based governmental frameworks that can balance innovation motives by exclusionary developments and growth trajectories that are inclusive of all. The findings indicate a need to have evidence-based, circumstances-based IPR approaches that creatively balance equitable access to technology and innovation. This will facilitate the shift to a knowledge based, innovation-oriented economy but also is compatible with inclusive growth targets with developmental needs.

detail.title: Long-Term Photovoltaic Power Generation Forecasting Using Long Short-Term Memory Network: Insights into Stochastic Dynamics
detail.abstract: Energy supply planning is crucial in modern energy systems, especially with the integration of renewable sources like solar and wind, which introduce significant stochasticity into the production process. Distributed photovoltaic generation, due to its intermittent nature, further complicates grid stability. Advanced machine learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been applied to address these challenges, improving forecasting accuracy for energy production and enabling better optimization and control of Smart Grid systems. Understanding how distributed photovoltaic energy impacts the grid is key to developing strategies for maintaining stability and integrating renewable sources effectively. The meteorological data for this study were sourced from the weather station at the Kamianka photovoltaic plant, which provided real-time measurements of key parameters. These data were then used to simulate the photovoltaic power output using a physical model of the photovoltaic system, taking into account the specific characteristics of the panels. This study focused on long-term forecasting of photovoltaic power generation for six months, using the LSTM model. The model demonstrated high accuracy, with an R2 value of 0.92 on the test set and 0.88 on the validation set, indicating a strong correlation between predicted and actual values. The RMSE for the test set was 1908.47 kW (6.12%), while for the validation set, it was slightly higher at 2107.35 kW (6.58%). The MAE was 1004.23 kW (3.24%) on the test set and 1152.89 kW (3.82%) on the validation set. These error values arise primarily due to the inherent stochasticity of photovoltaic energy, influenced by varying meteorological conditions such as cloud cover and sunlight intensity. The unpredictable nature of solar energy generation complicates the forecasting process and results in fluctuations in energy supply, challenging the ability to meet energy demand reliably. Consequently, this variability also affects energy demand, as grid operators must adjust consumption patterns or deploy backup generation to compensate for sudden dips or surges in photovoltaic output.

detail.abstract: As the usage of electric vehicle (EV) batteries continues to escalate globally, concerns regarding the management and disposal of these batteries post their active service life are gaining significant attention. These batteries, pivotal in powering electric vehicles, eventually reach a point where their efficiency declines, no longer making them suitable for transport functions. This juncture raises concerns about the most effective and environmentally responsible ways to handle these used batteries. In the article, an in-depth examination of global trends in managing post-use EV batteries reveals essential strategies for their sustainable handling. The analysis underscores two primary approaches: repurposing for secondary applications and recycling for material recovery. The study highlights the potential of repurposing EV batteries in applications like stationary energy storage, which extends their lifecycle and mitigates electronic waste. This approach is particularly beneficial in storing energy from renewable sources and supporting sustainable energy infrastructures. Furthermore, the article emphasises the significance of recycling EV batteries. Efficient recycling processes enable the extraction of valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel, conserving resources and reducing the environmental impact of raw material extraction. The findings suggest a combined strategy of repurposing and recycling as an optimal solution for managing post-use EV batteries. This approach aligns with circular economy principles, ensuring environmentally responsible and economically viable battery lifecycle management. The article concludes that developing suitable technologies, infrastructures, and regulations is crucial for enabling this sustainable management strategy, effectively addressing the challenge of post-use EV batteries.

detail.abstract: We analyse a subscription platform that commits to capacity, bargains bilaterally with subscribers over data provision or paid privacy, and then charges a market-clearing access fee. Because failed negotiations can be replaced by other subscribers, the platform's capacity commitment (and the resulting subscriber base) determines the size of the replacement pool and hence bargaining power. Under opt-in (the platform buys data), capacity tends to expand to depress data payments; under opt-out (users buy privacy), capacity tends to contract to raise privacy charges. Privacy prices internalise the opportunity cost of foregone data.

detail.abstract: Modelling is carried out of the coverage of electric energy consumption for an electrical power node, which includes consumers with the maximum possible consumption power during one hour at the level of 4 MW, distributed generation power plants, namely wind, solar, reserve gas power plant and energy storage system. The costs necessary for the implementation and further operation of distributed generation power plants and energy storage systems were formed, and the income level was determined for the case of synchronous and isolated mode of operation of the studied electrical power node with the power system. In the study, it is assumed that in the synchronous mode, producers of electric energy carry out sales, and for consumers, suppliers carry out the purchase of electric energy on the “day-ahead” market, the operator of the energy storage system as a separate market participant provides auxiliary services for regulating the frequency and active power in the power system. In the isolated mode of operation, the consumption of an electrical power node is fully satisfied by its generating capacities, while the cost of electric energy for consumers is determined based on the total cost of electricity production and storage. According to the results of calculations, it was determined that when a switch from synchronous to isolated operation of a power node with the power system, the discounted payback period of distributed generation power plants with energy storage system increases from 5.5 to 8.7 years.

detail.abstract: China’s industrial policy, characterized by large-scale state intervention and funding, has evolved markedly over recent decades, underpinning China’s massive increase in industrial production while also moving up the ladder. First, objectives have evolved from general support to a more innovation-centered one aiming at reducing the unequal footing of private companies, in exchange for guiding their strategic investments. Second, the instruments used are much wider and complex than subsidies, which also means that it is quite difficult, if not impossible, to assess the degree of support. Landmark initiatives like Made in China 2025 and the 10,000 Little Giants program are good examples of the complexities. The success of China’s industrial policy is not generalized, as it varies across sectors, and has not yet managed to mitigate China’s decelerating productivity.

detail.abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are the backbone of the national economy due to their significant role in employment absorption, income distribution, and driving the local economy. However, MSMEs still face serious obstacles in accessing formal financial services, particularly financing. Limited collateral, low financial literacy, and relatively complex banking procedures are the main factors hindering this access. In this context, cooperatives exist as peoplebased economic institutions with unique characteristics, membership-based, and oriented towards shared prosperity. This paper aims to examine the role of cooperatives in increasing financial access for MSMEs, identify the opportunities and challenges they face, and formulate alternative strategies and adaptive measures that cooperatives can implement amidst economic dynamics and technological developments. The writing method used is a literature review with reference to various scientific journals, official agency reports, and related publications. The results of the study indicate that cooperatives have significant potential as providers of inclusive financing for MSMEs, but require institutional strengthening, service innovation, and adaptation to digitalization to optimize their role.

title: When GDP Is Not Enough: Puerto Rico, Statistical Boundaries, and the Limits of National Accounting in a Regional Economy

detail.title: When GDP Is Not Enough: Puerto Rico, Statistical Boundaries, and the Limits of National Accounting in a Regional Economy
detail.abstract: Puerto Rico exhibits one of the world's largest and most persistent gaps between gross domestic product (GDP) and gross national product (GNP). While the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) has substantially modernized Puerto Rico's GDP, this paper argues that the core interpretive problem is institutional rather than technical: the island is economically "external" yet statistically "internal" to U.S. survey and accounting architectures, preventing a consistently implemented resident/non-resident boundary across production, income, and financial accounts and thereby obstructing system closure. Drawing on primary-source documentation and official reports from 1989-2023, the paper reconstructs the evolution of Puerto Rico's macroeconomic accounts and shows why GDP modernization alone cannot resolve ambiguity about resident income and external dependence. It concludes by outlining what a credible macroeconomic system would require beyond GDP: outward-looking income-flow accounts, a regional balance-of-payments perspective, and flow-of-funds integration.

detail.title: When Private Equity Owns the Press: Easier Access to Finance for Entrepreneurs?
detail.abstract: This essay examines how media ownership structures shape news coverage of financial regulation. Drawing on the interest group theory of financial development and a model of media capture, I argue that controlling family owners of media firms have an incentive to slant news coverage toward a critical stance on regulation that encourages financial development. Due to new entrants' heavy dependence on external finance, a highly developed financial system promotes market competition. By obstructing financial development, families can protect their firms from competition. In contrast, private equity and hedge funds depend on well-functioning financial markets for their operations. Consequently, media outlets owned by such investment firms may instead report favorably on policies that promote market competition. The implication is that the recent wave of private equity takeovers in US media may have an unrecognized benefit: more favorable coverage of policies that improve access to finance for all entrepreneurs.

detail.title: A Roadmap for a Monopolization Case Against Google: Monopsony Power and AI Overviews

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Volume 175 of the University of Pennsylvania Law Review.

detail.abstract:
Google’s integration of AI-generated “Overviews” into general search marks a structural shift in how information is produced, distributed, and monetized on the internet. For years, Google incrementally altered its relationship with publishers that had been broadly symbiotic: publishers permitted Google to crawl their websites to build the search index, and in return Google directed traffic that could be monetized through advertising or subscriptions. The introduction of AI Overviews represents a decisive break from that arrangement. Google now uses publisher data not only to construct its search index, but also for AI training and grounding, while AI Overviews retain users on Google for longer instead of directing them to publisher websites. Google denies publishers the option to opt out of the AI uses without forfeiting search visibility. This Article argues that Google’s conduct is anticompetitive. Conditioning inclusion in the search index on the use of publisher data for AI-related purposes constitutes unlawful monopsonization and illegal tying in violation of Section 2 of the Sherman Act. 

Google’s conduct also constitutes an exploitative abuse that is actionable in several jurisdictions, including the European Union. The use of publisher data for additional and economically significant purposes, such as AI training and grounding, without corresponding compensation amounts to unfair pricing or the imposition of unfair conditions. The anticompetitive effects of this conduct have become increasingly evident. Traffic to publishers’ websites has declined, advertising revenues have fallen, and some publishers face foreclosure. 

Legal challenges are already underway, but regulators in the United States have not acted. Publishers have filed Section 2 claims in the US and the European Commission has initiated an investigation. Against this backdrop, the Article provides a roadmap for regulators and courts by identifying the illegal conduct, situating it within established theories of harm, and examining its anticompetitive effects on publishers and users. It then turns to remedies, arguing that effective relief must go beyond prohibiting unlawful conduct and also restore competitive conditions. The Article evaluates several remedial frameworks, including publisher opt-in with granular choice, limited collective bargaining, bilateral monopoly, and judicial or regulatory rate setting, and assesses their respective advantages and limitations. The anticompetitive exclusion of publishers is not merely a loss of competition in an ordinary product market, but a threat to the sustainability of independent journalism essential to democratic governance, underscoring the importance of timely and careful regulatory intervention.

detail.abstract: A critical issue in developing countries such as Pakistan is environmental degradation, especially rising CO₂ emissions in the country. The growing economy, energy consumption, population increase, and industrialization have created additional pressures on environmental sustainability in Pakistan. This study empirically examines the interrelationships between CO₂ emissions and economic growth, energy consumption, and final consumption expenditures in Pakistan during the sample period 1991-2022, employing an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) approach. This study estimated short- and long-run results using linear and non-linear terms to examine the EKC hypothesis. The empirical findings explained that economic growth and energy consumption are major contributors to CO₂ emissions, and final consumption does not have a significant effect in this regard in Pakistan during 1991-2022. The findings suggest a U-shaped curve between a country’s income and CO₂ emissions, and therefore, the EKC hypothesis does not support energy emissions in Pakistan, as Pakistan is still a fuel-consuming economy and has low technological efficiency.

detail.title: Analysis of the Effect of Poverty and Economic Growth on the Prevalence of Stunting in Indonesia
detail.abstract: Stunting is a condition where a child's growth is shorter than the standard for their age, and it remains a significant issue in Indonesia. In Indonesia, the prevalence rate of stunting is higher (24.4%) than the threshold set by WHO (20%). This condition is a serious concern for the government, and they aim to reduce the prevalence rate of stunting to 14% by 2024. One of the challenges faced in preventing stunting is the poverty prevailing in society. The purpose of the research is to analyze the impact of poverty and economic growth on the prevalence of stunting in Indonesia from 2000 to 2023. The data used are secondary data from national health surveys and economic indicators. The data analysis method employed is path analysis. The results of the study indicate that poverty and economic growth have an insignificant effect on parents' education level; poverty and economic growth also have an insignificant impact on the open unemployment rate; Poverty and economic growth have an insignificant effect on stunting prevalence through parental education level; poverty and economic growth have an insignificant impact on stunting prevalence through the open unemployment rate. The level of parental education has a significant effect on stunting prevalence, whereas the open unemployment rate affects stunting prevalence but is not significant. The recommendation from this study is the need for more inclusive policies to address stunting in Indonesia.

detail.abstract: Declining civic engagement increasingly strains welfare state institutions. This paper studies whether civic values can be shaped through early educational investments. I analyze Tax and School, a large-scale program implemented in Italian schools to promote fiscal and civic responsibility. Exploiting staggered cross-municipality adoption, I find that program participation increases students' intrinsic motivation for rule compliance and reduces antisocial behaviors, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged contexts. These individual responses gradually translate into community-level outcomes: municipalities exposed to the program later exhibit higher voter turnout and stronger support for redistributive policies. Survey evidence indicates these effects operate through belief updating about the value of public goods and the role of government in mitigating inequality. Counterfactual simulations suggest that scaling the program would slow the secular decline in turnout, though long-term effects depend on whether low-civic areas can retain civic capital.

title: A Parsimonious and Interpretable Factor Model of the Implied Volatility Surface
affiliations: Monash University, Monash Business School and Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics

detail.title: A Parsimonious and Interpretable Factor Model of the Implied Volatility Surface
detail.abstract: The implied volatility surface (IVS) is a key gauge of market uncertainty with implications for derivative pricing, risk management, and macro-financial analysis. This paper introduces a parsimonious factor-based model that decomposes the IVS into five components: level, tail asymmetry, term structure, curvature, and deviation. By incorporating the asymptotic properties of the IVS, the proposed framework offers a structurally grounded representation with enhanced interpretability. Empirical application to S&P 500 European options demonstrates that our model (i) captures the global geometry of the IVS; (ii) outperforms traditional polynomial-based benchmarks in both surface fitting and forecasting; and (iii) provides superior predictive power for both realized variance and macroeconomic conditions. The factors are particularly informative during episodes of heightened uncertainty, including the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 shock.

title: The Right to Walk to School
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - Paul M. Hebert Law Center

detail.title: The Right to Walk to School
detail.abstract:
In 1969, half of all students walked or biked to school.  By 2023, only one in ten students did so.  Instead, the majority of children today get to school in a car driven by a parent. Although multiple forces drive this trend away from walking, school transportation policies play an outsized role in determining children’s mobility options.  Across the United States, school districts are quietly adopting policies that prohibit or restrict children from walking to school.  These policies are typically justified in the name of safety and administrative convenience, but they operate as significant restraints on parental rights and children’s everyday movement.  

This Article examines whether public school students have a right to walk to school. In doing so, the Article focuses on the intersection of parental authority, children's individual liberties, and the state's responsibility for child welfare and safe streets. First, the Article explores the right to walk to school from the state's perspective. This side of the conflict has two components: the state's powers to design unsafe streets; and the state's interest in student safety in light of those safety concerns. School districts often defend walking restrictions as measures to prevent traffic accidents. Yet this Article questions whether broad prohibitions are narrowly tailored to serve that interest, and whether alternatives (such as improved pedestrian infrastructure or more tailored walk-to-school policies) could achieve safety goals while preserving parental and student rights. 

The second inquiry considers the extent to which parental rights insulate decisions about school transportation from excessive state interference.  Building on the Supreme Court’s parental rights jurisprudence, which affirms the fundamental right of parents to direct the care, custody, and control of their children, the Article argues that restrictions on walking may impermissibly intrude on parental autonomy absent a compelling safety risk.

Finally, the Article explores whether children themselves possess a constitutionally protected right to walk to school.  Although the Constitution does not expressly provide such a right, some courts have recognized certain free movement rights (such as the right to intrastate travel or the right to locomotion) in other contexts.  This Article analyzes whether prohibitions on walking impose undue burdens on children’s freedom of movement, comparing them to curfew laws that have been invalidated for restricting individuals’ mobility without sufficient justification.

Taken together, these analyses provide a framework for evaluating the constitutionality of school transportation policies.  The Article concludes that restrictions on walking implicate foundational questions about parental authority, children’s liberties, and the scope of state power.  Courts, school districts, and urban planners should therefore adopt approaches that balance child safety with respect for family autonomy and student freedom of movement.

title: Income Distribution Sensitive Thirlwall’s Law: A Decomposition of Import Income Elasticities and Estimation for the Brazilian Economy

detail.title: Income Distribution Sensitive Thirlwall’s Law: A Decomposition of Import Income Elasticities and Estimation for the Brazilian Economy

keywords: income elasticity of demand for imports

detail.abstract: The relationship between inequality and growth has long attracted the attention of Post-Keynesian economists. The Balance-of-Payments-Constrained Growth (BPCG) approach, however, emphasizes that in the long run it is the external constraint that ultimately pins down the growth rate. This paper contributes to that literature by developing a theoretical version of an Income Distribution Sensitive Thirlwall's Law, in which import income elasticities are decomposed by income group and the aggregate elasticity becomes a weighted average of group-specific elasticities. Changes in personal income distribution therefore modify the balance-of-payments-constrained equilibrium growth rate. Using Brazilian household microdata for 2018, we estimate income elasticities for ten income groups and convert them into import income elasticities. The results show that these elasticities vary systematically across the distribution and that more unequal income distributions are associated with a higher aggregate import income elasticity and a lower growth rate compatible with balance-of-payments equilibrium, underscoring the need to incorporate inequality directly into Thirlwall's law.

detail.abstract: We examine how various aspects of family ownership affect both market and accounting performance for an emerging market like India. We also study whether non-family promoters help to reduce the expected agency problems arising between family promoters and outside shareholders. Using feasible generalised least squares for a sample of 1,100 firms listed on BSE during 2007 to 2014, we show that not only do family firms perform worse than nonfamily firms, but also that family ownership has a negative impact on both accounting and market performance of firms. Evidence also indicates that family ownership has a U-shaped relationship with firm performance suggesting that at higher levels of family ownership, convergence of interest hypothesis may be useful in explaining this positive relationship. Non-family promoters help to improve market value at lower levels of ownership but as their ownership increases, the beneficial effect of their active monitoring diminishes.

title: Homeowners insurance and the transmission of monetary policy

detail.title: Homeowners insurance and the transmission of monetary policy

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We document a novel transmission channel of monetary policy through the homeowners insurance market. On average, contractionary monetary policy shocks result in higher homeowners insurance prices. Using granular data on insurers’ balance sheets, we show that this effect is driven by the interaction of financial frictions and the interest rate sensitivity of investment portfolios. Specifically, rate hikes reduce the market value of insurers’ assets, tightening insurers’ balance sheet constraints and increasing their shadow cost of capital. These frictions in insurance supply amplify the effects of monetary policy on real estate and mortgage markets by making housing less affordable. We find that monetary policy shocks have a stronger impact on home prices and mortgage applications when local insurers are more sensitive to interest rates. This channel is particularly pronounced in areas where households face high climate risk exposure. Our findings highlight the role of insurance markets in amplifying macroeconomic shocks and the interconnections between homeowners insurance, residential real estate, and mortgage lending.

title: Vertical Integration as a Driver of Investment Efficiency: Evidence from China's Food and Beverage Sector
affiliations: University College of Technology Sarawak

detail.title: Vertical Integration as a Driver of Investment Efficiency: Evidence from China's Food and Beverage Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Vertical integration is widely used in China's food and beverage sector to secure supply and quality control, yet evidence on its financial benefits remains mixed and the mechanisms linking integration to stock-market outcomes are underexplored. Using a 15-year panel of 50 Chinese listed food and beverage firms (2008-2022; 750 firm-year observations), this study examines whether vertical integration affects stock yield directly and indirectly through firms' investment behaviour. Employing firm and year fixed effects and mediation analysis, we find that higher vertical integration is associated with greater investment intensity, and that investment intensity is positively related to stock yield. Once the investment channel is accounted for, the direct effect of vertical integration on stock yield becomes statistically insignificant, suggesting that the stock-market relevance of integration primarily operates through investment. These results refine Transaction Cost Economics and the Resource-Based View by showing that integration creates shareholder value not automatically, but when translated into disciplined capital allocation in a regulation-intensive, perishable-goods industry. The study offers a mechanism-based empirical framework for evaluating integration strategies in emerging-market settings.

title: Stabilizing Credit When Nonperforming Loans Surge: The Role Of Asset Management Companies
affiliations: National Bank of Slovakia, European Central Bank (ECB), Oberlin College and University of Oxford - Said Business School and St. Edmund Hall

detail.title: Stabilizing Credit When Nonperforming Loans Surge: The Role Of Asset Management Companies

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: When default losses elevate borrowing costs, expanding credit cannot stabilize the economy because default rates feedback to lending rates through bank balance sheets. Asset management companies (AMCs) break this loop by purchasing nonperforming loans at their long-run recovery values, thereby fixing the effective default rate that banks face. Government purchases of performing loans expand credit but leave this feedback intact. In a model calibrated to the eurozone, the AMC reduces quarterly default rates by 0.8 percentage points, lowers lending rates by 1.6 percentage points, and raises welfare by 0.2%. Government purchases crowd out bank deposits, contracting credit; default rates rise by 1.8 percentage points, lending rates increase by 1.2 percentage points, and welfare falls by 0.3%.

title: Multi-State and Diffusion Models for Goalie Pulling Towards the End of the Third Period
affiliations: and Michigan State University

detail.title: Multi-State and Diffusion Models for Goalie Pulling Towards the End of the Third Period
detail.abstract:
The question of when a hockey coach should pull the goalie when down by 1 or 2 goals has persisted since the early 1900s. A novel approach to quantifying this problem, utilizing the Bellman optimality principle (Bellman. Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press. 1957), was recently proposed by Asness and Brown (SSRN Electronic Journal. 2018). 

In this work, we seek to extend the ideas detailed by the authors in that seminal paper while presenting options for coaches with only a few minutes left in the third period. In doing so, we first borrow from multi-state model techniques commonly used in actuarial science (Dickson, Hardy, & Waters. Actuarial Mathematics for Life Contingent Risks. Cambridge University Press. 2019) and then diffusion models common in financial economics.

Specifically, we compute the optimal time a coach should pull once they have committed to pulling their goalie, both as excess expected points over a coach who never pulls and as absolute expected points. We show a time difference between these two scenarios, which may provide insight into why some coaches wait longer than others to pull. Finally, we upscale to a diffusion model for score difference that represents a coach's perspective on the current state of the game, reframing the decision to pull or not as a question of whether a barrier has been crossed by the score differential. We provide R code so readers can reproduce our results, experiment, and implement their ideas into our framework.

title: Congestion in General Equilibrium: Nodal Electricity Pricing, Production, and Welfare Working Paper

detail.title: Congestion in General Equilibrium: Nodal Electricity Pricing, Production, and Welfare Working Paper
detail.abstract: When a transmission network is congested, localized demand shocks change electricity prices at every node. Whether and how those price changes affect local wages and welfare depends on how firms and households adjust their electricity consumption, which in turn reshapes the dispatch and the prices themselves. This paper defines a power-flow general equilibrium (PFGE) that embeds the KKT conditions of a DC optimal power flow inside a general equilibrium model with production and factor markets, so that locational marginal prices, firm output, wages, and household income emerge as a fixed point. Because the OPF is solved endogenously, rather than fed observed nodal prices from an ISO, the model supports counterfactual policy analysis: a new load re-optimizes dispatch, shifts which lines bind, and changes prices throughout the network. We prove existence via Brouwer's theorem. The main analytical result is a decomposition: the standard CGE commits a spatial averaging error proportional to congestion rents, and the standalone OPF commits a demand rigidity error proportional to the price elasticity of electricity demand. Both models coincide with the PFGE if and only if a congestion-elasticity interaction term I is zero at every node. A three-bus illustration calibrated loosely to the PJM data center problem confirms that both error channels are quantitatively nontrivial and that the standalone OPF substantially overstates the cost of a new load when demand response is ignored.

title: Between Journalism and Political Advocacy: The Contested Position of Kashmir Times in The Kashmir Conflict
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Between Journalism and Political Advocacy: The Contested Position of Kashmir Times in The Kashmir Conflict
detail.abstract: This study explores the historical evolution, ideological positioning, and geopolitical entanglements surrounding Kashmir Times, one of the earliest English-language newspapers operating from Jammu and Kashmir. By examining the legacy of its founder Ved Bhasin and the contemporary role of executive editor Anuradha Bhasin, the paper analyzes the complex intersection between journalism, separatist political narratives, state patronage structures, and transnational advocacy networks. The study situates Kashmir Times within broader debates on media autonomy in conflict regions, examining controversies related to government patronage, eviction disputes, legal challenges to communication restrictions following the abrogation of Article 370, and alleged links to international lobbying platforms such as the Kashmiri American Council. Through institutional and political-economy analysis, the paper evaluates competing claims regarding press freedom, foreign influence operations, and national security imperatives. It argues that Kashmir Times represents a critical case study illustrating how media institutions in conflict zones become arenas of ideological contestation, geopolitical lobbying, and informational sovereignty struggles within modern democratic states.

title: Challenges and Limitations of Machine Learning Models in Financial Volatility Prediction

detail.title: Challenges and Limitations of Machine Learning Models in Financial Volatility Prediction
detail.abstract: Over the years, machine learning has been increasingly positioned as a way to make sense of this uncertainty. Flexible models, large datasets, and improved computation have created the impression that volatility can now be forecast with reasonable confidence. In this we takes a more cautious view. Rather than proposing new models or reporting performance numbers, it looks at the structural reasons why volatility prediction remains difficult, even with advanced machine learning techniques. Drawing data from existing research and practical observations, the paper discusses non-stationarity, noise, data limitations, overfitting, as recurring obstacles. The central argument is that many of these challenges are not engineering problems waiting to be solved, but reflections of how financial markets actually behave. Understanding these limitations is essential before placing too much faith in model-driven volatility forecasts.

It proposed to replace donors with market-based        transactions. detail.title: Begreifen or Verstehen in the Thought of Ludwig von Mises Is There a Difference

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Journal of Private Enterprise , Volume XL Issue 4 (Winter) 2025 pp.1-8
publicationDetails.journalName: Journal of Private Enterprise

detail.abstract: An increasing number of scholars have argued that the theoretical approach of Ludwig von Mises ought to be viewed along lines that are more favorably disposed to interpretive historical        methods than was once generally recognized. Despite Mises’s adamant statements about the apodictic certainty of theory derived from purposefulness, particular purposes were often seen by        Mises to be embedded in a specific context. While this essay does not deny that such “understanding” can be useful in the application of theory, it argues that there were very good reasons        why some of Mises’s students, particularly Murray Rothbard, took their teacher’s arguments in the more logically deductive and apodictic direction. The distinction between Mises’s idea of        Begreifen and the historically laden concept of Verstehen is seen to be more substantive than nominal. title: Using SET for Employment Decisions is Unethical
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Using SET for Employment Decisions is Unethical
detail.abstract: There is compelling evidence that student evaluations of teaching (SET) have little connection to teaching quality; that they have large unpredictable biases from things beyond the instructor's control, including the instructor's gender and other characteristics protected under employment law; that some fraction of student SET responses are objectively false;  that SET reflect grade expectations rather than learning; that SET are sometimes negatively associated with teaching effectiveness; that students cannot accurately assess their own learning (and thus cannot accurately assess pedagogical effectiveness); that faculty can raise SET by giving students cookies; and that some students use SET comments to harass instructors anonymously. Some studies claim that SET measure teaching quality or that biases in SET are negligible. The apparent contradiction arises largely from relying on data that cannot in principle measure bias, misinterpreting statistical tests, and faulty logic. But even a solid finding of no bias in some set of courses would not rule out bias elsewhere or elsewhen. This work summarizes key evidence about SET, explains errors in some arguments that SET are valid and fair, and explains why comparing SET scores across courses and faculty is unethical statistical mischief. The signal of teaching quality in SET is too weak and the biases are too numerous, complex, and variable to adjust SET to make them fair and valid.

title: The Silent Battles: The Challenges Encountered By The Women Workers In The Unorganized Sector
affiliations: Central University of South Bihar

detail.title: The Silent Battles: The Challenges Encountered By The Women Workers In The Unorganized Sector
detail.abstract:
This study examines the socio-legal challenges faced by women in India’s unorganized sector, who represent approximately 52.5% of the nation’s registered workforce. Focusing specifically on the Gaya and Nalanda districts of Bihar, the research identifies a precarious working environment defined by systemic wage discrimination, excessive workloads, and a critical deficit in social security coverage. Primary data collected through field interviews reveals significant psychological barriers, including a pervasive fear of job loss, physical abuse, and workplace harassment. The findings suggest that existing labor law frameworks suffer from ineffective implementation at the grassroots level. Consequently, this report advocates for the formal legal recognition of domestic workers, the establishment of dedicated protection wings within labor departments, and the implementation of localized dispute resolution mechanisms to effectively safeguard the rights of women workers. 
This is prepared as part of academic coursework of Labour Law at the Central University of South Bihar, Gaya.

detail.abstract: This paper provides three immersive lesson plans that showcase the intricate relationship between economic dynamism and economic growth, emphasizing the narrative power of images to        illustrate the concept of creative destruction. Economic dynamism is the process by which innovation, entrepreneurship, and market forces continually reshape industries and economies.        Creative destruction, a term coined by economist Joseph Schumpeter, embodies this transformative process in which new technologies, ideas, and business models replace outdated ones, leading        to economic progress. This work is especially timely, as Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how innovation and the        forces of creative destruction can drive economic growth.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence governance is commonly conceptualized through formal regulation, institutional oversight, and technical control mechanisms. However, the social processes through which responsibility is enacted across distributed actor networks remain insufficiently understood. This study analyzes several thousand publicly available professional posts and discussion threads contributed by over one thousand identifiable actors over a one-month observation period using inductive qualitative coding to examine how responsibility roles emerge in AI governance across healthcare, insurance, regulatory, research, and technological ecosystems. Drawing on sensemaking theory, socio-technical systems perspectives, role theory, and governance-as-practice approaches, the study identifies recurring patterns of influence, mediation, translation, and accountability that manifest as emergent governance roles. Findings suggest that responsibility in AI ecosystems is dynamically negotiated rather than institutionally fixed. The paper proposes an initial taxonomy of emergent roles and develops hypotheses for future empirical testing.

title: Technology Adoption and Women's Rights: Evidence from Switzerland

detail.title: Technology Adoption and Women's Rights: Evidence from Switzerland

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 03/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Gender equality and economic growth have historically tended to move together yet identifying causal effects has been difficult. This paper uses data on the support for female suffrage in Switzerland in order to explore the impact of technology adoption on gender norms. We argue that the early adoption of electricity was conducive to local economic development, which in turn led to more egalitarian views on gender. To identify causality, we exploit geographic differences in the potential to generate electricity from waterpower. Our results show that early electricity adoption (by the 1910s) had a lasting impact on municipality vote shares in support of female suffrage in the groundbreaking 1959 referendum. We complement this finding with Cantonal referendums on female voting rights and federal electoral results to show that higher support for female political participation is observed in the data since the 1920s. We then examine how technology may have shaped gender attitudes and find that increased educational investment explains part of the shift. Fertility appears to respond to changing gender norms and reinforce them, but is unlikely the keymechanism in the causal chain.

title: Public Service Stewardship: Authority, Legitimacy, and the Prevention of Administrative Evil in an Era of Persistent Crisis

detail.title: Public Service Stewardship: Authority, Legitimacy, and the Prevention of Administrative Evil in an Era of Persistent Crisis

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or primary data collection. As a conceptual and theoretical analysis drawing exclusively on publicly available sources, ethics approval or informed consent was not required.
