detail.abstract: Contemporary governance increasingly operates under conditions of persistent crisis in which emergencies are normalized, discretion expands, and legitimacy erodes incrementally rather than episodically. Under these conditions, traditional safeguards against ethical failure-including rules and compliance systems, values-based ethics training, and leadership-centered moral frameworks-have proven insufficient to prevent the routinization of harm through lawful, professional action. This paper advances Public Service Stewardship as a governing public service ethic designed to discipline authority under uncertainty, constraint, and cumulative legitimacy risk. Stewardship reframes authority as custodial rather than instrumental, treats legitimacy as finite and depletable, and insists that ethical responsibility persists despite incomplete control or hierarchical constraint. Rather than prescribing outcomes, it governs how discretion is held, justified, and constrained over time. By focusing on decision posture rather than episodic results, Public Service Stewardship functions as a preventive ethical architecture, capable of interrupting the normalization of administrative evil before harm consolidates into routine practice. The paper situates this framework as the individual-level ethical foundation of a broader stewardship architecture that includes Constitutional Stewardship and Multi-Polar Stewardship, forming a coherent cross-level approach to governing authority under permanent crisis. It concludes by examining implications for professional identity, institutional design, and future research, arguing that the endurance of democratic governance depends less on decisiveness or compliance than on the ethical stewardship of authority across time.

title: How Resilient are Decentralised Markets? Insights from a CME Outage into FX Market Functioning
affiliations: Swiss National Bank, Swiss National Bank and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: How Resilient are Decentralised Markets? Insights from a CME Outage into FX Market Functioning

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Economic Note No. 02/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss National Bank Economic Note Series

detail.abstract: On 28 November 2025, the failure of a single Chicago-based data centre disrupted several global financial markets. The foreign exchange (FX) market was among those affected as its most important trading venue for futures contracts as well as a key primary venue became unavailable. The outage provided a natural experiment, shedding light on the impact of the trading halt on market functioning and the resilience of the decentralised FX market. We find that trading on secondary venues and with banks continued, demonstrating how decentralisation can enhance resilience. However, transaction costs increased considerably, mainly because FX futures prices became unavailable. This indicates that price signals from transparent venues remain essential for price discovery in the FX market.

title: Tax-tualism
affiliations: Yale University, Law School

detail.title: Tax-tualism
detail.abstract:
Textualism has long bedeviled tax law. Many longstanding tax anti-abuse doctrines lack clear textual footing and therefore appear vulnerable in an era that prioritizes statutory text. This threat has sharpened in the wake of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which requires courts to determine the best reading of statutes and limits agency discretion. The problem is this: Will textualism undo tax law’s functionalist foundation?

This Article argues that the conflict between textualism and federal income tax law is overstated. It develops a method of interpreting the Internal Revenue Code—“tax-tualism”—that is rooted in textualism but harmonizes with tax law’s anti-abuse foundations. Tax-tualism’s core insight is that the unusual statutory history of the Code is especially susceptible to application of the reenactment canon. According to this canon, when Congress reenacts statutory language without significant change, it places the settled interpretation of the statute into positive law. Because the Code has been repeatedly reenacted, application of the reenactment canon is indispensable to any textualist approach to tax law.

In addition, the Article elaborates on the reenactment canon in the tax context, arguing that judicial interpretations, including those of the Tax Court, are central to determining settled meaning, though administrative pronouncements are not. It further contends that reenactment incorporates settled interpretations whether or not those interpretations were textually justifiable. 

As a case study, the Article applies tax-tualism to the so-called “judicial requirements” of tax-free corporate reorganizations. It concludes that tax-tualism saves two out of the three. In doing so, the Article demonstrates that many classic anti-abuse doctrines already survive on textualist terms as positive law, without resort to purposivism or administrative deference, thus preserving tax law’s structural integrity.

title: The Price of Knowledge Diffusion: Technology Licensing and Market Power
affiliations: and University of Turku - Turku School of Economics

detail.title: The Price of Knowledge Diffusion: Technology Licensing and Market Power

declarations.funderStatement: Lieto Savings Bank Foundation

detail.abstract: Business dynamism has been slowing globally over the last several decades. In a recent study, Akcigit and Ates (2023) examine the relative importance of different channels behind this development and highlight weakened knowledge diffusion from the technology frontier to followers as a dominant force. Their study also suggests that diffusion may weaken endogenously as the technology gap widens and market power accumulates, raising the question of how innovation policy can strengthen diffusion without reducing welfare. In this paper we study leader-to-follower licensing as a policy-relevant diffusion margin, and evaluate licensing subsidies relative to direct R&D subsidies. We develop an endogenous-growth general equilibrium model in which firms compete in prices and invest in R&D; the technology leader endogenously chooses whether to license to the follower, trading off higher static profits against faster follower catch-up through knowledge diffusion. We calibrate the model to Finnish data from 2014-2019. Our first exercise evaluates whether allowing licensing is desirable by shutting down the licensing channel in the calibrated economy. In the Finnish benchmark, shutting down licensing lowers growth but increases consumption-equivalent welfare, because the level effects of reduced concentration dominate the diffusion benefits of licensing. We then vary the diffusion rate through licensing and product substitutability to characterize when licensing becomes welfare improving. In that region, solving the policymaker's problem shows a non-trivial interaction: higher R&D subsidies can reduce equilibrium licensing by moving leaders more quickly into the monopoly-pricing states where licensing is privately unattractive, so the optimal policy mix augments R&D support with a non-negligible licensing subsidy to sustain diffusion.

title: The Year in Law & Technology 2025
affiliations: and George Mason University - Law Library

detail.title: The Year in Law & Technology 2025

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Green Bag Almanac and Reader 2026, Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
This article surveys developments at the intersection of law and technology during 2025, a year defined by the legal profession's rapid—and often turbulent—adoption of generative artificial intelligence. Organized as a month-by-month chronicle, it documents the proliferation of AI-powered legal research tools from Bloomberg Law, LexisNexis, and newcomers like Harvey and vLex; the wave of judicial sanctions imposed on attorneys who submitted AI-hallucinated case citations; and the emerging case law testing copyright, product liability, privacy, and evidentiary frameworks against new technological realities. The article tracks how law schools shifted from restricting AI use to requiring AI literacy, with institutions from Case Western Reserve to Stanford embedding generative AI training into their curricula. It examines landmark enforcement actions, including the largest CCPA penalty to date, a federal warrant for LLM chat histories, and the first AI copyright training settlement. It also catalogs judicial responses to AI-generated filings, from monetary sanctions to bar referrals, and notes the growing concern that hallucinated citations are weighing heavily on judicial resources. Throughout, the article highlights the tension between generative AI's transformative potential and the profession's obligation to ensure accuracy, competence, and ethical compliance. 

Join us as we peruse some of the happenings over the last year at the intersection of the legal and technology worlds.

detail.abstract: Economics has long been framed as a science of rational choice and incentives. This essay argues for a more fundamental starting point: affect, and specifically the primary motivator of interest-excitement. Following the work of psychologist Silvan Tomkins, we posit that interest is the engine of all human action-the force that directs attention, fuels curiosity, and makes learning and creation possible. Its opposite is not irrationality, but interruption-a motivational collapse experienced as profound confusion. This framework reveals that economic expansion is a function of cultivated interest, while contraction and alienation are the results of its systemic interruption. We argue that the painful social experience of economic humiliation is the consequence of a system that generates chronic interruption at the core of motivation. By reframing economics as the science of human attention, we can move beyond abstract models and toward.a discipline capable of addressing the systemic humiliation and motivational collapse that plague modern economic life.

title: Regulating Investment Advice in the Age of Social Media: Finfluencers, Sec Regulation, and Sec V. Constantinescu

detail.title: Regulating Investment Advice in the Age of Social Media: Finfluencers, Sec Regulation, and Sec V. Constantinescu
detail.abstract: The rise of financial influencers (“finfluencers”) has transformed investment advice, shifting financial persuasion from regulated intermediaries to algorithmically amplified social media personalities. The controversy surrounding SEC v. Constantinescu and the second Trump Administration’s pivot on SEC enforcement exposes a structural mismatch between traditional fraud doctrine and digitally mediated markets. Drawing on behavioral finance research, emerging empirical evidence of retail harm, and comparative international approaches, this Article contends that finfluencers function as de facto investment advisers. It proposes a three-tier regulatory framework combining targeted registration thresholds, enhanced disclosure obligations, and platform-level incentives. This framework aligns regulatory obligations with functional impact, closes doctrinal loopholes exposed by Constantinescu, and restores parity between traditional and digital markets to better protect retail investors.

title:
Private Equity's Zombie Firms: The Trapped Capital Dilemma 
A Rigorous Mathematical Framework for Analyzing Liquidity Crises in Illiquid Asset Markets
affiliations: Society of Actuaries

detail.title:
Private Equity's Zombie Firms: The Trapped Capital Dilemma 
A Rigorous Mathematical Framework for Analyzing Liquidity Crises in Illiquid Asset Markets
detail.abstract:
We develop a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing the “zombie firm” phenomenon in private equity (PE). The term refers to portfolio companies and funds that continue to survive on paper but are unable to achieve a viable exit or return meaningful capital to investors. Building on the foundational zombie lending model of Caballero, Hoshi, and Kashyap, we extend their analysis in four distinct directions.

First, we apply real options theory, as formalized by Dixit and Pindyck [1], to model the general partner’s exit decision as an optimal stopping problem. This approach treats the decision to sell a portfolio company as analogous to exercising a financial option: the GP must weigh the ongoing stream of management fees against the uncertain, one-time payoff from exiting. Second, we employ the optimal stopping framework of Peskir and Shiryaev [2] to prove that a well-defined “zombie equilibrium” exists. In financial terms, this equilibrium is the precise company valuation below which it is rational for the GP to hold indefinitely and collect fees rather than pursue a sale. Third, we use network contagion models, drawing on the work of Acemoglu et al. [3] and Battiston et al. [4], to quantify how distress at one fund can cascade across the PE ecosystem through shared LP commitments, co-investments, and lending relationships. Fourth, we borrow techniques from econophysics, following Bouchaud and Potters [5] and Sornette [6], to characterize abrupt, market wide regime shifts between liquid and frozen states.

On the theoretical side, we prove the existence and uniqueness of zombie equilibria under general conditions that allow for sudden valuation jumps (modeled via Lévy processes, which generalize the standard assumption that asset prices change smoothly). We derive sharp bounds on how much a localized shock can amplify as it propagates through the GP–LP network, using spectral graph theory to characterize the network’s vulnerability in terms of its most influential connection patterns. We identify the conditions under which the PE exit market undergoes a phase transition, a sudden, discontinuous shift from an active, liquid state to a frozen one, using a Landau-Ginzburg free energy approach borrowed from statistical physics and adapted to model market-wide liquidity. Finally, we construct incentive-compatible fee mechanisms, contracts designed so that the GP’s self-interest naturally aligns with the LP’s objective of timely exits, using the revelation principle from mechanism design theory [7].

Calibrating the model to data from 2018 through 2025 fund vintages, we estimate that zombie prevalence ranges from 23 to 31 percent of funds, and we project that the associated deadweight losses, representing capital stuck in unproductive holdings rather than being recycled into new investments, amount to between $180 billion and $240 billion annually. Our model predicts that the current $1.2 trillion trapped capital crisis is a structural equilibrium that requires fundamental mechanism redesign, not merely a cyclical downturn that will self-correct.

detail.abstract: Contemporary societies face a structural coordination crisis: fragmented institutions, decisions detached from territorial reality, and advanced technologies applied in isolation without an integrated understanding of the system they aim to optimize. In this context, artificial intelligence, classical strategic planning, and digital governance frameworks often fall short of enabling coherent, traceable, and sustainable outcomes in complex environments. This article proposes Structural Intelligence (IE) as a new discipline focused on understanding, organizing, and governing complex systems—human, organizational, and technological—through the analysis of their structures, interactions, and territorial dynamics. IE is not limited to automating decisions or processing data; it introduces an integrative framework that allows a system to observe its own architecture, detect dysfunctions, coordinate actors, and optimize decisions adaptively while preserving global coherence. The paper provides a formal definition of IE, establishes its guiding principles, differentiates it from existing approaches, outlines key domains of application, and proposes a research agenda for its academic and institutional consolidation.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh witnessed the worst flood crisis of recent times in 2024. The severity of the flood was striking not only during the flood but also at the time of the rescuing period when people died due to, inter alia, heavily contaminated water. Overflow of pollutants into water supplies further escalated widespread outbreaks of water-borne diseases. As a climate-vulnerable country, this flood exposed Bangladesh's infrastructural weakness in tackling such crisis circumstances just like any other global south country. This weakness includes public health, environmental legal policy framework, and inconsistency in implementing international standards and sustainable development goals. declarations.funderStatement: The second author acknowledges the National Research Foundation, Singapore, under its AI Singapore Pro gramme (AISG) [Grant AISG3-GV-2021-006]. The fourth author acknowledges National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72325002 and 72421001].

detail.abstract: This study investigates how AI recommendation algorithms shape complementor strategies and market equality on digital platforms. Using two quasi-natural experiments from a food-sharing platform, we examine impacts of sequential algorithmic upgrades: from a location-based baseline to popularity-based (PopRec) and then personalization-based (PersRec). Analyses of over 1.7 million observations reveal that PopRec drives complementors to concentrate on a few offerings, while PersRec encourages new product introduction; yet these strategic shifts come at the expense of one another. Furthermore, PopRec reduces revenues of superstars but boosts revenues for long-tail complementors, enhancing market equality. Conversely, PersRec exacerbates market inequality by asymmetrically benefiting superstars. By bridging platform orchestration and AI frontiers, this study demonstrates the strategic potential of AI in platform management while underscoring the importance of algorithmic accountability. Managerial Summary: Digital platforms increasingly deploy AI recommendation algorithms to manage ecosystem performance. This study reveals that these algorithms also function as effective orchestration mechanisms, incentivizing and shaping complementor offering strategies at scale. We find that popularity-based algorithms incentivize complementors to specialize and concentrate on a few core product offerings, while personalization-based algorithms foster broader new product introduction. Our results demonstrate the vital strategic value of AI for managing platform ecosystems. Crucially, both algorithms present inherent trade-offs for complementor strategies and trigger unforeseen market dynamics. Platform owners must meticulously design and implement algorithmic systems, balancing ecosystem generativity with operational control and considering far-reaching market inequality implications.

title: Decentralized Finance (DeFi): A Review and Research Agenda
affiliations: Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management

detail.title: Decentralized Finance (DeFi): A Review and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Decentralized finance (DeFi) has emerged as a significant financial innovation, using blockchain technology and smart contracts to replicate and expand traditional financial services without intermediaries. This review synthesizes the literature across seven dimensions: token financing, trading and liquidity, cryptocurrency as an asset class, governance, risk, monetary system implications, and infrastructure. We identify several key findings: tokens solve coordination problems but face design trade-offs; cryptocurrency markets exhibit distinct risk factors, yet most price volatility reflects beliefs rather than fundamentals; decentralization is partial and endogenous, with concentration emerging in mining, staking, and governance; novel risks including stablecoin fragility and MEV extraction require new frameworks; and infrastructure constraints shape feasible applications. We conclude by proposing directions for future research.

title:
Bank Failures: 
The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title:
Bank Failures: 
The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity
detail.abstract: Bank failures can stem from runs on otherwise solvent banks or from losses that render banks insolvent, regardless of withdrawals. Disentangling the relative importance of liquidity and solvency in explaining bank failures is central to understanding financial crises and designing effective financial stability policies. This paper reviews evidence on the causes of bank failures. Bank failures-both with and without runs-are almost always related to poor fundamentals. Low recovery rates in failure suggest that most failed banks that experienced runs were likely fundamentally insolvent. Examiners' postmortem assessments also emphasize the primacy of poor asset quality and solvency problems. Before deposit insurance, runs commonly triggered the failure of insolvent banks. However, runs rarely caused the failure of strong banks, as such runs were typically resolved through other mechanisms, including interbank cooperation, equity injections, public signals of strength, or suspension of convertibility. We discuss the policy implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

title: Default-Triggered Acquisition (III): The European Option-to-Acquire
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Default-Triggered Acquisition (III): The European Option-to-Acquire
detail.abstract: Cheung and Satchell (2004) and Cheung (2004a) address the default-triggered acquisition issue and derives some analytical results for risky bond pricing. Instead of modelling from the bond investors' point of view, this paper analyses the default-triggered acquisition problem from the potential acquirers' perspective and develops a structural model of a potential acquirer's position, the European option-to-acquire, with analytical results. A comprehensive numerical comparative static analysis is also undertaken which provides some insights for the Greeks of the option. Abstract Addendum (2026): This paper anticipates the modern shift towards strategic distressed debt investing. By modelling the 'Option-to-Acquire' from the buyer's perspective, it provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for Real Options analysis in M&A. As Private Equity and Special Situations funds increasingly utilise 'Loan-to-Own' strategies, the analytical results and 'Greeks' derived herein offer a vital framework for valuing the strategic optionality inherent in distressed acquisitions.

title: Strategic Disclosure to Rivals and Suppliers Under the Threat of Screening
affiliations: East China University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Strategic Disclosure to Rivals and Suppliers Under the Threat of Screening
detail.abstract: Firms often operate in environments in which private information has strategic value for multiple stakeholders, including rivals and vertically related partners. This paper develops a framework in which a privately informed producer interacts with both a distributor and a rival. The producer may disclose information horizontally to the rival, vertically to the distributor, or both. Our key contribution is to allow the distributor to acquire information endogenously through screening. We show that the presence of screening fundamentally reshapes disclosure incentives. Horizontally, disclosure is no longer governed by the classical trade-off between outcomes in favorable and unfavorable states: only rival responses in unfavorable states matter, and, under quantity competition, disclosure becomes profitable when intra-industry correlation is sufficiently positive. Vertically, disclosure eliminates informational rents and quantity distortions associated with screening, making it profitable when the producer's outside option is sufficiently strong. Because of the strategic reaction of the rival, vertical disclosure may prove profitable in both favorable and unfavorable states of the world.

detail.abstract: We develop a microsimulation model that can identify Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) as financially distressed due to their inability to meet short term losses with cash (liquidity distress) or to meet their debt repayments (solvency distress). We estimate that – on these metrics – around one-in-six Irish SMEs may have been financially distressed at the end of 2020, or 14 per cent when weighted by debt balances. The model can be used for policy assessment: we calibrate the model to fiscal support implemented in Ireland during the first three quarters of 2020 and estimate that it reduced the share of distressed SME debt by two-fifths. On targeting, we show that a hypothetical scheme selecting firms with the smallest losses first could reduce distress rates from 19 to 7 per cent – albeit we do not suggest this is the welfare-optimising approach. On policy design, we show that debt-based support schemes reduce distress rates by less than grants, and this is driven by the greater role played by solvency over liquidity concerns in a debt-based support regime.

title: Using Supervised Machine Learning to Predict Exploration-Exploitation Vacillation

detail.title: Using Supervised Machine Learning to Predict Exploration-Exploitation Vacillation
detail.abstract: When and how do firms vacillate between exploration and exploitation? While firms face tensions in balancing exploration and exploitation, research on ambidexterity and punctuatedequilibrium is often treated separately. We reconcile these by reframing technological reorientation as a forecasting problem, operationalizing vacillation occurrence, time-tovacillation, and vacillation magnitude. Using patents data from U.S. public firms from 1991 to 2024, we compare econometric baselines, supervised machine learning, and Bayesian hierarchical models to predict vacillation from portfolio signals. Results indicate that machine learning improves PR-AUC for occurrence and C-index for time-to-vacillation compared to baselines. Focused accumulation in new IPC categories increases vacillation occurrence, accelerates time-to-vacillation, and amplifies vacillation magnitude, while concentration and scale delay switches. This advances strategy research through predictive validation under nonlinearity, and uncertainty quantification.

detail.abstract:
The Paradox of Technological Dependence The modern operational landscape is characterized by a precarious paradox: as our technological capabilities for managing critical sectors—from healthcare to energy grids—advance exponentially, the foundational human skills required to maintain these systems in the absence of automation are degrading at an alarming rate. This phenomenon, often termed "deskilling," creates a unique vulnerability profile for contemporary society. We are building "high-ceiling" systems capable of unprecedented efficiency while simultaneously lowering the "floor" of basic competence, leaving communities exposed to catastrophic failure when the technological assistance layer is disrupted. 
This report provides an exhaustive analysis of twelve critical domains where this tension is most acute. It examines the "Perishable Skills" that are eroding—such as manual clinical triage, agricultural intuition, and analog navigation—and evaluates the "Tech Assistance Layers" currently being deployed to augment them, ranging from AI diagnostic bots to satellite-guided precision farming. Crucially, it delineates the specific "Failure Risks" associated with the collapse of these technical layers and proposes robust "Replacement / Backup Strategies" that integrate community-led initiatives with resilient, appropriate technologies.The central thesis analysis is that resilience cannot be achieved solely through better hardware or smarter algorithms. True resilience requires a hybrid architecture: one that leverages High-Tech efficiency (AI, IoT, Microgrids) for routine operations but maintains a "warm backup" of Low-Tech, high-social-capital human systems (Peer Support, Seed Banks, Gravity-Fed Water) to prevent systemic collapse during High-Impact Low-Probability (HILP) events

title: Currency as a Phase System: Data Expansion, Monetary Abstraction, and the Structural Erosion of Trust

detail.title: Currency as a Phase System: Data Expansion, Monetary Abstraction, and the Structural Erosion of Trust
detail.abstract: Modern economic systems exhibit a recurring pattern: prolonged periods of apparent stability followed by abrupt and often disproportionate collapse. Conventional economic models struggle to explain this phenomenon because they focus on observable variables such as growth, liquidity, and information availability, while neglecting the structural role of trust. This paper proposes a phase-based framework in which currency evolves through increasing levels of abstraction-solid, liquid, and gas-each enabling expansion while progressively diluting trust density. As monetary systems abstract faster than verification mechanisms can scale, instability accumulates invisibly, masked by liquidity and data abundance. The core contribution of this work is the formalization of trust as a structural variable rather than a psychological or institutional byproduct. Collapse is reframed not as an event triggered by shocks, but as a threshold failure in representational coherence, occurring when trust falls below the minimum level required for shared belief in value. By introducing phase transitions, temporal compression, and a terminal "fire" state of rapid revaluation, the framework explains why modern crises appear sudden despite long gestation periods. The model is non-ideological, predictive in form rather than in dates, and applicable across fiat, asset-backed, and digital monetary regimes.

title: Structural Hysteresis and Priority Reversal in Hybrid Capital Instruments: A Forensic Analysis of Irreversible Trigger Events

detail.abstract: The advent of contemporary financial regulatory frameworks, such as Basel III and IFRS 9, has catalyzed the proliferation of highly complex Hybrid Capital Instruments. While these instruments exhibit distinct debt attributes and repayment seniority under normal market conditions, this study identifies an endogenous "Priority Reversal" mechanism within their contractual structures that activates only under specific regulatory or liquidity stress thresholds. This paper proposes a Binary Forensic Audit Model, designed to detect latent clauses that cause a divergence between "Nominal Priority" and "Effective Priority." We demonstrate that once specific covariance events are triggered, the reversal process exhibits thermodynamic Irreversibility, rendering post-event valuation recovery futile. Consequently, ex-ante structural audits must shift focus from yield optimization to "Seniority Rigidity" under stress scenarios.

title: Evaluating Data Center Power and Resilience at Scale: Physically Grounded Surrogates versus LLM-Based Inference
affiliations: Blend Tiger

detail.title: Evaluating Data Center Power and Resilience at Scale: Physically Grounded Surrogates versus LLM-Based Inference
detail.abstract: Rapid growth in data center capacity driven by cloud computing and artificial intelligence is pushing facility power demand, electricity consumption, and resilience requirements to scales that challenge both physical infrastructure and conventional evaluation methods. System-level planning of large data centers requires repeated evaluation of facility power, annual energy use, and long-duration backup requirements across wide parameter ranges, yet direct execution of deterministic techno-economic models becomes computationally expensive as scenario counts increase. At the same time, emerging approaches based on large language model (LLM) inference introduce substantial computational and energy overhead while lacking intrinsic enforcement of physical constraints. This paper develops a physically explicit deterministic kernel model for data center power demand, energy consumption, and long-duration resilience sizing, in which all relationships are encoded algebraically using first-principles scaling. A machine-learning surrogate is trained exclusively on synthetic data generated from this kernel to emulate the deterministic mapping at dramatically reduced computational cost. The surrogate preserves physical consistency by construction while enabling rapid evaluation across large scenario ensembles. The framework is benchmarked against direct kernel execution and LLM-based inference for the same evaluation task, with comparison focused on execution time, computational energy use, and physical fidelity rather than predictive intelligence. Results show that the surrogate reproduces kernel outputs with high accuracy across the full operating domain while reducing evaluation time and computational energy by orders of magnitude relative to both direct kernel execution and LLM-based inference. In contrast, LLM-based inference incurs substantially higher computing and energy cost and does not inherently enforce physical constraints. The analysis clarifies the conditions under which surrogate-accelerated, physically grounded modeling is preferable for large-scale data center system planning under sustained growth and long-duration resilience requirements.

title: Building Sustainable Competitive Advantage: An SDG-Aligned Strategic Framework for Oil & Gas EPC Firms Purpose

detail.abstract: The paper aims to develop a decision-oriented strategic framework that explains how oil and gas EPC firms can translate SDG commitments into consistent enterprise-level and project-level execution. It argues that persistent sustainability underperformance is not mainly a reporting or compliance issue, but a governance and decision-making challenge rooted in how strategic and operational trade-offs are made. The study reframes SDG integration as a decision architecture problem, positioning SDGs as decision criteria embedded within enterprise governance and execution routines. By integrating SDG priorities with GRI and ISSB standards, the paper seeks to explain how sustainability can shape decision-making and performance in project-based, highrisk environments. a diagnostic and governance blueprint for embedding sustainability into enterprise strategy and execution, thereby supporting sustainable competitive advantage.

title: Individual vs. Integrated Privatization of Complementary Airports under Air-Rail Competition
affiliations: Otaru University of Commerce,  and Hiroshima University - Economics

detail.title: Individual vs. Integrated Privatization of Complementary Airports under Air-Rail Competition
detail.abstract: This study investigates the strategic effects of airport privatization arising from competition with high-speed rail. It also compares the outcomes of the individual privatization of two complementary airports with those of their integrated privatization. We develop a model with two airports in distant regions, connected by two transport modes: air and high-speed rail. Three scenarios are analyzed: full nationalization, individual privatization, and integrated privatization. We find that when the degree of substitution between the two modes is moderate, airport privatization can enhance social welfare through strategic effects driven by competition with the railway, even in the absence of improvements in cost efficiency. Furthermore, we show that integrated privatization can enhance social welfare even when the degree of substitution is sufficiently low that individual privatization would reduce it.

title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Military Operations: Complicity, State Responsibility and Individual Criminal Responsibility under International Law
affiliations: University of Reading - School of Law

detail.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Military Operations: Complicity, State Responsibility and Individual Criminal Responsibility under International Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Caitlin Chiaramonte and Ashley Deeks (eds.), Artificial Intelligence and Multilateral Military Operations: Prospects and Challenges (Oxford University Press, forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines how AI systems employed in military operations can impact the law of state responsibility, especially the notion of attribution of conduct, and individual responsibility in international criminal law. States and individuals can incur responsibility under international law in a variety of scenarios involving AI systems in military operations. The development of an AI system can constitute an internationally wrongful act, for example, because the AI system is trained on data obtained in violation of the human right to privacy. The buying, selling, or otherwise transferring AI systems, or transferring data for the development or use of the AI system, can also be internationally wrongful. Finally, the use of the AI system can be wrongful. For instance, in the context of weapons or decision support systems, their use could result in attacks that are indiscriminate or fail to satisfy the requirement to take all feasible precautions.

In all of these contexts, states can be responsible for breaching a variety of rules coming from different branches of international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law. State responsibility can also exist concurrently with individual responsibility. The criminal responsibility of individuals is somewhat more circumscribed under international law than under domestic law, in that it generally requires higher levels of mens rea, such as intent and knowledge. But, at least in principle, AI systems can all be used to commit the four core crimes for which international law directly imposes responsibility on individuals, namely aggression, genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The scenarios that interest me the most here are those of complicity (broadly understood), which can be relevant both as a matter of state responsibility and as a matter of individual criminal responsibility. Before I can discuss complicity, however, I need to make a few more general points on AI, agency, personhood and intention. I then cover some preliminary questions under the law of state responsibility and under international criminal law, before focusing on complicity scenarios in more detail. My main argument is that existing international criminal law can adequately address challenges posed by AI, whether in perpetration or complicity-type scenarios. The law is technology-neutral, and can accommodate most new developments through reasonable interpretations that remain within the bounds of the legality principle. Where it matters the most, existing law does not require radical departures, reinvention or amendment – except with regard to the (possible, but uncertain) advent of AI systems which can be said to attain a level of independent personhood.

When it comes to criminal responsibility in particular, the problem of AI as an impenetrable “black box” does not necessarily make evidentiary inquiries fantastically more difficult. The situations that concern us the most from an accountability perspective are those in which violations of international law are committed systematically and at scale. In such situations, it will generally be possible to infer intent, or other types of fault, of the individuals concerned, be it with regard to the commission of wrongful acts or their facilitation. And if these individuals act on a state’s behalf, the conduct and the fault with which they acted can also be imputed to that state for the purpose of state responsibility.

To be clear, in arguing that existing law is adequate, I am not denying that the characteristics of AI development and use, in particular the unpredictability of outcomes in some cases, entail that in some cases their developers and operators could not be prosecuted internationally, since they would not possess the high mens rea required for criminal responsibility at the international level, especially at the International Criminal Court. But the same goes for many other situations, including the development and use of non-AI-enabled systems and weapons, all of which can result in mistakes and unintended outcomes. The responsibility or accountability gap, such as it is, really is not radically different when AI is added into the mix. That the existing law is good enough, and that AI is (at least not yet) a game changer in terms of attributing state and individual responsibility, are perhaps not the sexiest conclusions ever in selling a paper – but they are the right conclusions.

title: Authority-Mission Misalignment in Complex Innovation Systems

detail.abstract: Complex innovation systems frequently fail to deliver mission outcomes despite the availability of capital, technical competence, and formal governance. Conventional explanations attribute these failures to funding gaps, incentive misalignment, or cultural resistance. This paper advances a different diagnosis: execution failure often arises from a structural misalignment between authority cycles and mission cycles. Drawing on Regenerative Cycle Architecture (RCA), the paper introduces authority as a first-class architectural variable governing time-bounded commitment. Failure emerges when authority to commit resources operates on slower temporal cycles than mission viability windows, producing decision delay, fragmented accountability, and authority looping. The paper formalises this condition, identifies recurrent symptom clusters, and distinguishes authority from governance as commonly conflated constructs. The analysis is general and non-attributive, applying across public, quasi-public, and multi-stakeholder innovation systems. The contribution is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, providing a structural lens for identifying execution failure modes that persist despite aligned capital and intent.

title: Unlocking Households’ Flexibility Potential - on the Barriers to Real-Time Pricing

detail.title: Unlocking Households’ Flexibility Potential - on the Barriers to Real-Time Pricing
detail.abstract: Many countries intend to electrify most of their energy consumption in the near future, which can raise the flexibility of electricity consumption significantly. To unlock this flexibility potential, consumers require appropriate price signals, achieved through real-time pricing (RTP) contracts. Building on the stylized market model of Borenstein and Holland (2005), this paper identifies potential barriers to the adoption of RTP. We find substantial synergies between RTP and flexibility of consumption. As flexibility increases, so does the adoption of RTP. However, this relationship weakens if consumers' electricity bills are dominated by non-energy components such as grid fees, taxes, and retail markups. When these costs are substantial, RTP becomes less attractive and adoption remains limited.

title: SHIELD: A National Resilience Policy Framework Strategic Hub for Innovation, Economic Leadership and Development Author: ADJ Visoko Darvo Foundation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: SHIELD: A National Resilience Policy Framework Strategic Hub for Innovation, Economic Leadership and Development Author: ADJ Visoko Darvo Foundation
detail.abstract: This paper presents SHIELD, a conceptual framework for national resilience grounded in balance-sheet stewardship rather than sectoral policy design. Modern states possess substantial assets and institutional capacity yet increasingly struggle to convert these into durable resilience under conditions of persistent economic, technological, demographic, and geopolitical stress. The central problem is not absent sophistication-central banks, sovereign wealth funds, pension systems, and infrastructure banks already operate with balance-sheet logic-but fragmentation. These functions evolved in isolation, optimized for specific risks, and were never integrated into coherent national stewardship. Value generated from collectively enabled assets leaks, reinvestment becomes discretionary, and the dividends of growth appear unstable or unevenly distributed. SHIELD articulates governing principles for how assets may be recognized, how yield may be retained, how reinvestment may be disciplined, and how resilience may become visible and legitimate over time. The framework establishes a closed cycle: assets generate yield, participation retains value, reinvestment compounds capacity, and dividends anchor legitimacy. It includes institutional design principles for durability (mission-lock, anti-capture geometry, entropy resistance) and addresses implementation through worked examples and failure mode analysis. Unlike sectoral interventions or project-based policy, SHIELD provides integrating logic for how states compound existing capacity under permanent stress. The paper explicitly acknowledges that many implicated decisions-asset definition, participation mechanisms, reinvestment priorities-are inherently political. Its contribution lies in clarifying where such choices should be made deliberately and where discretion should be structurally constrained to prevent extraction, drift, and short-termism.

detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term impact of childhood exposure to Glacier Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) on adult human capital outcomes in the High Mountain Asia (HMA) region. Using historical GLOF data and geospatial mapping of downstream flood pathways, we identify treatment and control groups based on geographic proximity. Exposed children attain 1.4 to 1.7 fewer years of schooling and have a 1.9 to 2.2 kg/m² lower Body Mass Index (BMI) in adulthood compared to non-exposed children. Moreover, rural adolescents face greater educational losses, whereas urban residents experience more pronounced health impacts. Our findings provide valuable insights into the long-term costs of climate-induced disasters and underscore the need for targeted risk reduction strategies in vulnerable mountain communities.

title:
The Oversight Sentinel Doctrine 
A Systems Guide to Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Oversight Sentinel Doctrine 
A Systems Guide to Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness
detail.abstract:
Oversight failures in complex institutions rarely originate in isolated misconduct or discrete breakdowns. Instead, they emerge through gradual, often invisible misalignment between system design and system behavior—a process this paper describes as drift. Traditional oversight models, oriented toward retrospective detection and compliance verification, frequently arrive after this drift has matured into exposure, escalation, or failure.

This paper introduces the Oversight Sentinel Doctrine, a systems-based framework for understanding how organizations adapt under sustained pressure and why economy, efficiency, and effectiveness degrade long before failure becomes visible. Drawing on systems theory, organizational behavior, and applied oversight experience, the Doctrine reframes oversight as an interpretive and orienting function rather than a purely corrective one.

To support this orienting function, the doctrine employs what is referred to conceptually as the Sentinel Compass. The Compass is not a tool or metric, but a way of organizing attention—integrating system purpose, architectural conditions, observed adaptations, and emerging outcomes to assess directional movement rather than static performance. Its value lies in helping oversight recognize when systems are converging toward alignment or drifting away from it, even when surface indicators suggest stability.

The Oversight Sentinel Doctrine offers a unifying lens for Inspectors General and comparable oversight authorities across public, private, and hybrid environments, emphasizing foresight, alignment, and institutional stewardship over post hoc accountability. It contributes a structured vocabulary and conceptual architecture for diagnosing drift, preserving oversight authority, and strengthening institutional resilience in complex systems.

title: Mandatory Sustainability (ISSB) Reporting: Early Evidence from Türkiye
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School, , London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: Mandatory Sustainability (ISSB) Reporting: Early Evidence from Türkiye
detail.abstract: This paper provides evidence on mandatory sustainability reporting. We exploit the introduction of IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 in Türkiye, which incorporated the standards into domestic law without material modification and mandated their application for public issuers beginning in 2024. We document issuers' initial reporting practices in the first year of mandatory adoption. We find a high degree of formal compliance with the new standards, but substantial heterogeneity in key reporting choices, including materiality approaches, climate scenario selection, emissions measurement boundaries, and base year and target year in carbon emission reduction plans. These differences arise due to the flexibility offered by the standards. Our findings raise questions about the extent to which flexibility in ISSB standards may limit cross-firm comparability, at least in early adoption periods.

title: Evidence on Firm-to-Firm R&D Collaboration Intensity

detail.title: Evidence on Firm-to-Firm R&D Collaboration Intensity
detail.abstract: Firm-to-firm R&D collaborations have become increasingly common, and firms have been assigning more inventors to these collaborative projects. Despite this trend, existing research on collaboration subsidies has mainly focused on the existence of collaborations rather than their intensity. In this paper, I develop a model in which firms jointly choose their R&D collaborators, the intensity of each collaboration, and their R&D investment. Accounting for heterogeneity in intensity is central to the optimal subsidy design. Using U.S. patent and accounting data, I find that increasing collaboration intensity from below-median to above-median raises collaboration costs by 23% but increases benefits from technological complementarities by more than twelvefold. Counterfactual analysis shows that, under a constrained government budget of less than $26 billion, targeting high-intensity collaborations is more cost-effective than subsidizing all collaborations uniformly. Although targeting high-intensity collaborations increases network congestion and attracts less R&D-efficient firms, it accelerates technological complementarities.

detail.abstract: This preprint concludes the "Economic Security Guarantees" series published in SSRN in December 2025-January 2026, and represents the final element in a series of developed economic and financial mechanisms for preventing armed conflict. This paper examines Surprise Attack Bonds (SABs) as an underlying asset for constructing derivative financial instruments designed to deter armed aggression during periods of rising political tension and prewar uncertainty. It is shown that combining SABs with options mechanisms-including mutual placement, swap, and cross-collateralization schemes-transforms political risk into an endogenous market variable, altering the structure of expected losses for both parties and rendering preemptive aggression economically irrational, regardless of the subjective interpretations of the adversary's intentions. We propose a model of an exotic barrier option with a cross-trigger, whereby a decline in the SAB price of one party following a confirmed act of aggression automatically activates the right to redistribute property claims under the obligations of the other party to the agreement. This "option barrier" enhances the disciplinary effect of SABs, reduces the requirements for their par value, and creates an automatic, depoliticized mechanism for enforcing peace agreements. Derivatives within the proposed framework embed mechanisms for enforcing international treaties directly into the global financial architecture, creating a new level of economic deterrence that goes beyond classic sanctions regimes and traditional security guarantees.

title: Consumer Social Responsibility in Experimental Markets with(out) Sellers
affiliations: Leuphana University of Lueneburg and Leuphana University of Lueneburg

detail.title: Consumer Social Responsibility in Experimental Markets with(out) Sellers

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study obtained ethics approval from the Ethical Review Board of the German Association for Experimental Economic Research e.V. (Institutional Review Board Certificate No. UnC9jn1X).

detail.abstract: We make a methodological contribution to the experimental study of socially responsible consumer behavior by examining whether the presence of sellers is essential to identify the drivers of this behavior. Our experiment compares buyer choices in two main treatments: (i) a baseline with sellers who choose product type (socially responsible or harmful) and price; (ii) a treatment without sellers in which buyers face the same offers as in the baseline, predefined rather than chosen by sellers. Buyer behavior proves strikingly stable across treatments. The probability of buying the socially responsible product or abstaining from consumption does not differ significantly between markets with and without sellers. Instead, market prices emerge as the dominant driver of buyer behavior. While full market designs involving sellers remain indispensable to study market dynamics and buyer-seller interactions, our findings suggest that simplified seller-free designs can validly capture the socially responsible dimension of consumer behavior. This design preserves key strengths of classic market experiments (real economic incentives, controlled moral trade-offs), while avoiding the hypothetical bias common in survey-based methods (e.g., contingent valuation).

title: Who Should Control Government Information?

detail.title: Who Should Control Government Information?
detail.abstract: This Article argues that the high risk of politically driven manipulation of data collected by agencies within the executive branch—combined with the Supreme Court’s growing embrace of the Unitary Executive Theory—undermines the credibility of federal data and weakens Congress’s institutional capacity.  It proposes moving the government’s core statistical functions currently located in the executive branch to congressional statistical agencies insulated by bipartisan appointment and removal, fixed terms, and professional standards.  The Article demonstrates that shifting these functions to congressional statistical agencies would improve data availability and accuracy, increase public trust, and strengthen Congress’s capacity.  Furthermore, the Article explains that moving statistical agencies to Congress is consistent with actions taken by Congress in the past, that it can be implemented without violating the Constitution’s separation of powers, and that it would be politically feasible.

title: Heat Shocks and Labor Market Dynamics: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: and World Bank

detail.title: Heat Shocks and Labor Market Dynamics: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effects of extreme heat on formal establishments in Brazil, leveraging high-resolution climate reanalysis data combined with comprehensive employer-employee administrative records covering the universe of formal establishments over two decades (2000-2019). Using a fixed-effects panel specification for short-run analysis and a long-differences approach for medium-run effects, we find that aggregate responses to heat shocks mask substantial heterogeneity across productivity levels. In the short run, additional days of extreme heat increase the probability of exit among low-productivity establishments while high-productivity establishments expand employment and exhibit greater resilience. These redistributive patterns are particularly pronounced in agriculture and manufacturing, where direct impacts on output and labor productivity are more salient. In the medium run, municipalities experiencing larger increases in heat days witness a decline in the entry of high-productivity establishments without a corresponding reduction in the low-productivity ones. These findings suggest that climate change may reshape the establishment distribution by accelerating the exit of less productive plants while simultaneously discouraging the creation of more productive ones, with potential implications for aggregate productivity growth in emerging economies.

title: Structural-State Mathematical Economics
affiliations: and Suzhou Goldennanox Research Institute

detail.title: Structural-State Mathematical Economics
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a Structural-State Mathematical Economics framework for stockmarket research. Its central claim is simple but consequential: the primary object of modeling should not be prices, returns, or isolated indicators, but rather a structure system jointly determined by multiple structural dimensions and their intrinsic constraints. Within this view, a stock market is represented as the structure object S stock = (D, F, R, Φ), where D denotes the set of structural dimensions-quality, growth, valuation, trend, momentum, volatility, volume-price, and macro constraints. The library R collects intrinsic cross-dimensional constraints, Ω ⊂ ∏ d∈D X d is the feasible set of admissible structural states induced by these constraints, and Φ is a manifestation operator that maps structural states to observable market outcomes (e.g., trend manifestation and regime-shift risk). Accordingly, a market state is defined as an admissible configuration (a structural state), and market dynamics are interpreted as transitions in a constrained state space, including boundary reconstructions when feasibility shrinks or constraints are reshaped. This unified language allows us to characterize structural consistency, structural mismatch, and structural collapse, while clarifying the hierarchy between price signals and structural causes. Our contribution is methodological and representational rather than predictive. We do not aim to deliver a trading strategy or to improve forecasting accuracy. Instead, we provide an extensible structure-first representation that diagnoses the structural changes behind model breakdowns and supplies structural priors and applicability boundaries for factor models, technical analysis, and machine-learning approaches. As an illustrative application, we use NVDA as a case study to describe its structural-state path under the coupling of technology cycles, expectation expansion, and macro constraints. The case demonstrates how the structural-state framework can explain phase stability, rising tension, mismatch manifestation, and the subsequent divergence into repair versus collapse, without relying on heavy econometric regressions.

title: Modeling Observation Lens in Co-Occurrence Network Analysis: Four Window Approaches and Implementations
affiliations: FernUniversitat in Hagen, University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne, University of Eastern Finland and University of Eastern Finland

detail.title: Modeling Observation Lens in Co-Occurrence Network Analysis: Four Window Approaches and Implementations

publicationDetails.detailsText: Transition Network Analysis Workshop, April 27-28, 2026, 16th International Conference on Learning Analytics & Knowledge (LAK), Bergen, Norway

detail.abstract: Modeling how collaboration unfolds in digital learning environments requires analytical approaches that account for both temporal structure and the local organization of learner actions. Co-occurrence Network Analysis (CNA) offers a flexible framework for representing these relationships; however, the choice of co-occurrence window remains an under-examined methodological decision with substantial interpretive consequences. We present a systematic comparison of four window implementations: single-message, multi-message, fixed-duration, and duration-gap. Using two simulated datasets that represent synchronous (dense) and asynchronous (sparse) collaboration patterns, we examine how each window approach shapes the resulting network structures, including co-occurrence patterns, self-connections, cross-actor links, and their sensitivity to different temporal dynamics. Our findings underscore that defining the co-occurrence window is not a neutral pre-processing step but a central modeling decision that directly shapes the interpretation and conceptualization of collaborative processes.

title: Separation of Powers or Division of Labor? Patent Interference Disputes, the Grand Narrative, and the History of the Administrative State, 1790-1940
affiliations: and

detail.title: Separation of Powers or Division of Labor? Patent Interference Disputes, the Grand Narrative, and the History of the Administrative State, 1790-1940
detail.abstract: We use the history of the Patent Office to challenge the Grand Narrative of separation of powers that the current Supreme Court is using to invalidate congressional designs for administrative agencies.  Focusing on the adjudication of patent interference disputes—cases in which two or more inventors applied for patents for essentially the same technology—we find that the division of labor between the Patent Office and the courts shifted repeatedly and dramatically over the century and a half preceding the Administrative Procedure Act.  Rather than worries about separation of powers, the main drivers of change were (1) the Patent Office’s efforts to curb inventors’ exploitation of interference procedures to delay the award of patents to rivals and (2) the need to manage the workload that interference appeals imposed on the overburdened Patent Office and courts.  Innovations in Patent Office procedures led to dramatic improvements in the efficiency of its frontline adjudication of interferences, but officials found it much more difficult to prevent losing parties from abusing appeals opportunistically.  At the behest of the Patent Office, Congress repeatedly revised the appeals process for interferences, trying out direct review by ad hoc arbitration panels, individual judges, and variously constituted courts.  It even eliminated direct appeals of interference decisions from 1870 until 1893, while continuing to provide for appeals from rejections of patent applications (where opportunistic delays posed less serious problems).  Although interference parties sometimes raised legal challenges to these review structures, they reached a dead end in the Supreme Court, which throughout the nineteenth century deferred to Congress’s authority to design the system.  Finally, in 1939, after a century of trial and error, the Patent Office convinced Congress to eliminate all internal appeals in interference cases within the Patent Office, to authorize the Patent Office to issue patents based on its frontline adjudications of priority, and to shift review of interference decisions entirely to the courts.  Again, this change did not apply to rejections of patent applications, which were still reviewed internally before they could be appealed to the courts. Both the great variety of appeal structures enacted over the years and the repeated divergence in the treatment of appeals of interferences and rejections support our emphasis on the primary role that pragmatic concerns played in the evolving division of labor between the Patent Office and the courts. This history reveals flexible adaptation over time rather than conformity to a standard model of separation of powers traceable to the framers.

title: Agile Democracy

detail.title: Agile Democracy

detail.abstract: Agile Democracy is presented as a governance architecture addressing temporal misalignment between policy decision cycles and the emergence of downstream social impacts. In many institutional settings, policy evaluation occurs under conditions where the observable consequences of prior decisions have not yet stabilized, leading to evaluative feedback that is structurally premature or disconnected from the policy’s intended time horizon. This document renders explicit a configuration in which decision-making, evaluation, and impact realization operate on partially asynchronous temporal layers. Under such conditions, policy performance cannot be reliably inferred from contemporaneous indicators, and revision cycles risk optimizing for short-term evaluability rather than long-term system stability. Agile Democracy introduces revisability as an architectural condition for governance systems operating in environments characterized by delayed observability and distributed policy effects. Rather than proposing specific institutional reforms, this document frames revisability as a structural property enabling decision systems to maintain adaptive coherence under temporal uncertainty. This definition is intended as a conceptual rendering of governance configurations under delayed-feedback conditions and does not prescribe implementation strategies or institutional arrangements.

detail.abstract: Researchers typically collect experimental data sequentially, allowing early outcome observations and adaptive treatment assignment to reduce exposure to inferior treatments. This article reviews multi-armed-bandit adaptive experimental designs that balance exploration and exploitation. Because adaptively collected experimental data through bandit algorithms violate standard asymptotics, inference is challenging. We implement an estimator that yields valid heteroskedasticity-robust confidence intervals in batched bandit designs and compare coverage in Monte Carlo simulations. We introduce bbandits for Stata, a tool for designing experiments via simulation, running interactive bandit experiments, and implementing and analyzing adaptively collected data. bbandits includes three common assignment algorithms-ε-first, ε-greedy, and Thompson sampling-and supports estimation, inference, and visualization.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series No. 3, 2021
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this paper, we use new survey data on the Irish SME population to trace out the impact of the pandemic on revenues, firms' capacity to adjust their cost base and their usage of policy supports. Over 70 per cent of firms experienced some fall in turnover with a median fall of 25 per cent. The impact of the shock appears uncorrelated with past firm performance which highlights its exogenous nature. Expenditure fell by 8.5 per cent on average with 40 per cent of firms cutting spending. Losses were incurred in over 30 per cent of enterprises with a further 30 per cent just breaking even. We find that about 61 per cent of SMEs received wage subsidies, 20 per cent of firms used tax warehousing while fewer than 6 per cent of firms used lending initiatives. Policy support take-up is more likely among those more affected by the downturn, while the smallest firms appear less likely to use support than larger firms.

title: Policy Brief: The OCC's Unlawful Proposal to Preempt State Interest-on-Escrow Laws Reveals That the Agency's Ultimate Goal Is to Revive Its Illegal De Facto Field Preemption Regime for National Banks
affiliations: George Washington University Law School

detail.title: Policy Brief: The OCC's Unlawful Proposal to Preempt State Interest-on-Escrow Laws Reveals That the Agency's Ultimate Goal Is to Revive Its Illegal De Facto Field Preemption Regime for National Banks

keywords: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-17
publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Law School Public Law Research Paper No. 2026-17
publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In December 2025, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (“OCC”) issued a proposal to preempt all state laws that require national banks and federal savings associations to pay interest on borrowers’ funds held in mortgage escrow accounts. The OCC’s proposal is unlawful and must be rescinded. Under 12 U.S.C. § 25b and the Supreme Court’s decisions in Cuomo v. Clearing House and Cantero v. Bank of America, the OCC does not have authority to preempt state interest-on-escrow (IOE) laws.

The OCC’s proposal for a categorical, across-the-board preemption of state IOE laws violates three requirements set forth in 12 U.S.C. § 25b. First, the OCC’s proposal violates § 25b’s governing preemption standard, which provides that a state consumer financial law can be preempted “only if” that state law “prevents or significantly interferes with the exercise by a national bank of its powers.” A careful analysis of state IOE laws demonstrates that they do not prevent or significantly interfere with the exercise of any national bank power. The OCC’s proposed categorical preemption of state IOE laws also contravenes provisions in § 25b that require the OCC to proceed on a “case-by-case basis” and to support its findings of preemption with “substantial evidence, made on the record of the proceeding.”

The potential implications of the OCC’s proposal extend far beyond state IOE laws.  The aggressive preemption claims advanced in the OCC’s proposal indicate that the agency’s ultimate goal is to revive its discredited regime of de facto field preemption for national banks.  The OCC created that illegal regime by issuing blanket preemption rules in 2004.  In 2010, Congress repudiated the OCC’s 2004 preemption rules by adopting § 25b, after determining that the OCC’s rules contributed to the severity of the financial crisis of 2007-09.  Similarly, the Supreme Court rejected the OCC’s field preemption rationale for its 2004 rules in Cuomo and Cantero.  Despite those setbacks, the OCC’s proposal to override state IOE laws continues to assert an unbounded power to preempt state consumer protection laws, and the proposal ignores the limitations imposed on the OCC’s preemption authority by Congress and the Supreme Court.

Based on its past record, the OCC will probably use its proposal as a launching pad for a larger campaign to revive its discredited de facto field preemption regime. Such a regime would heavily favor large multistate national banks, which provide most of the funding for the OCC’s budget and are its most influential regulated constituents. The OCC has frequently tried to expand the powers and privileges of national banks beyond their statutory limits, and the OCC has also refused to comply with judicial decisions upholding those limits. Accordingly, federal courts and Congress must be prepared once again to rein in the OCC and preserve the states’ authority to protect their consumers, businesses, and communities under 12 U.S.C. § 25b.

title: Unveiling Women’s Crucial Role in Africa’s Development: An Introduction
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University

detail.title: Unveiling Women’s Crucial Role in Africa’s Development: An Introduction
detail.abstract: This introductory chapter establishes the conceptual and thematic foundation for Women in Africa’s Development: In Memory of Prof Alice Ndu by foregrounding African women as central, rather than peripheral, actors in the continent’s development trajectory. It challenges dominant historical and policy narratives that marginalise women’s contributions, and instead repositions women as architects of social, economic, educational, and institutional transformation across Africa. Drawing on evocative contextual narratives and an integrative overview of the volume, the chapter maps how women’s agency manifests in diverse spaces—ranging from households, markets, and communities to education systems, leadership structures, entrepreneurship, health, law, communication, and faith-based institutions. The chapter further situates the volume within a broader intellectual and moral project by honouring the life and legacy of Professor Alice Ndu, whose academic leadership, commitment to education, and advocacy for women’s empowerment exemplify the ideals explored throughout the book. By synthesising the contributions of subsequent chapters, this introduction provides a coherent analytical lens through which women’s roles in Africa’s development are examined as systemic, intergenerational, and transformative. The chapter concludes by framing women’s empowerment not as a sectoral concern, but as a foundational imperative for sustainable and inclusive development in Africa.

title: A Citizen Killed, Minneapolis Occupied: Death of Urban Trust
affiliations: Catholic Theological Union, Chicago

detail.title: A Citizen Killed, Minneapolis Occupied: Death of Urban Trust
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the erosion of urban trust through the lens of a fatal federal immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis in January 2026. The killing of Renee Nicole Good during an ICE operation is analyzed not merely as an isolated security failure, but as a structural rupture in the moral and spatial foundations of the modern city. Drawing on urban theory, spatial justice, and the concept of the “right to the city,” the study argues that when federal security logics—borrowed from border enforcement and counterinsurgency—are imposed on everyday urban life, the city ceases to function as a space of civic coexistence. Streets transform from shared social infrastructure into zones of fear, suspicion, and coercion, undermining the tacit social contract that allows strangers to live together without constant threat.

The paper further contends that militarized federal interventions in local urban space represent a form of internal occupation that bypasses local governance, weakens municipal autonomy, and fractures community trust. By analyzing the spatial consequences of concepts such as “reasonable suspicion,” racialized surveillance, and the collapse of consensual encounters in public space, the study highlights how security policies can actively produce urban insecurity. Ultimately, the article calls for a re-centering of human dignity, locality, and civic trust in urban governance, arguing that genuinely safe cities are not built through force and domination, but through justice-oriented, human-centric approaches to security and urban design.

title: Reconciling Economic Growth With Environmental Sustainability in BRICS: Panel Econometric Evidence on the Environmental Kuznets Curve
affiliations: HSE University, Nizhny Novgorod, Russia

detail.title: Reconciling Economic Growth With Environmental Sustainability in BRICS: Panel Econometric Evidence on the Environmental Kuznets Curve
detail.abstract: This study examines the interplay between economic growth and environmental sustainability in the enlarged BRICS economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Iran, Indonesia, and the United Arab Emirates), focusing on the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis amid rising CO₂ emissions. By integrating trade openness, natural resource rents, sectoral value-added, renewable energy consumption, and foreign direct investment (FDI) into a unified framework, it addresses gaps in fragmented analyses. Utilizing annual panel data from 2000 to 2024, the research employs a robust multi-method approach, including pooled OLS with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, fixed effects, first-difference, GMMstyle IV, and random effects GLS estimators. Findings robustly validate the EKC, revealing an inverted U-shaped relationship with a turning point at approximately $15,134 (constant 2015 USD), indicating most BRICS nations remain in the emissionsrising phase. Trade openness exacerbates emissions, supporting the pollution haven hypothesis, while renewable energy consistently mitigates them. Natural resource rents offer conditional mitigation, sectoral effects vary, and FDI shows no significant impact. Policy implications emphasize channeling resource rents into green investments, embedding environmental clauses in trade agreements, and accelerating renewables to align with Sustainable Development Goals, fostering equitable global climate governance.
