detail.abstract: Classical decision theory relies on the Nash Equilibrium (NE) for strategic stability. This paper argues that NE is insufficient for autonomous systems as it ensures stability in Decision Space (DS) but ignores the coherence of the underlying Meaning Space (MS). We introduce "Semantic Physics" to measure Semantic Instability using the Semantic Gap (SG) and Interpretive Synchrony (IS). We propose Semantic Equilibrium as a necessary condition for robust AI, illustrating how "Hollow Equilibria" lead to systemic failures.

title: The Transparency Trap: Quality of Public Information and the Intensity of Revolutionary Violence

detail.title: The Transparency Trap: Quality of Public Information and the Intensity of Revolutionary Violence

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 570
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management & Statistics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework to study how the quality of public information shapes the intensity of revolt in global games of regime change. Building on the canonical literature, I model citizens deciding whether to attack a regime where intensity determines both effectiveness and failure costs. I extend the framework by endogenizing total conflict intensity through the strategic interaction of vanguard groups seeking to maximize the potential of the attack, and including the regime's response. The analysis reveals a non-monotonic "transparency trap": at intermediate beliefs, the relationship between information quality and total violence becomes Ushaped. Intensity is high when information is scarce (serving as a substitute coordination device), minimizes at intermediate levels, and surges again when high transparency facilitates violent coordination. These dynamics persist when intensity is the outcome of decentralized strategic choice. Moreover, as the number of competing vanguard groups increases, so does the equilibrium intensity. I empirically test these predictions drawing 177 events from the Revolutionary Episodes dataset (1900-2014), combined with historical Freedom of Expression indices. The results provide robust support for the U-shaped hypothesis and confirm that higher vanguard competition structurally escalates conflict. These findings highlight that transparency reforms can have counterintuitive effects, providing relevant policy implications.

title: Time in Residence and Entitlement to Resources: A Neglected Dimension of Migration Politics
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Time in Residence and Entitlement to Resources: A Neglected Dimension of Migration Politics

declarations.funderStatement: The data used in this work come from the Civic Health and Institutions Project (chip50.org). The funders and the principal investigators of the CHIP50 Project bear no responsibility for the analyses reported here or the content of the work.

detail.abstract: Do people favor the long-time residents of a place over newer arrivals—even if the context is not international migration? Public opinion on immigration can only partially illuminate favoritism based on time-in-residence because access to residence is controlled via nationality. I turn to domestic mobility in the US to investigate whether US adults value residence independent of shared nationality or ethno-racial identity. Respondents split a college scholarship pool between hypothetical US citizens, whose profiles varied in terms of the duration of their in-state residence and race/ethnicity. Respondents favor in-state students over out-of-state students and, among in-state students, favor those who have been in-residence longest. Pro-resident discrimination appears across every ethno-racial and ideological sub-group. Respondents rewarded racial out-groups for longer residence even at the expense of students from their own race. Favoritism toward residents of one’s own state was present regardless of respondents’ own domestic migration history, feelings of closeness to their state, or affinity for the US. In-state favoritism is strongly related to opinions about immigration. People who wanted large cuts to immigration were also the most biased in favor of longtime residents of their state over Americans from elsewhere. Theories of migration politics should incorporate the belief that time-in-residence creates entitlement, a dynamic that is not reducible to well-known biases favoring co-nationals and co-ethnics.

title: Open Code, Unequal Access: How Complementary Skills and Local Talent Shape Responses to Open-Source Releases
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and

detail.title: Open Code, Unequal Access: How Complementary Skills and Local Talent Shape Responses to Open-Source Releases
detail.abstract: While open-source technologies lower the cost of accessing advanced tools, it remains unclear which establishments are particularly likely to act on these opportunities. Such cost reductions could democratize investment by making it easier for less-endowed establishments to find and invest in technology-related human capital or instead amplify existing advantages if establishments with complementary capabilities or in talent-rich markets are best positioned to respond. We study how U.S. high-tech establishments responded to Google's unexpected open-source release of TensorFlow, which sharply reduced the cost of acquiring AI-related skills. Using data from Revelio Labs and a matched difference-indifferences design, we show that establishments with complementary skills and those in talent-rich labor markets increased AI human-capital investments the most following the open-source release of TensorFlow. These factors also shaped how establishments invested in AI human capital, with complementary skills associated with internal redeployment and external hiring, and local talent driving external hiring alone. The findings reveal that while open sourcing enables widespread access to advanced tools, it does not necessarily democratize establishments' investment in them.

title: RECLAIM Framework and the Evolution of Mine Closure Policy in India: A Community-Centric Framework for Just and Sustainable Transition
affiliations: Coal India Limited

detail.title: RECLAIM Framework and the Evolution of Mine Closure Policy in India: A Community-Centric Framework for Just and Sustainable Transition
detail.abstract: Mine closure has long been treated as a technical and environmental compliance exercise, often overlooking its socioeconomic consequences for mining-dependent communities. In India, the introduction of the RECLAIM framework in 2025 marks a significant shift in mine closure governance by embedding principles of community participation, livelihood transition, and ecological regeneration into closure planning. Developed by the Coal Controller Organisation in collaboration with the Heartfulness Institute and launched by the Union Minister for Coal, RECLAIM aligns with the revised Mine Closure Guidelines (2025) for coal and lignite blocks. This paper examines the genesis of mine closure policy in India, analyses the conceptual framework and components of RECLAIM, and evaluates its integration with Progressive and Final Mine Closure Plans. The study argues that RECLAIM represents a paradigm shift from reclamation-oriented closure towards a holistic, peoplecentric and just transition model capable of fostering long-term socioeconomic resilience and environmental sustainability in mining-affected regions.

title: When Time Is Local: γ-Space and the Structural Universality of Temporal Coordination
affiliations: School of Economics and Management of the University of Bologna

detail.title: When Time Is Local: γ-Space and the Structural Universality of Temporal Coordination

detail.abstract: Time is often treated as a universal parameter: a single magnitude against which events can be compared, coordinated, and evaluated across different domains. In practice, however, every temporal instant we ever access is obtained through a concrete act of measurement, by a clock, a device, or a process, along a specific trajectory. Such an instant is therefore unavoidably local. The difficulty is not that local measurements exist, but that they are routinely taken to represent a universal temporal order without further justification. This paper addresses this tension by clarifying the status of local time and its relation to temporal universality. Rather than proposing a new physical theory of time, it develops an epistemological framework in which local time is understood as the observable realization of an underlying coordination structure. The central proposal is γ-space: a non-Euclidean, non-temporal space of admissible coordination relations that governs how locally measured temporal instants can be related to one another. γ-space itself is not directly observable. What we observe instead are its local realizations: the times measured by clocks, which appear as projections of this deeper structure. Within this framework, temporal universality does not consist in a shared temporal value, but in the stability of the coordination structure that constrains how local temporal measurements can be meaningfully compared. The paper illustrates the relevance of this perspective through an application to health economics and policy, where time-based metrics often fail to reflect heterogeneous biological and clinical trajectories. By making explicit the structural conditions under which temporal coordination is achieved, the γ-framework provides a foundation for rethinking temporal measurement, interpretation, and decision-making across scientific domains.

title: Intellectual Property, Personality, and Misrepresentation
affiliations: University of Washington - The Information School

detail.title: Intellectual Property, Personality, and Misrepresentation
detail.abstract: Incentives-based utilitarian arguments justify intellectual property rights as tools to bring about good consequences. By promising and protecting various rights, institutions of intellectual property-copyright, patent, trade secret-incentivize authors and inventors to create new and useful intellectual works. This innovation, in turn, leads to higher levels of health and wellbeing for everyone. 1 A second kind of justification offered for intellectual property is the natural rights tradition championed by John Locke. In general, the intuition is that laboring, producing, thinking, and persevering are voluntary, and individuals who engage in these activities are entitled to what they produce. Subject to certain restrictions, rights are generated when individuals mix their labor with unowned objects or when they create new intellectual works. 2 * I would like to thank

title: Political economy of bank insolvency: instability and social reaction to financial collapse

detail.title: Political economy of bank insolvency: instability and social reaction to financial collapse
detail.abstract: This paper examines bank insolvency from a political economy perspective, showing that its dynamics do not depend only on economic variables, but also on the institutional architecture that defines who decides, who bears the costs, and how uncertainty is distributed in society. The analysis proposes an integrated reading of bankruptcy law-aimed at the protection of credit-and banking law-focused on financial stability and the protection of depositors-, highlighting how both regimes overlap and condition each other in crisis contexts. It is argued that this convergence is essential to understanding the specificity of bank failures and constitutes a decisive component of economic policy, influencing the state's ability to prevent instabilities, manage the social costs of collapse, and preserve confidence in the financial system.

title: The 'Japa' Syndrome And It's Effect On National Economy: The Way Forward
affiliations: University of Ibadan, Ibadan, Nigeria

detail.title: The 'Japa' Syndrome And It's Effect On National Economy: The Way Forward
detail.abstract: Emigration is an occurrence that is inevitable in all nations of the world. Many nations have their citizens constantly leaving and citizens from other nations coming in. This paper addresses the nuances of this normal emigration occurrences and emigration in Nigeria. In Nigeria, the rate at which young people leave the country has attracted the attention of nationalists, economists and analysts. This mass migration nicknamed the "japa syndrome" is caused majorly by push factors from Nigeria which includes poor economic conditions, inflation, high cost of living and low standard of living, insecurity, corruption, unemployment/underemployment, poor working conditions, etc. The japa syndrome has since had a number of negative effects on the economy of Nigeria including the risk of brain drain. This paper highlights the effects which the japa syndrome has had on the national economy. It goes ahead to suggest the way forward by first drawing insight from China and how it overcame its brain drain, it then makes some recommendations that are Nigeria-focused. The recommendations are drawn from a study which shows that the government's focus on the educational sector and the health sector would go a long way in reducing the rate at which human capital leave to other nations in search of greener pastures.

title: Regional Heterogeneity in Environmental Responses to a Macroeconomic Shock: Evidence from China's 2008 Stimulus
affiliations: and Beijing Normal University - Zhuhai Campus

detail.title: Regional Heterogeneity in Environmental Responses to a Macroeconomic Shock: Evidence from China's 2008 Stimulus
detail.abstract: This study examines the heterogeneous environmental consequences of China's 2008 four-trillion RMB economic stimulus package across provinces with differing industrial structures. Using a rigorous difference-in-differences (DID) design with dynamic event-study specifications and comprehensive parallel trends validation (including graphical analysis, placebo tests, and Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator robustness), we analyze a balanced provincial-level panel dataset spanning 1997–2022, covering all 31 Chinese provinces (806 province-year observations). Provinces are classified as "high-industry" (treatment) or "low-industry" (control) based on pre-2008 CO2 emission intensity. The analysis yields three key findings. First, the stimulus drove a substantial aggregate increase in CO2 emissions across all provinces (73.2–82.5% higher post-stimulus, p < 0.001), consistent with scale effects from expanded economic activity. Second, high-industry provinces exhibited gradually improving relative environmental performance, with significant divergence emerging only after nine years and peaking at an 11.3% reduction relative to expected trends (p = 0.006). Third, effects were substantially larger and more significant in coastal provinces (-2.8%, p = 0.027) than inland, highlighting the moderating role of regional institutional and technological capabilities. These temporally dynamic and spatially heterogeneous outcomes demonstrate that large-scale fiscal interventions can produce complex environmental footprints. The study contributes to debates on the Environmental Kuznets Curve and Porter's Hypothesis, while offering policy insights for designing more sustainable and equitable stimulus measures. Extensive robustness checks, including alternative treatment definitions, placebo tests, subsample analyses, and mediation tests, affirm the validity of our causal estimates.

title: Stakeholder Perceptions of the Impacts of Fish Stock Collapse in Lake Victoria: Insights into Mental Models
affiliations: Tanzania Fisheries Research Institute, Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute, National Fisheries Resources Research Institute, Tanzania Fisheries Research Institute, Tanzania Fisheries Research Institute, Tanzania Fisheries Research Institute, Tanzania Fisheries Research Institute and Utrecht University

detail.title: Stakeholder Perceptions of the Impacts of Fish Stock Collapse in Lake Victoria: Insights into Mental Models
detail.abstract: Fishery resources support millions of people However, in recent years, fishers perceive that the stocks are declining. Perceptions about changes are vital as they shape behaviour, compliance and support for management interventions. Although previous studies have documented the ecological and economic drivers of stock change, little is known about how local stakeholders view and conceptualize its consequences. This study employed a mental models approach to investigate how stakeholders anticipate and interpret the impacts of a potential Nile perch fishery collapse in Lake Victoria. Data was collected using structured surveys via Kobo Toolbox and mental mapping via M-Tool with participants including boat owners, fish traders/processors, law enforcers and researchers in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. The survey questionnaire included questions on demographics, conservation perceptions, and adaptation strategies. The findings show that (1) stakeholders expect a potential collapse to result in poverty, livelihood loss and food insecurity, (2) many perceive current conservation measures as ineffective, and (3) adaptation preferences vary by country, with Tanzanians prioritizing training and technical support while Ugandans and Kenyans emphasizing financial assistance. These findings point to poverty and socioeconomic vulnerability as the main perceived outcomes of the potential Nile perch collapse, highlighting the need for inclusive and context-specific management strategies.  Beyond Lake Victoria, this study shows how mental models can illuminate connection between perceptions and conservation behaviour, offering understandings for theory and practice in fisheries governance more broadly.

detail.abstract: We provide a systematic and bibliometric synthesis of research at the intersection of deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), and portfolio optimization. Using a transparent Scopus-based search strategy and a twostage screening protocol, we construct a curated dataset of 329 peer-reviewed journal articles (up to 07/08/2024). We combine descriptive statistics with bibliometric maps (keyword co-occurrence, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling) and a manual taxonomy that labels each study by (i) problem focus (forecasting, portfolio optimization, or hybrid), (ii) DL architecture, and (iii) RL/DRL algorithmic family. Results reveal a consistent division of labour: DL is predominantly employed for forecasting market variables (returns, volatility, correlations), whereas RL/DRL is mainly used for direct sequential allocation and tradingstyle formulations. Across DRL papers, generic feedforward networks dominate, while LSTM/CNN architectures are prevalent in forecasting-driven studies. Despite rapid growth after 2017, we identify persistent gaps in (a) long-horizon, institutionally relevant objectives (e.g., pension/ALM/endowment problems), (b) standardised benchmarks and reproducible protocols, and (c) robustness and interpretability required in regulated settings. We conclude by outlining a research agenda connecting stochastic-control structure with modern RL, with a particular emphasis on long-term portfolio design.

title: Cognitive Infrastructure and the Integrity of Attention: A Protocol for Truth-Preserving Sponsored Visibility (TPSV) in the Agentic Economy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Cognitive Infrastructure and the Integrity of Attention: A Protocol for Truth-Preserving Sponsored Visibility (TPSV) in the Agentic Economy
detail.abstract: Truth-Preserving Sponsored Visibility (TPSV) is a mechanism design and software architecture proposal for funding high-cost, agentic AI services without distorting recommendations. It responds to two converging pressures: (a) the expansion of consumption-based pricing in software and AI as compute costs scale with task complexity, weakening seat-based subscriptions (Metronome, 2025), and (b) emerging ad deployments in consumer AI alongside policy commitments that advertising will not influence answers (OpenAI, 2026; Reuters, 2026). TPSV shifts integrity from policy to architecture by enforcing ranking and monetisation separation through a Blind-Ranking firewall and auditable commitment logs. The protocol uses a two-lane output: Lane A (Anchor) provides a fiduciary-optimal recommendation under a disclosed and contestable welfare function (the user benefit score), while Lane B (Market) offers sponsored alternatives restricted to "variance capture", that is, legitimate trade-offs driven by secondary preferences. Transparency is operationalised via an Agent-Readable Transparency (ART) protocol that standardises total cost of ownership fields, warranty and return conditions, shipping latency, and cancellation friction, supported by a verification ladder. Incentive compatibility is achieved through an Uncertainty Penalty that discounts unverified disclosures in Lane A and conditions Lane B eligibility on ART verification. Because standards adoption is a coordination problem, TPSV specifies progressive onboarding: platforms auto-extract "Tier 0.5" ART fields from public pages, vendors attest to upgrade, and verification costs can be subsidised for small sellers.

detail.abstract: This paper explores how spatial spillovers define neighborhoods and drive neighborhood change through a stylized computable equilibrium model of income-based residential sorting. We find three main results. First, stronger spillovers create larger, more distinct neighborhood clusters even when the spatial scope of externalities is small. Second, spillovers make neighborhoods resistant to small change but also susceptible to rapid shifts between equilibrium states. Third, stronger spillovers concentrate change at cluster boundaries and isolated locations rather than neighborhood interiors. Extending Schelling-like insights to income sorting dynamics, the model treats neighborhood shape as an endogenous outcome determined by decentralized household location choices mediated through housing markets. The framework helps explain persistent urban segregation patterns, neighborhood resilience, and the geography of neighborhood change, offering new approaches for linking spatial spillovers to urban spatial structure and dynamics.

detail.title: Demand-Based Asset Pricing in General Equilibrium

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-12

detail.abstract: I develop a general equilibrium macro-finance model that integrates demand-based asset pricing. Assets are held by financial intermediaries (“funds”) with investment mandates that induce downward-sloping demand curves. A representative household seeks out profitable investment opportunities by shifting its savings across funds, but it does so only gradually due to frictions in adjusting its portfolio. The aggregate demand for assets in this economy is inelastic and depends on the distribution of net worth across funds. Consequently, shocks to asset supply and unanticipated financial flows have meaningful effects on asset prices. The framework is general enough to accommodate an arbitrary set of intermediaries and assets, so it can be applied to several questions in macro-finance. Analytically, I characterize sufficient statistics to construct counterfactual asset price responses to shocks and show how these statistics relate to estimates of asset demand elasticity in the literature. Quantitatively, I demonstrate that the model can account for the “excess volatility”  in asset prices.

detail.abstract: Notional Defined Contribution (NDC) pension schemes convert accumulated pension wealth into an annuity, based on an average life expectancy at retirement. When longevity differs across social groups, a single conversion factor implies systematic transfers from shorter-lived to longer-lived individuals. This motivates proposals to differentiate benefits by socio-demographic characteristics related to life expectancy. We study whether such differentiation is perceived as fair using a survey experiment involving 3,004 Italian residents aged 18-66. Respondents completed an incentivised allocation task used to elicit their fairness views and then evaluated six reform scenarios that adjust pension benefits based on gender, region, income, household wealth, workplace fatigue, and health status. The results show that the fatigue-based and wealth-based scenarios receive the highest support, whereas the gender-based and region-based scenarios are strongly opposed. Self-interest predicts approval, with higher support among those who stand to gain from a reform. Respondents with libertarian views are consistently less supportive of changes in benefits, while egalitarians and, to a lesser extent, liberal egalitarians are more favourable. Our results inform policymakers on the importance of citizens' fairness perceptions for the implementation and communication of financially sustainable pension reforms.

title: A Review of Scientific Studies on Improving Enterprise Efficiency within Financial Services: Digital Transformation and FinTech
affiliations: Azerbaijan State Oil and Industry University, Baku, Azerbaijan.

detail.title: A Review of Scientific Studies on Improving Enterprise Efficiency within Financial Services: Digital Transformation and FinTech
detail.abstract: This article presents a detailed, systematic review of recent scientific studies and business data on how FinTech innovations and digital initiatives improve operational performance, profitability, and capital efficiency in the financial services industry. The study, drawing on peer-reviewed sources and business studies published over the last decade, examines fundamental efficiency factors, including process automation, advanced data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) implementation, regulatory technology (RegTech), cybersecurity upgrades, and FinTech mergers and partnerships. Automation and AI implementation have been shown to reduce operational costs by 20%-30% across several banking tasks while improving transaction speed, accuracy, and efficiency (Berruti et al., 2017; McKinsey, 2025). The empirical findings across the payments, wealth management, and regulatory compliance segments indicate a substantial efficiency gain, while cost-to-income ratios are declining and, in parallel, asset turnover is improving. However, this research also reveals critical implementation challenges as many institutions launching automation-focused technologies achieve only modest efficiency improvements due to poor process integration and insufficient change management (Berruti et al., 2017). Furthermore, FinTech-driven transformations are fundamentally restructuring financial services employment patterns and displacing routine clerical and back-office roles while creating higher demand for technically skilled talents in data science, cybersecurity, and other similar roles. In a nutshell, this analysis concludes that while FinTech and digital transformation enable significant efficiency improvements, realizing full value requires a strategic implementation combining tech, cultural adaptation, and, more importantly, security and compliance frameworks. This review synthesizes current empirical findings, highlights practical implications for financial institutions, and identifies critical gaps for future research on optimizing efficiency outcomes through FinTech innovation.

title: Why Financial Event Sequences Require Temporal Transformers: Necessity Theorems for Default Prediction
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why Financial Event Sequences Require Temporal Transformers: Necessity Theorems for Default Prediction
detail.abstract: Credit risk models typically aggregate transaction histories into tabular features, discarding temporal structure. We prove this approach is fundamentally limited. Three architectural components are mathematically necessary for optimal default prediction from financial event sequences: discrete event embeddings preserving transaction identity, spectral encoding of timestamps, and learned attention over account history. Each component is individually irreducible. Removing any one provably reduces predictive performance. The central result establishes that standard positional encoding, which assumes uniform event spacing, is categorically incorrect for financial data where transactions carry intrinsic timestamps. A payment at day 15 of the billing cycle differs predictively from the same payment at day 45, independent of sequence position. Ordinal encoding discards this temporal geometry. We further prove that default outcomes shape the entire account trajectory representation through gradient flow during training, creating second-order structure where early transactions modify interpretation of subsequent events. This formalizes the credit intuition that payment history must be read as a whole. The theoretical framework identifies minimal requirements for financial sequence modeling and explains observed performance gaps between sequential and tabular approaches in credit scoring.

title: Ownership Concentration and Firm Performance in India
affiliations: and University of Delhi South Campus

detail.title: Ownership Concentration and Firm Performance in India
detail.abstract: Ownership concentration is considered an important corporate governance mechanism because owners with concentrated shareholding influence the operations and management of a company. The ownership structure in developing countries is quite different from that in the developed markets, thus, we provide empirical evidence from an important emerging market like India. This study used panel data models and instrumental variables techniques using GMM on a large sample of 11,136 firm-year observations to get efficient and reliable results. The endogeneity of ownership concentration has not been examined in India before. In this paper, ownership concentration is measured by Herfindahl's index as suggested by Demsetz and Lehn (1985); and Leach and Leahy (1991). Other Indian studies in this area have used promoter shareholding as a proxy of ownership concentration. After controlling for endogeneity, we find that ownership concentration affects both market and accounting performance of a company, positively. The results suggest that concentrated ownership reduces agency costs as blockholders actively monitor the management of the company, thereby leading to better firm performance.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the concept of Antitrust 5.0, a new analytical framework for understanding the transformation of competition law in the context of geopolitical rivalry, economic fragmentation, and national security imperatives. It challenges the traditional view of antitrust as a neutral instrument of market correction and argues that competition policy has become a central tool of state power, industrial strategy, and geoeconomic defense.

Drawing on recent regulatory developments in the United States, China, and the European Union, the paper demonstrates how competition law is increasingly deployed to protect strategic sectors, foster national champions, secure critical supply chains, and advance broader geopolitical objectives. Antitrust 5.0 reflects a paradigm shift from efficiency-based enforcement toward sovereignty-oriented competition policy, where economic regulation operates as an extension of national security and foreign policy.

The paper proposes a conceptual model for Antitrust 5.0, identifies its core pillars, and explores its implications for global markets, international trade, regulatory convergence, and institutional design. It argues that this emerging paradigm reshapes the foundations of competition law, transforming it into a strategic instrument for navigating the new era of economic confrontation, technological rivalry, and multipolar governance.

title: Ask a Political Scientist: A Conversation with Yuen Yuen Ang about China and Political Science

detail.title: Ask a Political Scientist: A Conversation with Yuen Yuen Ang about China and Political Science

detail.abstract:
In this interview with Polity, Yuen Yuen Ang reflects on China’s political economy through a broader meta-critique of disciplinary practice in political science. Ang critiques the “publication-friendly” disciplinary incentives that privilege narrow, linear inquiry and thereby reduce scholars’ capacity to interpret consequential, disruptive problems as well as their relevance to policy making. She advances a complexity-oriented lens by distinguishing complicated from complex systems (mutual causality; outcomes influenced rather than controlled) and highlights “meta-institutions” that enable adaptive problem-solving. Applying her framework to China and drawing on her book How China Escaped the Poverty Trap (2016), Ang revisits “directed improvisation” under Deng as an adaptive development pattern, and characterizes Xi’s era as a structural break in which improvisation persisted but was redirected toward “zero-COVID,” contributing to the 2022 protests and abrupt policy reversal.

This article first appears in Polity, Volume 55, Number 3 (July 2023)

detail.abstract: This article explores the integration of Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) principles within living labs, particularly focusing on engineering and innovation practices. It reviews the evolution of living labs over the last 20 years, their roles in fostering co-responsibility among stakeholders, collaborative knowledge production and directing innovations toward socially desirable ends. It proposes the concept of Responsible Research and Innovation Labs (RRI Labs) tailored for engineering practices.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces The Theory of Intelligent Compression (TIC), a first-principles framework in management science that connects cognitive intelligence with organizational architecture. As intelligence—facilitated by AI and cognitive systems—becomes a scalable instrument, organizations undergo a fundamental transformation defined by structural contraction and cognitive expansion.

The theory formulates the Regulation of Intelligent Compression, supported by six mathematical formulations including Structural, Cognitive, Equilibrium, and Entropy regulations. TIC argues that organizations naturally evolve toward a Cognitive Steady State (CSS)—a condition of minimal structural mass and maximal intelligence. This work provides the mathematical logic and feedback models necessary to quantify AI's effect on organizational evolution across global sectors.

title: Main Bank Ties and the Co-insurance Effect: Evidence from the Japanese Corporate Bond Markets
affiliations: Waseda University - Graduate School of Business and Finance, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) - Department of Management Science, Loyola University Maryland and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Main Bank Ties and the Co-insurance Effect: Evidence from the Japanese Corporate Bond Markets
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the interplay between traditional stakeholder governance and modern market risk assessments in the Japanese corporate bond market (2006–2023). We examine how local (R&I) and global (S&P) rating agencies incorporate "soft" governance—specifically main bank ties and cross-shareholdings—into debt pricing. Our findings reveal an "informational diarchy": local ratings superiorly explain yield spreads, while global ratings dominate the CDS market. We find robust support for the "co-insurance" hypothesis, as speculative-grade firms utilize higher main bank loan ratios to mitigate distress. However, a "signaling paradox" emerges for globally rated firms, where bond guarantees are perceived as signals of latent weakness rather than risk mitigants. After addressing selection bias via a Heckman two-step model, we show that S&P ratings exhibit significant selection bias while R&I ratings remain standardized. These results highlight how persistent relationship-based governance in Japan exerts diverging influences on domestic and international risk pricing.​

title: Outside Director Tenure Limit: Expertise-Enhancement versus Entrenchment
affiliations: Korea University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Korea University Business School

detail.title: Outside Director Tenure Limit: Expertise-Enhancement versus Entrenchment
detail.abstract: We study Korea’s 2020 tenure-limit rule, barring reappointment of outside directors after six years at a firm (nine within a business group), and examine its effects on valuation and board behavior. Announcement returns are positive for firms with long-tenured outside directors (LTODs), especially where agency problems are high and transparency low, but weaker in R&D-intensive firms. Implementation timing matters: early LTOD replacement is rewarded, while extensions are penalized. Post-reform, monitoring strengthens—dissent against management rises, non-performance pay falls, pay–performance elasticity increases, CEO turnover rises, and board agendas expand. The surge in dissent stems from removing historically acquiescent LTODs and appointing newer directors. Contrary to expectations, final-term directors do not dissent more than others. We reconcile this by documenting a labor-market penalty: dissenting directors are less likely to be nominated elsewhere. These findings highlight how tenure limits reshape market valuations and director incentives.

title: Anti–Money Laundering Regulations and Bank Performance: Evidence from Global Panel Data
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Griffith University - Griffith Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Griffith University - Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics and Griffith University

detail.title: Anti–Money Laundering Regulations and Bank Performance: Evidence from Global Panel Data
detail.abstract: The past 25 years have witnessed a considerable expansion in the depth and scope of global Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing standards. This has been primarily driven by the efforts of the global watchdog, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), which evaluates AML/CFT regulations across 200 countries. Using a global panel dataset covering 132 countries, we employ a staggered heterogeneous DiD design to study the impact of the FATF’s mutual evaluation process on banking costs that are proxied by the ratio of non-interest expense to gross income. Our results show that banks experience an average 8.6% increase in short term operating costs after FATF evaluations.

detail.abstract: Boards of directors function as teams. We study how board composition - diverse or homogeneous - affects shareholder value. In our model, two directors jointly design the CEO's compensation contract and monitor performance, while the CEO chooses productive effort and earnings manipulation. Repeated interactions between the two directors shape monitoring incentives, CEO compensation, manipulation, and ultimately, shareholder value. Directors with longer team tenure and/or stronger incentive alignment with shareholders exert greater monitoring effort and offer higher-powered CEO bonuses. While these higher bonuses increase productive effort, they also incentivize manipulation. Nonetheless, shareholders always prefer stronger board monitoring. Although these results hold for both board types, board composition alters their relative strength. Diverse boards exert greater monitoring effort and offer higher-powered CEO bonuses when incentive alignment is strong and team tenure is moderate, whereas homogeneous boards do so when director tenure is long. Our model also predicts that governance measures aimed at strengthening board monitoring may either succeed or backfire, depending on board composition.

detail.abstract: China is experiencing rapid population aging and a declining workforce, posing significant economic and fiscal challenges, especially to the pension system. This paper examines the evolution of China’s pension system, assesses its gaps relative to international peers, and evaluates the macro-fiscal implications of population aging and various pension reforms. Using a calibrated overlapping generations model that explicitly incorporates the rural–urban disparities, we project that population aging alone can slow annual GDP growth by about 2 percentage points between 2024 and 2050, while pension spending can rise by nearly 10 percentage points of GDP. The 2024 retirement age reform eases some of the long-term growth and fiscal sustainability pressures, raising GDP growth by 0.2 percentage points annually and reducing pension spending from 15.3 percent to 11.9 percent of GDP by 2050. We also use the model to examine a set of policy-relevant reforms—doubling Residents Pension Scheme benefits which are currently inadequate, linking benefits to life expectancy, further increasing the retirement age, and promoting urbanization—and find significant effects on fiscal and macroeconomic outcomes.

detail.abstract: Health systems face growing pressure from population ageing, multimorbidity, and persistent workforce shortages. In this context, intermediate care is internationally positioned as time-limited, recoveryoriented care that prevents unnecessary hospital admissions, shortens length of stay, and supports safe transitions to follow-up care. However, the concept remains heterogeneous in the literature, and in the Netherlands its underlying functions are institutionally fragmented across multiple provisions, funding domains, and governance structures. This article develops a conceptual clarification of intermediate care for the Dutch context. We conducted (1) a systematic narrative synthesis of international literature and (2) a qualitative analysis of Dutch policy documents. Across health systems, publications converge around three interrelated core functions of intermediate care: recovery-oriented temporality, organization of care transitions, and substitution of hospital care. In Dutch policy, these functions are recognizable but dispersed across separate care arrangements and regulatory frameworks, without an overarching conceptual articulation. Our integrative synthesis shows that intermediate care in the Netherlands is best understood as a system function rather than as a discrete facility or service. We propose a working definition and a three-layer conceptual framework that organizes intermediate care along: (1) core functions (what it does), (2) organizational dimensions (how it is structured), and (3) intended system outcomes (what it aims to achieve). This framework provides a shared analytical language for policy, research, and practice. By shifting the perspective from individual provisions to system-level coordination, it supports regional governance of access, triage, care transitions, and capacity management.

detail.abstract: We study the uneven impacts of reducing mobility barriers arising from land market frictions by leveraging two major land reforms that strengthened land rental rights in China. We construct a novel county-level reform index by tracing the reforms’ spatial and temporal rollout. Combining this index with a large panel dataset, we show that, relative to men, the reforms facilitate rural women’s transition out of agriculture while reducing urban women’s employment and wage income. We embed the reform index in a two-sector model with household-level employment decisions. Interactions between land market frictions and gender roles in market and home production drive these uneven impacts. Counterfactual analyses suggest that alleviating these frictions substantially affects female labor allocation and agricultural productivity.

detail.abstract: Background The growing number of patients with multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs) in the UK presents significant challenges for individuals, carers, professionals, and healthcare systems. Objectives This qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) identifies key problem areas in continuity and coordination of care from the perspectives of patients, carers, and healthcare professionals. Methods We searched nine electronic databases (Ovid: MEDLINE, Embase, HMIC, PsycInfo, SPP; EBSCO: CINAHL Ultimate, AgeLine, AMED, CDAS) from inception to 12/02/2024. We included English-language, peer-reviewed qualitative reviews reporting on continuity or coordination of care for MLTCs from the perspective of patients, carers, or healthcare professionals. Primary studies and quantitative reviews were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened, appraised (using CASP), and extracted data. A novel pluralistic synthesis approach was used to identify cross-stakeholder themes. This review was pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024512922). Results From 1847 records, 42 reviews were included, covering 1576 primary studies. We identified seven priority problem areas, triangulating experiences of patients, carers, and clinicians to highlight shared and divergent concerns. Conclusions Frustrations reported by patients and carers were often echoed by professionals, pointing to systemic failings. Comparing perspectives revealed system-level insights to inform the design of more coordinated care for people with MLTCs.

detail.abstract:
The BIS withdrawal from Project mBridge in October 2024 exposed a structural gap in cross-border finance: no CBDC settlement platform spans both Western and non-Western monetary authorities using a politically neutral asset. This paper specifies the Gold Bridge Protocol, a permissioned framework that bridges heterogeneous CBDC systems through tokenised allocated physical gold—held for seconds during atomic settlement, not as a monetary standard. The design adapts CLS Bank governance, LBMA custody, and PFMI oversight to a neutral bridge asset, introducing corridor-level sanctions ring-fencing, sovereign-partitioned settlement, and confidential-computing compliance.

Calibrated Monte Carlo simulations (10,000 iterations, 250 days) across four corridors—UAE–China ($102B), Saudi Arabia–China ($108B), India–UAE ($122B trade and remittances), and Brazil–China ($167B)—yield $4.88B in combined annual savings with 86–92% cost reduction, sub-8-second settlement, and a total gold collateral requirement of just 2.7 tonnes (0.03% of London vault holdings). A triangular network analysis demonstrates that multilateral netting and collateral pooling emerge naturally as corridors connect.

detail.abstract: United States' technology transfer law and policy (TTLP) integrates government, academia, and industry-a "triple-threat" research and development ("R&D") methodology-and harnesses commercial incentives to stimulate market application of federal government-funded invention. TTLP, which has proven a potent catalyst for remarkably prolific biomedical R&D since Congress enacted its cornerstone legislation in 1980, is transforming U.S. medicine to molecular medicine-to personal genome medicine (PGM)-in real time. A genomics (gene function in the context of an organism's entire genome, meaning its full set of genetic instructions) complement to the Human Genome Project (HGP) emerged in the 1990s. Genomics has given rise to a portfolio of "omics" !elds that represent a biomedical research perspective shift over the last two decades to multifaceted systems of biology on the molecular level, with simultaneous analysis of thousands of molecules and the way they influence each other. During more than four decades of expansive implementation, TTLP has directly infused industry influence from the laboratory bench to clinical research, and on the stakeholders (individuals and institutions) engaged in both. During this same span of time, U.S. medicine has become much more commercial through cumulative waves of managed care, conversions from not-for-prof!t to for-prof!t, consolidation, and private equity ownership of medical practices. An ongoing proliferation of inauthentic authorship, research misconduct, and outright fraud in peer-reviewed science and medical literature undermines research integrity and reliability. TTLP, while a profound prescription medicines ("Rx") R&D enabler, has not been complemented with regulation-self-regulation by the U.S. medical profession, governmental regulation, or a combination of the two to sufficiently protect the evidentiary-science base of medicine in an age of omics commensurate with the way the base of U.S. medicine was established, protected, and promoted during its formative twentieth century. This article discusses the preceding and introduces law-policy proposals to reinforce the evidentiary-science base of U.S. medicine in our omics century.

detail.abstract: Financial intermediation in Montenegro has been on a declining trend since independence, with domestic credit to the private sector decreasing from a peak of 86.5 percent of GDP in 2008 to 46.4 percent in 2024. Net interest margin (NIM)—a common indicator of intermediation costs—has remained elevated, ranking among the highest in the Western Balkans. This paper analyzes the determinants of NIMs using a unique bank-level dataset comprising quarterly observations on all commercial banks in Montenegro during the period 2013–25. The empirical analysis reveals three key findings, each with important policy implications. First, larger banks tend to exhibit lower NIMs, reflecting economies of scale, diversification, and stronger market power. Second, higher asset quality is associated with narrower margins, underscoring the role of effective credit risk management. Third, greater operational efficiency correlates with lower NIMs, highlighting the importance of cost control and managerial effectiveness. Taken together, these results underscore the need for policy initiatives that support banking sector consolidation, reinforce credit risk management practices, and promote operational efficiency improvements.

title: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and Offshore Energy: Unlocking Ocean Rents for National Development
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University

detail.title: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and Offshore Energy: Unlocking Ocean Rents for National Development
detail.abstract: The strategic exploitation of Nigeria's offshore energy resources presents a critical opportunity for national development, yet the effectiveness of fiscal mechanisms in capturing ocean rents remains insufficiently examined within legal scholarship. In Nigeria, where offshore hydrocarbons constitute a dominant source of public revenue, the central challenge lies in optimising tax-based rent capture to finance sustainable development while maintaining investment attractiveness and economic competitiveness. This study critically interrogates the positioning of the Nigerian Tax Act as a framework for offshore energy governance, assessing its adequacy in capturing ocean rents and facilitating equitable and sustainable fiscal outcomes. Adopting a doctrinal and analytical methodology, the research examines the structure and scope of offshore taxation under the Tax Act, the effectiveness of rent-capturing instruments, and the alignment of fiscal provisions with national development imperatives. The analysis evaluates corporate income taxation, royalties, incentives, profit-based levies, and fiscal concessions in offshore energy operations, highlighting persistent gaps in revenue capture, transparency, and intergenerational equity. Drawing insight from Nigeria's fiscal regime and offshore tax governance, the study reveals that while the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 provides a formal legal basis for revenue collection, it is constrained by weak valuebased rent mechanisms, fiscal leakages, and misalignment with sustainable development objectives. The research recommends strengthening rent-capture provisions, instituting ringfenced development funds, enhancing transparency and accountability, and integrating fiscal design with national Blue Economy and post-oil transition strategies, thereby positioning offshore energy taxation as a transformative instrument for national development.

detail.title: Peer-to-peer carsharing as an effective way to reduce car overuse
detail.abstract: We study the market of peer-to-peer carsharing, a market where owners rent their cars out to nonowners in exchange for a price. In a model where individuals take into account the effects of their mobility decisions on the environment, but this green sensitivity is heterogeneously distributed across them, we show that the introduction of peer-to-peer carsharing may lead to both an increase or a decrease in total car usage (and thereby emissions), but is likely to yield more beneficial effects in less green populations or when the distribution of green sensitivity is more polarized. We consider the possibility that individuals suffer from present bias and therefore end up using the car more than they originally intended. We show that peer-to-peer carsharing can curb this behavior and, in some cases, fully prevents car overuse.

detail.abstract: We study optimal monetary and exchange rate policy in a small open economy facing oil price shocks. In a model with segmented financial markets that generate endogenous UIP deviations, the first-best allocation is achieved through a combination of interest rate policy and foreign exchange intervention (FXI). Monetary policy stabilizes domestic inflation and the output gap, while FXI targets the UIP wedge to offset financial frictions. Oil price shocks endogenously move the net foreign asset position, giving rise to financial imbalances that make FXI essential—a mechanism distinct from exogenous financial shocks highlighted in the literature. Quantitatively, for a calibrated oil exporter, suboptimal regimes such as a free float or a simple peg entail sizable welfare losses of around 2% in consumption-equivalent terms, though peg, and especially peg with fuel subsidies, can outperform free floats. Overall, FXI is crucial to break the destabilizing link between real commodity shocks and financial risk premia.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a nowcasting model to produce timely estimates of quarterly GDP growth for Kenya. Nowcasting combines official monthly indicators with digital transaction data. Exploiting strong comovement of macroeconomic time series, a few latent factors summarize aggregate dynamics and enhance forecasts. The model is updated with each data release, decomposing revisions into predictable and news components. Results demonstrate robust performance of the nowcasting model in data-constrained environments and show that nowcasting is applicable to low-income countries.

title: Tiered Climate Clubs: Global Abatement Without Global Agreement
affiliations: Colorado State University, Fort Collins

detail.title: Tiered Climate Clubs: Global Abatement Without Global Agreement
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel two-tier climate policy structure to mitigate global carbon emissions without requiring broad multilateral cooperation. Extending Nordhaus's (2015) climate club, countries in the ``second tier'' must price carbon at a fixed fraction of the average carbon price within the first tier, or face trade penalties. This matching rule creates two reinforcing mechanisms. First, by requiring partial carbon pricing by non-participating countries, the policy shifts abatement toward lower-cost opportunities outside the coalition, substantially improving global cost-effectiveness. Second, higher abatement by first-tier countries induces additional abatement by second-tier countries, strengthening incentives for leadership. The stable first-tier coalition consists of the United States and the European Union. In equilibrium, this coalition sets carbon prices at roughly 60\% of the global Social Cost of Carbon. The resulting agreement achieves global abatement four and a half times higher than the uncoordinated Nash equilibrium and approximately one-third of the globally efficient level. If participation by the United States is exogenously constrained, the remaining stable first-tier coalitions consist of the EU paired with either the UK or Australia. In these cases, equilibrium abatement rises by only a modest amount relative to the uncoordinated Nash outcome, compared to the much larger gains achieved under EU--US leadership.

title: Medals and Mindsets: How Women's Olympic Competitiveness Advances Gender Equality

detail.title: Medals and Mindsets: How Women's Olympic Competitiveness Advances Gender Equality
detail.abstract: Can female athletic success reshape beliefs about women's competitive capacity and advance gender equality? We study this question in the context of China's return to the Olympics, combining comprehensive athlete records from 1984-2004 with detailed census data. Exploiting variation in the timing of each prefecture's first female Olympic medalist and differential exposure across birth cohorts, we find that hometown female medalists significantly narrow gender gaps in educational attainment, while male medalists produce no comparable effects. To address potential endogeneity, we employ a Bartik-style instrument leveraging the 1991 Soviet collapse as an exogenous shock to medal opportunities across sports. We further show that media coverage framing female achievements as evidence of women's competitiveness helps explain these effects, and that female medalists shift fathers' beliefs about daughters' competitive capacity rather than directly inspiring girls. Taken together, our findings suggest that publicized female success can challenge gender stereotypes and promote equality.

detail.title: The Intersection of Biodiversity and Climate Change: Implications for International Enviromental Law
detail.abstract: The intersection between biodiversity and climate change presents profound challenges for global ecosystems and human societies. This article explores how these two critical environmental issues intersect, highlighting the implications for international environmental law. As climate change accelerates, it threatens species diversity and disrupts ecological balances, leading to dire consequences for both wildlife and human populations that rely on ecosystem services. The article analyzes existing legal frameworks and their effectiveness in addressing the dual crises of biodiversity loss and climate change. It emphasizes the need for a cohesive legal approach that recognizes the interconnectedness of these issues and advocates for stronger international cooperation. By examining case studies and policy responses, this work underscores the urgency for legal reform to protect biodiversity while combating climate change. Ultimately, it calls for innovative legal solutions that not only safeguard our planet's rich biological heritage but also foster resilience in the face of an uncertain climate future.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes a structural separation between order, geometry, and dynamics to clarify why Pareto efficiency, equilibrium selection, and regime shifts must be treated as distinct objects. We formalize Pareto efficiency as an order-theoretic property induced by dominance, invariant to any metric. We then separate this invariant order from geometry by distinguishing dominance from distance to efficiency, yielding an inefficiency decomposition Γ(𝑦) into a dominance state and a metric-dependent magnitude. Dynamics are introduced as a third, independent layer; dynamics select realizable outcomes via attractors. Regime shifts correspond to topological changes in the efficient set, in attractor structure, or in their alignment, and cannot be resolved by geometric re-scaling. The framework provides a substrate-independent foundation for analyzing optimization, equilibrium selection, and regime change across strategic, economic, and ecological systems.

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In 2021, the Republic of Georgia established a Large Taxpayer Office (LTO) to strengthen tax administration and improve compliance among firms that contribute a disproportionate share of revenue. This paper draws on that quasi-experiment to estimate the causal impact of intensive oversight, with no change in tax rates, on taxpayer behavior and revenue collection using administrative data from 2017–2024. Our study exploits both the 2021 introduction of the LTO and the revision of eligibility thresholds in 2024. Estimating a weighted difference-in-differences design, we find that LTO assignment raised annual tax assessments by about 0.4–0.7 percent of GDP, concentrated in VAT and withholding taxes. When we examine the channels, we find that the LTO raised compliance by combining targeted enforcement with improved taxpayer services, while audits became fewer but more selective. The impacts are largest in sectors with strong third-party reporting and high transaction traceability. Our findings underscore that reforms to tax administration can deliver significant gains in fiscal capacity, generate fiscal space, and support development.

title: Legacy-to-Cloud Semantic Regression Validation: A Framework for Detecting Meaning Drift in Modernized Systems
affiliations: Independent,  and

detail.title: Legacy-to-Cloud Semantic Regression Validation: A Framework for Detecting Meaning Drift in Modernized Systems
detail.abstract: Modernization and cloud migration of legacy systems are typically confirmed using functional regression testing, data reconciliation testing, and performance testing methods. Functional regression testing methods confirm that a new system works as expected technically but do not identify semantic regression-another type of defect wherein the new system works functionally, but has different meanings, interpretations of intent, and/or policy interpretation compared to the legacy system. These types of regressions are particularly risky for regulated and mission critical environments as they contain decades worth of business logic, edge cases, and institutional knowledge. Legacy-to-Cloud Semantic Regression Validation (LCSRV)-A structured process for identifying, measuring and mitigating semantic drift during system modernization-was developed to address this issue. LCSRV enhances traditional regression testing through the addition of semantic checkpoints, invariant-based validation, domain-aligned scenario models, and meaning-preserving comparison methodologies. LCSRV also allows for the systematic validation of the intended behavior of the system rather than simply determining whether the outputs are equivalent. An applied case study based on a healthcare eligibility modernization program demonstrates the use of the LCSRV Framework in practice. Controlled test scenarios and pseudo-metrics were used to illustrate how semantic regressions may occur and how they can be identified, even when conventional regression tests pass. The results showed that semantic drift can occur in the order of precedence for rules, the conditional interpretation of rules, and temporal logic, and therefore indicate that explicit semantic validation should be an integral part of modernization programs. The proposed methodology offers modernization teams a defendable, repeatable, and auditable process for maintaining the meaning of their systems throughout cloud transformations, which will enhance the quality assurance and compliance practices currently employed by many organizations.

title: Olympic Success and Gender Equality: How Media Narratives Shape Social Norms

detail.title: Olympic Success and Gender Equality: How Media Narratives Shape Social Norms
detail.abstract: Does female athletic achievement in the Olympic Games influence broader gender equality? We study this question in the context of China's return to the Olympics in 1984, combining comprehensive athlete records from 1984-2004 with detailed census data. Using a two-way fixed-effects design, we exploit variation in the timing of each prefecture's first female Olympic medal and differential exposure across cohorts who still could make education decisions versus those beyond that window. We find that the emergence of a hometown female medalist significantly reduces gender gaps in education and improves women's labor market outcomes. To address potential endogeneity in medal timing, we construct a Bartik-style instrument based on shifts in Soviet presence and relative strength across sports following the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union, which generated exogenous variation in Chinese prefectures' medal opportunities. Mechanism analyses indicate that media framing-rather than coverage intensity-drives these effects: in People's Daily, female medalists are disproportionately portrayed through genderequality narratives rather than national pride. Together, the results suggest that publicized female achievement can challenge entrenched gender stereotypes and foster broader gender equality.

title: Time Is Not Authority: On the Structural Failure of Temporal Control Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Time Is Not Authority: On the Structural Failure of Temporal Control Systems
detail.abstract:
This paper identifies a structural failure mode underlying modern digital systems: the substitution of temporal order for legitimacy. In many automated infrastructures: financial markets, blockchains, AI agents, and social media platforms; actions execute because time advanced, not because they were explicitly permitted. We argue that this represents a category error: time can order events, but it cannot authorize them.

We introduce the concept of temporal control systems, in which execution is triggered solely by temporal progression, and show that such systems are inherently unstable because they lack a mechanism to revoke, pause, or deny action. Drawing on control theory, financial instability, blockchain economics, and AI safety, we demonstrate that this failure mode appears across domains whenever execution is justified by continuity rather than permission.

The paper proposes explicit authorization as a missing control primitive and argues that no large-scale automated system can remain stable without it. By reframing recent crises in finance, computation, and attention as failures of temporal authority, the paper provides a unifying structural explanation for instability in digital civilization.

detail.abstract: High-quality video presentations generate scope-sensitive willingness to pay (WTP) for Amazon rainforest conservation as effectively as immersive virtual reality (VR), while offering greater accessibility and lower cost. Using a preregistered 2×2 between-subjects experimental design, participants were randomly assigned to VR or video presentations and asked their WTP for conservation programmes protecting 20% and 50% of the Amazon rainforest. Both formats successfully elicited scope-sensitive valuations, with scope elasticities of 0.588 for VR and 0.576 for video, within the empirically plausible range for environmental goods. With equivalent scope sensitivity, video represents the recommended approach for most stated preference applications. Exploratory within-VR analyses revealed that presence, realism, and discomfort moderated scope sensitivity, with higher presence and realism strengthening scope responsiveness and discomfort weakening it. These findings validate immersive VR as capable of eliciting scope-sensitive valuations for remote ecosystems with high non-use values, while establishing video's equivalent performance at substantially lower implementation costs.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the sectoral performance of India’s Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY 2.0) by analysing the relationship between training intensity and employment placement outcomes across skill sectors. Using officially reported sector-wise data, the study highlights substantial heterogeneity in placement performance and finds that higher training volumes do not consistently result in better employment outcomes. The results suggest mismatches between skill provision and labour market demand in several sectors, underscoring the need for demand-driven training, stronger industry linkages, and improved programme targeting. The paper offers policy-relevant insights for improving the effectiveness of large-scale skill development initiatives in India.

title: Structural Localization and Regime Selection: Multi-Seed Validation of Telegraph Dynamics via Operational Detection

detail.title: Structural Localization and Regime Selection: Multi-Seed Validation of Telegraph Dynamics via Operational Detection
detail.abstract: We demonstrate that graph-based telegraph dynamics exhibit structural localization that statistically selects dynamical regimes (underdamped vs. overdamped), and that this selection is operationally detectable from partial, noisy timeseries observations without spectral knowledge. Using 50 independent graph realizations (500 graphs total, n = 60-103 nodes) and analyzing 18 nontrivial Laplacian eigenmodes per graph, we establish three core findings via multi-seed validation: (C1) Certain topologies generate localized eigenmodes (272/500 graphs, 54% hit rate), (C2) localization exhibits population-level coupling to regime selection (∆r = 0.211, CI 95 = [0.175, 0.247], p < 0.001) with 38% seed-to-seed stability validating Causal Memory Gravity (CMG) predictions, and (C3) regimes are operationally detectable achieving PR-AUC = 0.853. The 50-fold sample increase (10 → 500 graphs) yields 7× tighter confidence intervals and establishes statistical significance for the localization-regime coupling that was ambiguous in single-seed analysis. The 38% seed stability validates CMG's prediction that "structure may fluctuate while causal constraints persist," distinguishing genuine structure-dependence from null effects (≈5% expected) or universal laws (≈90% expected).

title: The Three-Stage Transition: How Institutional Tolerance-Language Shifts from Act-Constraint to Judgment-Sanction
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: The Three-Stage Transition: How Institutional Tolerance-Language Shifts from Act-Constraint to Judgment-Sanction
detail.abstract: This article identifies and analyses a structural transition in UK equality and anti-harassment law through which normative language originally constraining acts of interference has been progressively extended to constrain evaluative judgment itself. Drawing on close doctrinal analysis of the Equality Act 2010, s 26, university conduct codes, criminal communications statutes, and the Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023, the article documents a three-stage pattern: from act-constraint (Stage 1), through an evaluative gateway created by subjective-effect tests (Stage 2), to judgmentas-sanction-target (Stage 3). Case law analysis-spanning Forstater v CGD Europe, Miller v College of Policing, Lee v Ashers Baking Company, Ngole v University of Sheffield, and cognate decisions-reveals that courts have intermittently recognised and corrected this transition, but that the statutory architecture continues to enable it. Comparative analysis confirms that the transition is strongest where legal frameworks provide evaluative gateways and weakest where strict act-speech distinctions are maintained. The article concludes that stable rights-protective frameworks require explicit statutory differentiation between act-constraint and judgment-constraint, and that the 'purpose or effect' formulation in s 26 constitutes a structural vulnerability that legislative reform has not yet adequately addressed.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Finance: A Comparative Evaluation of Vector, Hierarchical, and Graph-Based RAG Models

detail.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Finance: A Comparative Evaluation of Vector, Hierarchical, and Graph-Based RAG Models
detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have emerged as a powerful paradigm for enterprise knowledge retrieval, particularly in large, distributed corporate information environments. We develop and evaluate a RAG-based knowledge retrieval framework over BlackRocks corporate website corpus. We implement and systematically benchmark five RAG architectures-Vanilla RAG, RAPTOR, CRAG, LightRAG, and LinearRAGacross seven representative query types spanning factual, thematic, and comparative questions. To assess retrieval quality in enterprise settings where ground truth is distributed and context-dependent, we introduce three evaluation metrics: Wrong Category Rate, Context Deficiency Rate, and Incorrect Link Retrieval Rate. Empirical results indicate that graph-based architectures demonstrate superior retrieval robustness, with LinearRAG achieving zero observed failures across all metrics. Hierarchical approaches such as RAPTOR excel at thematic synthesis, while CRAGs self-correcting mechanism with web-search fallback improves resilience to corpus limitations. The system processes 1,130 BlackRock articles into a unified, searchable knowledge base supporting multiple retrieval paradigms. Our findings highlight the trade-offs between flat, hierarchical, corrective, and graph-based RAG architectures, offering practical design insights for deploying retrieval-grounded LLM systems in large-scale financial enterprise environments.

title: AI-Driven Deployment and Cloud Migration Strategies for Stable Software Releases

detail.abstract: The growing complexity of modern software systems has made manual deployment difficult to manage at scale. Artificial intelligence offers practical support across the deployment lifecycle, from traffic control to rollback decisions. This article discusses how AI supports blue and green deployment strategies through automated traffic orchestration, anomaly detection, predictive rollback, performance tuning, and user experience monitoring. It outlines the role of machine learning, deep learning, generative models, and reinforcement learning in improving release safety and system reliability. Common operational use cases such as load testing, circuit breakers, chaos engineering, caching, and cloud migration are also examined. The discussion shows how AI-enabled deployment reduces downtime, lowers release risk, and supports continuous improvement in production environments. The AI-Integrated Enhanced Deployment Strategy leverages machine learning and intelligent automation to revolutionize software delivery, optimizing CI/CD pipelines for greater speed, reliability, and accuracy. By automating testing, proactively detecting errors, and dynamically managing resources, this approach reduces deployment risks, overcomes infrastructure complexities, and ensures faster, more secure release cycles. This approach is critical for modern MLOps, allowing organizations to manage model drift and ensure AI models are consistently updated in production environments.

Globalization has become a key dynamic shaping renewable energy investment through technology transfer, capital mobility, and trade networks. This study examines the impact of economic globalization and its dimensions on renewable energy investments for the global economy, using global data from 1970 to 2022. The Johansen co-integration test confirmed the existence of long-run relationships in the study. Long-run coefficient estimates were made using the DOLS and FMOLS methods. The findings show that economic globalization generally has a positive impact on renewable energy investments. The long-run coefficient results show that a 1% increase in the economic globalization index increases renewable energy investments by approximately 0.06–0.07%. Analyzing the sub-components, the impact of trade globalization is significantly stronger. A 1% increase in the trade globalization index increases renewable energy investments by 0.10–0.12%. In contrast, financial globalization was estimated with negative coefficients. A 1% increase in the financial globalization index was found to reduce investments by approximately 0.05%. This result indicates that short-run capital movements, exchange rate fluctuations, and financial instability have a negative impact on long-run energy projects. Furthermore, economic growth was also found to support renewable energy investments. Overall, it emerged that the impact of globalization is not one-sided; while it offers opportunities for renewable energy investments, financial integration harbors vulnerabilities when appropriate policy frameworks are lacking.

detail.abstract: In today's hyper-competitive business landscape, organizations are increasingly recognizing the pivotal role that sustainable engineering management plays in achieving market differentiation and enhancing brand value. This paper examines the integral relationship between sustainable engineering practices and their impact on brand perception, consumer loyalty, and overall market positioning. By integrating principles of sustainability into engineering management, companies can not only improve operational efficiencies but also foster innovative solutions that resonate with environmentally conscious consumers. The first section of this study provides a comprehensive overview of sustainable engineering management, defining its key components, methodologies, and frameworks. It highlights the importance of aligning engineering strategies with sustainability goals, noting how this alignment supports long-term business viability and market competitiveness. A focus on the Triple Bottom Line—balancing economic, environmental, and social impacts—serves as a foundational element in this exploration, demonstrating how sustainability can drive value creation across multiple dimensions. Subsequent sections delve into empirical case studies that illustrate successful implementation of sustainable engineering practices across various industries. These case studies provide insight into how organizations like Tesla and Interface have effectively leveraged sustainability as a core component of their engineering strategies, resulting in enhanced brand loyalty and a differentiated market presence. By prioritizing sustainable innovations, these companies have not only captured significant market share but have also established themselves as leaders in corporate social responsibility. Furthermore, the paper investigates the mechanisms through which sustainable engineering enhances brand value. It discusses the role of consumer perceptions, stakeholder engagement, and regulatory compliance in shaping brand reputation. Ultimately, the findings indicate that organizations that prioritize sustainable engineering management not only elevate their operational capabilities but also strengthen their brand equity in an increasingly sustainability driven marketplace. This study concludes by advocating for a paradigm shift in engineering management practices, encouraging organizations to adopt sustainable models that align with evolving consumer expectations and regulatory landscapes. By embracing this approach, firms can position themselves favorably in the market, ultimately achieving a competitive edge that drives both profitability and positive societal impact.
