title: Smarter Deregulation
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Vanderbilt Law School and Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: Smarter Deregulation

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Citing high regulatory costs, the Trump administration has taken drastic steps towards administrative deregulation, prioritizing the repeal of existing regulations and discouraging the promulgation of new regulations. Executive directives advancing this deregulatory agenda encourage agencies to subvert the procedural and analytical requirements governing agency action, including reasoned decisionmaking, public participation, and regulatory impact analysis. The administration has directed agencies to prioritize compliance-cost reductions, most concerningly, by excluding public health impacts from regulatory impact analysis altogether. Myopic prioritization of compliance-cost reductions fails to account for the true quantitative and qualitative impacts associated with regulation and represents an unprecedented shift away from a regulatory decisionmaking process long-premised on social welfare maximization. The Trump Administration's policies do not constitute a defensible approach to deregulation. The revocation of a regulation can be desirable in some circumstances, for example, when it becomes inefficient due to technological advancements or changed circumstances. However, a rational and well-reasoned approach to deregulation is both economically preferable and legally mandated. We propose a smarter approach to deregulation by arguing that decisions to rescind existing regulations should be made by leveraging the empirical principles of cost-benefit analysis to prioritize deregulatory efforts towards regulations that are comparatively less costeffective. Under the proposed framework, agencies facing an upper bound on the regulatory costs an administration is willing to incur should compare the cost-effectiveness of similar regulations. Regulations that rank low on this metric are relatively less cost-efficient and therefore are the proper target for deregulatory action intended to achieve compliance cost savings. Conversely, agency action revoking regulations that are comparatively more costeffective is unjustified and will be vulnerable to legal challenges. The proposed approach serves to justify efficient deregulatory action while ensuring well-reasoned and transparent agency decisionmaking. Applying this approach to environmental regulations, which are a main target of recent deregulatory efforts, this paper demonstrates that many of these regulations are comparatively highly cost beneficial. Although environmental regulations account for the largest share of U.S. regulatory costs, they also generate substantial economic and public health benefits by mitigating future harms associated with climate change. Consequently, attempts to roll back these regulations are likely unjustified and violative of legal standards requiring agency action to be well-reasoned, evidence based, and transparent.

title: Quality Assurance Frameworks for Scalable Roll-to-Roll Production Lines
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Quality Assurance Frameworks for Scalable Roll-to-Roll Production Lines
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes frameworks for the Quality Assurance (QA) of scalable roll-to-roll (R2R) production lines, focusing on defects, yield, and process stability under high-throughput manufacturing (Pingale and Altay, 2025; Martin et al., 2025). It analyses, integrates, and reviews the literature related to the QA of in-line metrology, virtual sensing, statistical process control, and AI-enabled monitoring to delineate the versatility of working systems in integrated quality assurance (Jin, Shui, and Shpitalni, 2019). The findings indicate that most hybrid quality assurance frameworks, which incorporate physical sensor networks, virtual metrology, and predictive process control systems, outperform stand-alone inspection or monitoring systems in early defect detection, waste reduction, and process optimization (Maguluri et al., 2024). Moreover, the results stress the necessity of flexible, smart quality systems that can address the variability in materials, process drift, and changing conditions characteristic of R2R manufacturing. The study recommends that for scalable and resilient R2R production, there needs to be a movement from static, post-process inspection models to integrated, real-time quality assurance systems that are in tune with the process and the prevailing digital manufacturing frameworks (Zheng 2018). This further refines the emerging quality assurance frameworks for next-generation R2R production ecosystems.

detail.abstract: Technology diffusion is central to economic development. This paper examines diffusion patterns for 31 technologies for 139 countries over two centuries, extending existing databases to include recent digital technologies and renewable energy technologies. Using cross-country panel regressions, we find that while adoption lags have declined from 50 years (pre-1950) to 15 years (post-2000), adoption intensity in developing economies remains at 53% of advanced economy levels. We document diverging intensity for older technologies but emerging convergence for post-2000 technologies, suggesting digital innovations may reduce the technology gap. These findings inform policies aimed at accelerating technology diffusion to developing economies.

title: Digital Twin Applications for Yield Prediction in Roll-to-Roll Manufacturing
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Digital Twin Applications for Yield Prediction in Roll-to-Roll Manufacturing
detail.abstract: The idea of roll-to-roll (R2R) manufacturing is at the core of scalable production of flexible electronics, but is often limited by unstable yield, high material waste, and a lack of understanding of the process transparency. These issues drive the implementation of digital twin technologies as one of the methods of industrial robustness and sustainability preservation that will be able to keep high-throughput scalability (Pingale and Altay 2025; Nguyen et al. 2025). This paper follows a comparative and analytical approach by summarizing the latest developments in AI-based architecture and digital twins, data-driven yield prediction, and control-based R2R process implementations (Gafurov et al. 2025., Ali et al., 2025). The analysis incorporates reported models and case studies to assess the ability of virtual replicas of R2R systems to capture the dynamics of processes, material behavior, and defect evolution under different operating conditions. The most recent findings also suggest that digital twins allow identifying the mechanisms of yield loss earlier, enhance the causal nature of understanding the variability of processes, and make data-informed decisions across interrelated R2R subsystems (Shakeel et al. 2023; Ng et al. 2024). All in all, the research suggests that digital twins are an excellent integrative instrument to accomplish yield forecasting, process modelling, and sustainable manufacturing in further-generation R2R production areas (Nguyen et al. 2025).

title: Do U.S. Sanctions Significantly Impact the Financing Constraints of Chinese-listed Firms?
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Shenzhen University, Department of Accounting and Corporate Governance and

detail.title: Do U.S. Sanctions Significantly Impact the Financing Constraints of Chinese-listed Firms?
detail.abstract: This study examines whether U.S. sanctions significantly impact the financing constraints of Chinese listed firms. Using a uniquely constructed dataset of Chinese A-share firms spanning the 2007 to 2021 period that were directly impacted by the U.S. sanctions, we provide strong evidence showing a positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints. Additional analyses indicate that the positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints is more (less) pronounced for firms with greater risk exposure (strong market position, strong innovation and research capabilities, and effective government support policies). Sanctions also increase the financing costs for affected firms, shorten their financing duration, and complicate their access to financing. Finally, various endogeneity tests and robustness checks confirm our baseline results. Overall, our study provides important insights into the detrimental effect of U.S. sanctions on Chinese firms' financing constraints.

title: Lean Manufacturing Implementation in Flexible Display and Sensor Printing
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Lean Manufacturing Implementation in Flexible Display and Sensor Printing
detail.abstract: This research paper examines the implementation of lean manufacturing principles in flexible display and sensor printing processes with specific reference to waste minimization, increase in yield, and stability of the processes in a roll-to-roll system and hybrid printing system. The study is based on empirical case studies, industry publications, and peer-reviewed literature, which discusses the interactions of conventional lean instruments with the new digital manufacturing technologies, such as cyber-physical systems, RFID, artificial intelligence, and Industry 4.0 architectures (Pingale and Altay 2025; Rahardjo et al. 2023). The approach is an integrative one that has combined comparative literature examination and process-driven mapping data based on the printing and electronics production settings (Chan and Tay 2018; Maddipatla et al. 2020). The results show that the implementation of lean in flexible printing facilities will be the most efficient with support provided by such aspects as the real-time data acquisition, the digital twins, and the soft sensors that will be used to enforce better control over process variability and material sensitivity (Sekhar et al. 2023; Qu et al. 2023). The paper then concludes that lean manufacturing enabled digitally is a scalable and sustainable production methodology to flexible electronics. Nevertheless, the successful implementation is limited due to the organizational preparedness, the ability of the workforce, and the difficulty in implementing digital technologies into the current manufacturing environments (Rossini et al. 2022).

title: Driven to Collusion: Competitive Pricing under Independent Demand Model and Price Imitation
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen -School of Data Science and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: Driven to Collusion: Competitive Pricing under Independent Demand Model and Price Imitation
detail.abstract: In online markets crowded with similar sellers, pricing algorithms play a decisive role in shaping market competition. Yet firms often find it difficult to observe or track all competitors' prices. Facing informational limits and rapid price adjustments, some firms may ignore competitors' information and use simple independent demand models (IDMs) to predict demand and update prices, while others anchor their prices to selected competitors. Despite its prevalence, their dynamic interactions remain poorly understood. To this end, we establish a competitive learning framework where firms either update their beliefs via IDMs or imitate competitors' prices. We prove that when all firms learn independently through IDMs, they overestimate market intercepts, and prices converge to the Nash equilibrium. However, as more firms adopt imitation, they underestimate price sensitivity, pushing prices toward perfect collusion. We also identify a free-rider effect that firms not directly involved in price imitation always benefit the most. These results stand in sharp contrast to traditional static, full-information models of price competition, highlighting how independent learning and price imitation can interact in dynamic competitive environments and offer new implications for regulating algorithmic collusion. We further extend our results to settings where firms adopt the market average price or an affine function of a competitor's price. Moreover, numerical experiments show that our key results still hold when firms adopt other learning algorithms, such as gradient-based or nonparametric methods (e.g., bandit algorithms).

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence in public governance has generated strong optimism about faster processes, smarter decisions, and more modern administrative systems. Yet despite this enthusiasm, we still know surprisingly little about how AI actually takes shape inside different layers of government. Especially in federal systems where authority is fragmented across multiple levels. In practice, the same algorithm can serve very different purposes. This study responds to that gap by examining how AI is used across federal, state, and municipal levels in the United States. Drawing on a comparative qualitative analysis of thirty AI implementation cases, and guided by a digital-era governance framework combined with a sociotechnical perspective, the study identifies two broad modes of algorithmic governance: control-oriented systems and support-oriented systems. The findings reveal a clear pattern of functional differentiation across levels of government. At the federal level, AI is most often institutionalized as a tool for high-stakes control: supporting surveillance, enforcement, and regulatory oversight. State governments occupy a more ambiguous middle ground, where AI frequently combines supportive functions with algorithmic gatekeeping, particularly in areas such as welfare administration and public health. Municipal governments, by contrast, tend to deploy AI in more pragmatic and service-oriented ways, using it to streamline everyday operations and improve direct interactions with residents. By foregrounding institutional context, this study advances debates on algorithmic governance by demonstrating that the character, function, and risks of AI in the public sector are fundamentally shaped by the level of governance at which these systems are deployed.

title: Constant Maturity Swaps and CMS Linked Notes: A Unified Quantitative Framework for Structuring, Pricing, and Hedging

detail.title: Constant Maturity Swaps and CMS Linked Notes: A Unified Quantitative Framework for Structuring, Pricing, and Hedging
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified and operational quantitative framework for the structuring, pricing, and hedging of Constant Maturity Swaps (CMS) and CMS-linked structured notes. Starting from the economic rationale and underlying structuring of a CMS, the study formalizes the decomposition of CMS cash flows and derives a systematic methodology for computing forward swap rates and their convexity adjustments. The framework is then applied to two major categories of CMS-linked notes: CMS Floating-Rate Notes (CMS FRNs) and CMS Steepeners. For each product, the paper examines the respective motivations of issuers and investors, identifies the embedded CMS structures, and presents consistent pricing and hedging processes grounded in the proposed framework. The results highlight how CMS-based instruments allow market participants to express views on the level, slope, and dynamics of the yield curve. At the same time, the proposed framework provides a consistent and transparent approach for valuing and managing their interest-rate risk exposures. Overall, the study contributes to the literature by offering a rigorous, pedagogical, and practitioner-oriented methodology applicable to a broad range of CMS configurations and CM-linked products.

detail.abstract: This paper models and analyzes the dynamics after a client's shock in a private Bank-N-Client network. Following an exogenous shock to client's savings preference, deposits decline, reducing the bank's income and compressing the commercial activity. Since the pre-shock state becomes unreachable, the bank faces a fundamental trilemma: acceptance, maintaining its policy; self-protection, rationing loans to protect its own savings; or commercial reactivation, sacrificing its own savings to restore the commercial activity. The optimal response depends critically on client size: while rationing loans to small clients is feasible, self-protection against systemic clients is counter-productive and can trigger signaling-driven contagion. Overall, the framework provides a tractable model for dynamic stress-testing in the private banking sector.

title: State ENDS Taxes and Cigarette Smoking in Two-Parent Households

detail.abstract: Background: Exposure to secondhand smoke causes harm in children. Fortunately, smoking prevalence, and therefore exposure to secondhand smoke, has been declining for generations. However, states shifting policy targets to nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) through taxes and regulations may have unintended consequences. How ENDS taxes impact childhood exposure to cigarette smoking remains unknown. Methods: We analyzed National Survey of Children's Health data for two-parent households (2016-2024). Our outcomes were parental 1) smoking status and 2) smoking behavior inside the home. Our exposure variable was a standardized measure of ENDS taxes. Two-way fixed-effect linear-probability models adjusted for household sociodemographic factors, and incorporated robust standard errors and analytic sampling weights. Subgroup analyses stratified by parental education. Marginal analysis estimated the association between a $1 increase in ENDS tax and the probability of a child's exposure to parental smoking. Results: The sample of 291,667 children represented 484.6 million weighted child-years. 13% of children lived with an adult who smoked and 2% were exposed to smoking inside the house. We found that a $1 ENDS tax increase was associated with a 0.51 (CI = 0.09, 0.94) percentage-point increase in household smoking and a 0.33 (CI = 0.08, 0.57) percentage-point increase in smoking inside the home. These associations were only found in lower-education households, reflected a 7% and 16% relative increase from baseline, and corresponded to an additional 1.5 million children exposed to secondhand smoke. Conclusions: Childhood exposure to secondhand smoke continues declining but ENDS taxes may have reversed progress for children in lower-education households.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the dangers of emotionally charged nationalism by analyzing Donald Trump’s “America First” policy and drawing historical parallels with regimes such as those of Hitler, Saddam Hussein, Muammar Gaddafi, Enver Hoxha, Pol Pot, and Nicolae Ceaușescu. It argues that patriotism, when uncoupled from institutional governance and international cooperation, often mutates into a destructive force. The study advocates for a model of institutional patriotism—where national pride is guided by rule of law, diplomacy, and strategic foresight—especially in the context of an increasingly interconnected world.

detail.abstract: This paper reviews the concepts, mechanisms, and empirical evidence on the diffusion of digital technologies (DTs) in developing economies, focusing on the distinct infrastructural layers of connectivity—from first-mile submarine cables to last-mile mobile and broadband networks. It examines how infrastructure gaps, usage disparities, and technological divides shape digitalization pathways and their socio-economic impacts, with a particular emphasis on lower-income regions like Sub-Saharan Africa. The analysis highlights how submarine cables reduce connectivity costs and expand Internet access, yet also reveals uneven benefits due to limited absorptive capacity and new digital vulnerabilities. By synthesizing evidence on rural mobile coverage, urban Internet spillovers, and trade integration, the paper emphasizes the need for coordinated policies to bridge digital divides and foster inclusive digital transformation.
